items.title: Researchers propose ComplianceGate, a classifier-gated multi-tier routing system for large language models that enforces data residency and reduces latency and costs in regulated industries [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: ComplianceGate: Classifier-Gated Multi-Tier LLM Routing for Inference in Regulated Industries
items.summary:
Researchers have developed ComplianceGate, a classifier-gated multi-tier routing system designed for large language models (LLMs) used in regulated industries. This system enforces data residency compliance by routing queries containing personally identifiable information (PII) to local endpoints before any model processing, preventing data from crossing jurisdictional boundaries. It also improves efficiency by directing simple queries to smaller, faster models, reducing latency and costs.

The architecture uses a trained encoder classifier to assess each query's complexity and sensitivity, enabling geographic and size-appropriate routing. Evaluations on 600 queries showed a 39% median latency reduction, 33-52% cost savings depending on query distribution, and significantly higher token generation throughput compared to baseline models. The classifier achieved 99.2% accuracy with near-perfect PII recall and minimal inference overhead, demonstrating a practical approach to compliance-by-design in LLM deployment.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31163v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models deployed in regulated industries operate under two constraints: compliance enforcement and cost efficiency. Personally identifiable information (PII) in user queries can reach model endpoints before the system determines whether that data should leave its jurisdictional boundary. Serving all queries through a single large model consumes full GPU capacity regardless of query complexity while offering no mechanism for geographic routing. Mixture-of-Experts architectures do not address this routing occurs between expert layers within the model after data has already arrived at the endpoint, with all experts loaded in memory regardless of query complexity. We propose a classifier-gated routing architecture that enforces compliance by design. A trained encoder classifier sits before any decoder inference, evaluating each query for complexity and data sensitivity, then routing it to an appropriately sized dense model in the appropriate geographic location. PII-containing queries route to local endpoints before any LLM computation begins, making data residency violations structurally impossible. Simple queries reach small, fast models at a fraction of the cost. Our evaluation on 600 queries demonstrates 39% median latency reduction, 33-52% cost savings depending on query distribution, and generation throughput of 122-200 tokens/second versus 50-64 for the baseline. The encoder classifier achieves 99.2% accuracy with near-perfect PII recall at 7ms inference overhead, establishing pre-inference classification as a practical path to compliance-by-design LLM deployment.

items.title: Researchers develop reinforcement learning framework for coachable AI agents with real-time style control, demonstrated in Horizon Forbidden West, Gran Turismo, and humanoid walking domains [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Coachable agents for interactive gameplay
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a reinforcement learning framework that enables AI agents to be coached with real-time control over their behavior styles while performing tasks. This approach combines universal value function approximators with specialized training methods to allow users to influence how AI agents solve problems, demonstrated across diverse domains including the video games Horizon Forbidden West and Gran Turismo, as well as humanoid walking simulations. Each agent maintains task performance while adapting to style requests, offering flexible and interactive control over AI behavior during execution.

The framework was tested in complex environments with varying dynamics, such as car racing, stylized combat, and humanoid locomotion, showing consistent adherence to style modifications without compromising the core objectives. This advancement allows end users to dynamically select the AI's behavior style at runtime, enhancing the adaptability and user engagement of AI systems in interactive applications.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00642v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning has proven to be a valuable tool in the creation of advanced AI and robotic systems, contributing to everything from game playing to robotics to foundation models. Through trial-and-error, these AI systems typically learn one, near-optimal behavior to solve their tasks. However, there are many use cases in which one would like to assert some level of control, preferably in real time, over how the task is solved. We refer to these modifications of a core task as styles. We combine universal value function approximators (UVFAs) with carefully selected training scenarios, learning algorithms, and data augmentation to create a framework for coaching agents that exhibit styles in complex domains. We demonstrate the framework's application in the AAA video games Horizon Forbidden West and Gran Turismo, and in an open-source humanoid test domain. Despite the different nature of the domains -- car racing, stylized game combat, and humanoid walking -- each agent shows strong coherence to the style requests while still satisfying the main task in its domain. Importantly, the techniques outlined in this paper allow an end user to choose the final behavior at run time, giving them flexible control over the final executed performance.

items.title: Researchers develop Graph-PRefLexOR, a graph-native reinforcement learning model that improves traceable scientific hypothesis generation by 40-65% in materials science and mechanics tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Graph-Native Reinforcement Learning Enables Traceable Scientific Hypothesis Generation through Conceptual Recombination
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Graph-PRefLexOR, a graph-native reinforcement learning model designed to enhance scientific hypothesis generation in materials science and mechanics. This model improves reasoning traceability by 40-65% compared to base models, organizing the reasoning process into explicit phases such as mechanism exploration, graph construction, pattern extraction, and hypothesis synthesis. By integrating neural language generation with symbolic relational structures, it enables the construction and inspection of causal connections, making the reasoning process more interpretable.

Tested on 100 open-ended questions from relevant scientific literature, Graph-PRefLexOR demonstrated broader semantic exploration and two to three times greater semantic diversity than existing models. Analyses showed stronger alignment between structured reasoning and final answers, and additional computational effort primarily enhanced long-range conceptual recombination within a defined semantic space rather than simply expanding coverage. These findings suggest that graph-native reinforcement learning offers a promising approach for interpretable AI systems in scientific hypothesis generation and materials discovery.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00924v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accelerating materials discovery requires AI systems that can generate scientifically valid hypotheses through multi-step, domain-grounded reasoning. Standard large language models often produce fluent but weakly traceable responses to open-ended materials design problems, making it difficult to determine whether final answers are supported by coherent intermediate reasoning. We develop Graph-PRefLexOR, a family of graph-native reasoning models fine-tuned with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to organize reasoning into explicit phases for mechanism exploration, graph construction, pattern extraction, and hypothesis synthesis. This design links neural language generation with symbolic relational structure, enabling causal connections to be constructed, inspected, and reused. On 100 open-ended questions from materials science and mechanics literature, Graph-PRefLexOR achieves 40-65% improvements over corresponding base models, with the largest gains in reasoning traceability. Embedding analyses show broader semantic exploration and approximately 2-3 times greater semantic diversity than baselines. Semantic backtracking and layer-wise hidden-state analyses further show stronger alignment between structured reasoning and final answers. Finally, test-time graph expansion reveals that additional compute primarily increases long-range conceptual recombination within a bounded semantic space, rather than simply expanding semantic coverage. These results establish graph-native reinforcement learning as a pathway toward interpretable AI systems for scientific hypothesis generation in materials design and other scientific applications.

items.title: Theoria verification architecture rewrites AI reasoning into auditable state transitions, achieving 91.4% precision on expert problems and outperforming holistic LLM judges on adversarial tests [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Theoria: Rewrite-Acceptability Verification over Informal Reasoning States
items.summary:
Theoria is a new AI verification architecture that transforms candidate solutions into sequences of auditable state transitions, each justified explicitly by citations, computations, or problem facts. This approach ensures that every change between proof states is accounted for, exposing hidden premises as unlicensed changes. Tested on expert problem sets, Theoria achieved 91.4% precision and produced human-readable proof traces, allowing independent challenge of each step. It outperformed holistic large language model (LLM) judges on adversarial tests, particularly in detecting hidden premises and fabricated citations.

On a benchmark of 185 expert problems, Theoria certified 105 solutions with high precision, while holistic LLM judges showed similar precision but failed on different problems, indicating complementary strengths. In adversarial scenarios across multiple domains, Theoria's structured verification caught 94.7% of errors compared to 83.2% for holistic judging, with significant advantages in identifying subtle errors such as hidden premises. These results suggest Theoria offers a more transparent and reliable method for verifying AI-generated reasoning.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01223v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When should an AI system's answer be trusted? Formal proof assistants offer certainty but cannot reach most of the problem distribution; scalar LLM judges offer coverage but produce opaque scores that cannot be audited after the fact and are subject to the same coherence issues as any LLM. We present Theoria, a verification architecture that closes this gap. A candidate solution is rewritten into a sequence of typed state transitions, each licensed by an explicit justification, whether that be a citation, computation, or problem-given fact, and every transition is independently auditable. The foundational invariant is completeness of change: every difference between consecutive proof states must be accounted for, so hidden premises surface as unlicensed mutations rather than passing silently. On HLE-Verified Gold (185 text-only expert problems), Theoria certifies 105 at 91.4% strict precision (Wilson 95% CI [84.5%, 95.4%]). Every certification produces a human readable proof trace in which each step can be independently challenged. Holistic LLM judges achieve comparable precision at matched coverage but fail on different problems (Jaccard 0.14-0.36), making the approaches complementary. On 95 adversarial poisoned proofs across 15 domains, structured judges catch 94.7% versus 83.2% for holistic judging (p= 0.0017). The overall 11.5 pp gap concentrates in hidden premises (90.6% vs. 62.5%, a 28 pp difference) and fabricated citations (100% vs. 90%), the error classes where the formal analysis predicts an advantage; performance is identical on arithmetic and theorem-misapplication errors, where no advantage is predicted. On GPQA Diamond (n= 65), certified precision is 97.1% (Wilson CI [85.1%, 99.5%]).

items.title: Researchers introduce DigitalCoach, a multimodal dataset of 72 expert-novice computer coaching sessions to evaluate AI models' ability to teach software use and identify communication and grounding gaps [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: DigitalCoach: Communication and Grounding Gaps in Human and Agentic Computer Use Coaching
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced DigitalCoach, a comprehensive multimodal dataset comprising 72 expert-novice computer coaching sessions with over 22,000 dialogue turns and 28 hours of screen and input recordings across five software applications. This dataset is designed to evaluate how well state-of-the-art AI models can teach humans to use software. The study found that while AI models tend to give more direct instructions, they provide fewer explanations, error diagnoses, and knowledge-check questions compared to human coaches.

Further analysis revealed that even when AI coaching methods are aligned with human approaches, the models struggle with grounding their instructions in the visual context of the software interface. Interactive evaluations showed that learners guided by AI coaches often follow instructions passively without deeper engagement, highlighting gaps in communication and visual grounding. DigitalCoach aims to support the development of more collaborative and proactive AI agents for computer use coaching.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31980v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Agents are increasingly capable of automating software tasks, but can they teach humans how to use software themselves? We introduce DigitalCoach, a multimodal dataset of 72 human expert-novice computer use coaching sessions consisting of 22,752 dialogue turns grounded in 28.1 hours of screen and input event recordings across five software applications. We use DigitalCoach to evaluate whether state-of-the-art models can teach humans how to use computers. Automated evaluation shows that models differ from humans in how they coach: models provide more direct instructions, but fewer explanations, error diagnoses, and knowledge-check questions. When we fix the coaching method, models produce utterances similar to human references yet poorly grounded in visual context. Interactive evaluation confirms that model coaches cause learners to passively follow instructions without deeper engagement and fall short in visual grounding. DigitalCoach lays a foundation for collaborative and proactive computer use coaching agents.

items.title: Researchers identify vocabulary mismatch as cause of advanced encoders lagging in sparse retrieval and propose Vocabulary Transfer framework to improve performance on BEIR benchmark by 4.7 nDCG [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Why Advanced Encoders Lag on Sparse Retrieval? The Answer and an Approach to Bridging Vocabulary Gaps
items.summary:
Researchers have identified a vocabulary mismatch as the key reason why advanced foundation models like ModernBERT underperform compared to older models in learned sparse retrieval (LSR). They found that modern tokenizers use detailed, case-sensitive vocabularies that create redundant surface forms, which wastes model capacity and hinders effective lexical matching. To address this, the team proposed a Vocabulary Transfer (VT) framework that adapts advanced encoders to use sparse-friendly, normalized vocabularies, improving performance with minimal computational cost.

The VT framework includes Semantic Initialization to preserve geometric structure and Activation Potential Calibration to align pre-trained models with sparsity constraints, preventing common issues like dead neurons. Empirical results show that VT significantly boosts ModernBERT's performance on the BEIR benchmark by 4.7 nDCG points, revives struggling models such as RoBERTa-large, and generalizes well across different architectures and domains. This work demonstrates that the performance gap is due to vocabulary design rather than architectural limitations, offering a practical solution to enhance sparse retrieval models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00004v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While advanced foundation models like ModernBERT significantly outperform older architectures in dense retrieval, they surprisingly lag behind the aging BERT-base baseline in learned sparse retrieval (LSR). We identify the root cause as the \textit{Vocabulary Gap}: modern tokenizers utilize raw, case-sensitive vocabularies designed for lossless reconstruction, which map single semantic units to redundant surface forms, wasting model capacity on morphological noise and hindering lexical matching. We formalize this intuition through a theoretical framework, demonstrating that appropriate vocabulary coarse-graining can tighten the generalization bounds by reducing complexity of the hypothesis class, provided that semantic integrity is preserved. To resolve this, we propose \textbf{Vocabulary Transfer (VT)}, a model-agnostic framework that migrates advanced encoders to sparse-friendly, normalized vocabularies with minimal computational cost. VT utilizes a novel \textbf{Semantic Initialization} via spatial topology to preserve geometric structure and an \textbf{Activation Potential Calibration (APC)} mechanism to align pre-trained manifolds with sparsity constraints, preventing the dead neuron and dense collapse observed in standard fine-tuning. Empirically, VT is universally effective: it enables ModernBERT to achieve state-of-the-art performance on the BEIR benchmark (\textbf{52.4} nDCG, a \textbf{+4.7} improvement), resuscitates failing models like RoBERTa-large, and generalizes seamlessly to inference-free architectures and specialized domains. These results confirm that the performance lag is not an architectural deficiency but a solvable vocabulary mismatch. We've released our code and models.\footnote{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/vocab-transfer/. All details included.}

items.title: Researchers propose steering vectors and latent space-based calibrators to control and build trust in large language models with trillions of parameters [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Harnessing the Latent Space: From Steering Vectors to Model Calibrators for Control and Trust
items.summary:
Researchers have proposed new methods to enhance control and trust in large language models with trillions of parameters by harnessing their latent spaces. They introduce steering vectors to guide model behavior and latent space-based calibrators to assess the reliability of model outputs. These approaches aim to improve understanding of the internal representations of large language models and support safer, more trustworthy applications in decision-making and tool interaction.

As language models grow in scale and capability, interpreting their internal mechanisms becomes increasingly complex. The proposed techniques offer insights into managing model behavior and evaluating output trustworthiness, addressing the challenges posed by the widespread use of these models in medium- and high-stakes scenarios. This work contributes to demystifying latent spaces and advancing the development of more reliable language technologies.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00083v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models have changed from unreliable text generators to highly-capable large models with trillions of parameters. Capability increases come hand-in-hand with increases in scale, making understanding the internal representations of models more challenging. Since millions of users increasing rely on language models to interact with external tools or make decisions in medium or high-stakes scenarios, we need to establish control over model behavior and know when to trust model outputs. In this paper, we discuss our contributions on harnessing the latent spaces by proposing steering vectors for control and developing latent space-based model calibrators for trust. Together, our contributions help demystify the latent spaces of language models and offer new insights into how to harness model internals to build more trustworthy language technology.

items.title: Researchers present SNAP-FM, a sparse nonlinear accelerated projection method for physics-constrained generative modeling that speeds up nonlinear constraint projection using GPU sparse optimization on PDE benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SNAP-FM: Sparse Nonlinear Accelerated Projection for Physics-Constrained Generative Modeling
items.summary:
Researchers have developed SNAP-FM, a method that accelerates nonlinear constraint projection in physics-constrained generative modeling by leveraging sparse GPU optimization. This approach addresses the computational challenges of enforcing physical constraints such as conservation laws and boundary conditions during generative sampling without retraining, which typically involves costly projection and optimization steps. By exploiting the block-sparse structure of Jacobian and KKT systems induced by sample-wise batching and local PDE couplings, SNAP-FM efficiently solves sparse nonlinear programs using specialized tools and GPU sparse factorization.

Applied to Physics-Constrained Flow Matching on various PDE benchmarks with linear and nonlinear constraints, including one- and two-dimensional cases, SNAP-FM significantly speeds up constraint projection while maintaining exact constraint satisfaction. These results demonstrate that sparse GPU nonlinear optimization provides a practical and scalable foundation for constrained generative sampling in scientific machine learning, overcoming limitations of standard machine learning frameworks that rely on dense tensor operations and lack composability for sparse solvers.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00095v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative models have emerged as scalable surrogates for physical simulation, yet they offer no guarantee that their outputs respect the conservation laws, boundary conditions, and nonlinear invariants that govern the underlying physics. Constrained sampling closes this gap, enforcing such constraints exactly at inference time without retraining, but at a computational cost: projection, correction, and trajectory-optimization steps are repeated during sampling, with these steps becoming expensive for nonlinear constraints. Standard ML frameworks exacerbate this: their dense tensor algebra and limited sparse solver composability obscure the structure that physical constraints naturally induce, making efficient batched nonlinear optimization difficult to realize in practice. We address this bottleneck by exploiting the structure that sample-wise batching and local PDE couplings induce in the projection subproblems -- namely, block-sparse Jacobian and KKT systems -- exposing this structure using ExaModels.jl and solving the resulting sparse nonlinear programs with MadNLP.jl and GPU sparse factorization. Applied to Physics-Constrained Flow Matching (PCFM), on PDE benchmarks with linear, nonlinear, one-dimensional, and two-dimensional constraints, this approach accelerates nonlinear constraint projection while maintaining constraint satisfaction. These results show that sparse GPU nonlinear optimization is a practical foundation for constrained generative sampling in scientific machine learning.

items.title: Researchers propose a mechanism-driven theory identifying data-driven, transition, and model-driven phases in active learning dynamics, explaining strategy performance across datasets and architectures [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Mechanism-Driven Theory of Phase Transitions in Active Learning
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a mechanism-driven theory that characterizes active learning (AL) dynamics by identifying three distinct phases: data-driven, transition, and model-driven. This framework reframes budget regimes as shifts in the dominant generalization mechanism, explaining why different AL strategies such as representativeness, coverage, and uncertainty perform better at various stages. The theory is supported by experiments in natural and medical imaging, showing that AL efficiency depends on how well a strategy's inductive bias aligns with the current generalization bottleneck.

The study uses measurable proxies and segmented regression to detect these phase transitions and highlights that self-supervised representation shifts occur earlier in the labeling process, emphasizing the importance of representation quality in AL dynamics. This unified approach offers a foundation for developing transition-aware AL algorithms that adapt to changing learning conditions across datasets and architectures.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00144v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Active learning (AL) performance is known to be budget-dependent, yet regimes are typically defined by heuristic label counts that fail to generalize across datasets or architectures. We characterize AL dynamics by reframing budget regimes as shifts in the dominant generalization mechanism. By reinterpreting PAC-style risk components as dynamic interacting terms, we prove that dominance shifts are structurally unavoidable, creating a moving bottleneck for generalization. We operationalize this using measurable proxies and a segmented regression procedure to identify a tripartite taxonomy: data-driven, transition, and model-driven phases. Our framework explains the long-standing observation that representativeness, coverage, and uncertainty strategies excel at different stages. Experiments across natural and medical imaging show that AL efficiency depends on the alignment between the strategy's inductive bias and the active bottleneck. Moreover, self-supervised representation shift transitions earlier along the labeling trajectory, highlighting the role of representation quality in shaping AL dynamics. Overall, this work provides a unified framework for the next generation of transition-aware AL algorithms.

items.title: Researchers show GRPO, Dr. GRPO, and DAPO are variations of one standard deviation adjustment controlling training updates in language model reasoning tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: GRPO, Dr. GRPO, and DAPO Are Three Operations on One Number: The Group-Standard-Deviation Identity
items.summary:
Researchers have demonstrated that three popular methods for training language models to reason—Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), GRPO Done Right (Dr. GRPO), and Decoupled Clip and Dynamic Sampling Policy Optimization (DAPO)—are variations of a single underlying adjustment involving the standard deviation of model responses. This standard deviation measures how much sampled answers to prompts disagree, influencing the size of training updates. The study reveals that these methods represent different settings of one parameter that controls learning intensity based on answer disagreement, with split groups providing the most informative training signals and unanimous groups contributing none.

The paper confirms this insight through experiments on a large dataset (Big-Math) and controlled training runs, showing that what appears as a simple normalization step actually determines where and how strongly learning occurs. This finding clarifies the relationship between these techniques and offers guidance on weighting problems and the number of attempts needed during training to optimize language model reasoning performance.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00152v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Three of the most popular methods for training language models to reason look like three different tricks. They are not. All three adjust a single number: standard deviation, reflecting how much a prompt's sampled answers disagree. When such a model is trained, it answers each problem many times, and an automatic checker marks every answer right or wrong. The standard deviation of those marks measures the disagreement: largest when the answers split evenly between right and wrong, and zero when they all agree. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) divides by this number, GRPO Done Right (Dr. GRPO) drops the division, and Decoupled Clip and Dynamic Sampling Policy Optimization (DAPO) discards the groups where it is zero. Each is presented as its own fix, yet this paper proves they are three settings of one dial. That dial is not cosmetic: for right-or-wrong rewards, the disagreement is exactly the size of the training update, the group-standard-deviation identity. A split group teaches the most, while a unanimous group teaches nothing and falls silent. The same result says which problems deserve the most weight and how many tries each one needs. This paper confirms the intuition on a large real difficulty dataset (Big-Math) and in a controlled training run. What looks like a harmless normalization step is the dial that decides where learning happens and how strongly.

items.title: Researchers introduce EVOTS, an evolutionary neural architecture search framework for task-adaptive Transformer models in multivariate time-series forecasting, showing competitive results on ETT benchmark datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: EVOTS: Evolutionary Transformer Search for Time Series Forecasting
items.summary:
Researchers have developed EVOTS, an evolutionary neural architecture search framework designed to create task-adaptive Transformer-like models for multivariate time-series forecasting. This approach encodes architectures using a modular genome representation, allowing flexible combinations of attention, feed-forward, and projection components, and employs a repair mechanism to maintain structural validity during evolution. Evaluated on four ETT benchmark datasets across various forecasting scenarios, EVOTS demonstrated competitive or improved mean squared error compared to strong Transformer baselines, particularly in multivariate-to-multivariate predictions.

The framework explores a diverse architecture space without relying on hand-crafted design rules, enabling effective adaptation to different forecasting tasks and horizons. Additional analyses assessed performance variations across settings and reported training times to indicate computational costs. Overall, the results suggest that evolutionary search can efficiently discover flexible, high-performing Transformer-like architectures for time-series forecasting within practical runtime constraints.

items.title: Researchers develop scalable backpropagation algorithm for training thermodynamic AI models on Ising hardware, achieving up to 94.9% accuracy on CIFAR-10 and analyzing inference cost-performance tradeoffs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Scaling Up Thermodynamic AI Models
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a scalable backpropagation algorithm to train deep convolutional networks for thermodynamic AI models running on Ising hardware, achieving up to 94.9% accuracy on the CIFAR-10 image classification task. This approach leverages the time-averaged behavior of high-temperature Gibbs-sampled Ising systems to implement feed-forward neural inference, addressing previous limitations in training large models for such low-power AI devices.

The team also formulated and experimentally validated a mathematical theory linking inference cost to accuracy while managing autocorrelation times. Their analysis reveals a controlled tradeoff between inference cost and performance, and they propose algorithms to optimize inference schedules. These findings have significant implications for advancing hardware development and the future application of high-temperature thermodynamic AI models.

We turn this theoretical correspondence into a scalable and purely backpropagation-based algorithm for training deep convolutional networks for thermodynamic inference on Ising machine hardware. We then develop and experimentally validate a mathematical theory relating inference cost to accuracy and controlling autocorrelation times. Subsequently, we calculate asymptotic results showing that inference cost is bounded by a well-controlled tradeoff with performance and exhibit algorithms for computing optimal inference schedules. Finally, we discuss implications for hardware development and the future of high-temperature thermodynamic AI models.

items.title: Researchers introduce Latent Maps of Performance framework using StarCraft II data to generate counterfactual feedback for player improvement with four traversal strategies on amateur replays [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Play Like Champions: Counterfactual Feedback Generation in Latent Space
items.summary:
Researchers have developed the Latent Maps of Performance framework to generate counterfactual feedback aimed at improving player performance in real-time strategy games, using StarCraft II data. By training a Guided Variational Autoencoder on over 23,000 professional tournament replays, they created a model that enables traversal between losing and winning gameplay profiles. This approach applies four traversal strategies to amateur replays, generating multi-step improvement trajectories grounded in expert behavior to guide players toward winning configurations.

The framework extracts feedback at multiple levels to support players at various stages of development. The study highlights a trade-off among the path-finding methods used and suggests that future research should focus on refining model-based solutions to enhance human player improvement in competitive gaming environments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00190v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in reinforcement learning have produced superhuman agents across a wide range of competitive games. As a byproduct, researchers have begun studying how these agents play, extracting behavioral representations, analyzing decision structure, and modeling the latent geometry of expert performance. However, this growing body of work has overwhelmingly focused on defeating human players rather than providing feedback, leaving a critical gap in creating model solutions to improve human players. Unlike chess and Go, where AI has become integral to player training, real-time strategy (RTS) games lack principled frameworks for translating expert knowledge into actionable feedback. We introduce Latent Maps of Performance, a framework for counterfactual path generation. We focus on StarCraft~II data to model player improvement as an algorithmic recourse within a learned representation space. As inspiration for our work, we have looked at the championship model used in sports science. We trained a Guided Variational Autoencoder model on 23,305 professional tournament replays, enabling counterfactual traversal between losing and winning gameplay profiles. To fulfill our goal, we have devised and verified four traversal strategies on out-of-distribution (OOD) data randomly sampled from a dataset of amateur replays, namely linear interpolation, iterative optimal transport, density-regularized gradient ascent, and neural flow matching, each designed to generate multi-step improvement trajectories that remain grounded in observed expert behavior while moving a player's profile toward winning configurations. Feedback is extracted at multiple granularities to support players at different stages of improvement. Finally, we conclude that there is a trade-off between the path-finding methods we employ and hope that future research will focus on developing model solutions for human improvement.

items.title: Researchers propose HydraCollab, an adaptive collaborative-perception framework for distributed autonomous systems that reduces communication bandwidth by up to 74% while improving accuracy on V2X-R and V2X-Radar datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: HydraCollab: Adaptive Collaborative-Perception for Distributed Autonomous Systems
items.summary:
Researchers have developed HydraCollab, an adaptive collaborative-perception framework designed for distributed autonomous systems that enhances situational awareness while significantly reducing communication bandwidth. HydraCollab selectively transmits the most informative sensor features and dynamically adjusts collaboration strategies based on spatial confidence maps, achieving a better balance between perception accuracy and communication cost compared to existing methods.

Evaluations on the V2X-R, V2X-Radar, and UAV3D-mini datasets show that HydraCollab uses only 41% and 26% of the bandwidth on V2X-R and V2X-Radar respectively, while improving performance by approximately 0.75%. This framework outperforms the state-of-the-art Where2comm method, demonstrating its potential to optimize communication efficiency without sacrificing perception quality in multi-robot systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00191v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Collaborative-perception enables multi-robot systems to enhance situational awareness by sharing perceptual information. Existing collaborative-perception systems face an inherent trade-off between communication bandwidth requirements and perception accuracy, where methods that exchange more information achieve better perception results at the cost of increased communication overhead. However, real-world communication networks impose bandwidth constraints that require minimizing communication overhead without sacrificing perception performance. To address this challenge, we propose HydraCollab, an adaptive collaborative-perception framework that (i) selectively transmits the most informative sensor features and (ii) dynamically employs collaboration strategies (intermediate or late) based on spatial confidence maps. Extensive evaluations on the V2X-R, V2X-Radar and UAV3D-mini datasets demonstrate that HydraCollab achieves the best overall trade-off between accuracy and communication cost among existing collaborative-perception methods. Relative to SOTA Where2comm, HydraCollab uses only 41% of the bandwidth on V2X-R and 26% on V2X-Radar while improving performance by 0.78% and 0.75% respectively. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/AICPS/HydraCollab.

items.title: Researchers introduce SLIM-RL, a risk-budgeted random-masking reinforcement learning method for diffusion large language models that matches or surpasses TraceRL accuracy with fewer training samples and no trajectory slicing [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SLIM-RL: Risk-Budgeted Random-Masking RL for Diffusion LLMs Without Trajectory Slicing
items.summary:
Researchers have developed SLIM-RL, a new reinforcement learning method for diffusion large language models (dLLMs) that avoids the need for trajectory slicing used in previous approaches like TraceRL. SLIM-RL uses a tau-budget decoder to control commit risk during training and employs a trace-free random-masking objective with variance-reduction techniques. This approach matches or surpasses TraceRL's accuracy on benchmarks such as MATH500 and GSM8K while requiring fewer training samples.

SLIM-RL demonstrates significant improvements in efficiency and performance, achieving better results on math and code tasks compared to larger models like LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B. It also transfers effectively across different dLLM architectures without additional training. The method introduces a novel mask schedule and combines sequence-level importance sampling with deterministic quadrature to optimize training. The source code for SLIM-RL is publicly available for further research and development.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00208v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning for diffusion large language models (dLLMs) has largely moved to trajectory-aware methods. The current state of the art, TraceRL, holds that random masking is mismatched with the model's inference trajectory, and it reconstructs that trajectory during training by slicing each rollout into up to K/s trajectory-aligned training samples, a cost that grows with the block size K. We show that this mismatch can be mitigated without reconstructing the trajectory. Our method, SLIM-RL, bounds the commit risk of each rollout step with a tau-budget decoder, reducing aggregate commit risk in the training data. During optimization, SLIM-RL trains on these risk-controlled rollouts with a trace-free random-masking objective that adapts variance-reduction tools, combining sequence-level importance sampling, deterministic quadrature over masking levels under a mean-preserving, monotonically decreasing per-block mask schedule that we introduce. On SDAR-4B, SLIM-RL matches TraceRL's best MATH500 accuracy on only 0.46x its training samples at block size 16, improving over TraceRL by 6.32% on MATH500 and 11.05% on GSM8K under matched dynamic sampling. At block size 4, the 4B SLIM-RL surpasses the larger LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B dLLMs on math, exceeding LLaDA-8B by 10.76% on MATH500 while staying below the autoregressive Qwen2.5-7B. On code, it improves over TraceRL by 4.20% on MBPP and 3.65% on HumanEval. The tau-budget decoder transfers training-free across LLaDA, Dream, and SDAR. The source code is available at https://github.com/laolaorkkkkk/SLIM-RL .

items.title: Researchers introduce Causal Abstraction Error metric to validate high-level causal explanations across ten simulated complex systems with ground-truth benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Validating Causal Abstraction Metrics on Simulated Complex Systems
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a new metric called Causal Abstraction Error (CAE) to validate high-level causal explanations of complex systems. They tested this metric across ten simulated systems with known ground-truth causal structures, covering both discrete and continuous states as well as static and dynamic behaviors. Their findings show that CAE reliably distinguishes valid causal abstractions from invalid ones by incorporating a faithfulness test over unmapped variables, outperforming over thirty other candidate metrics from various families.

The study involved a comprehensive benchmark and systematic evaluation within a unified causal abstraction framework. CAE demonstrated strong performance by passing all discrimination tests across every system and converging with as few as 30 sampled interventions. This metric offers a continuous validity measure and is proposed as a general-purpose tool for discovering and validating high-level causal explanations in scientific research.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00267v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A central goal of science is to produce valid explanations of complex systems: high-level causal accounts that faithfully reflect the behavior of lower-level mechanisms. Yet no consensus exists on how to measure whether a proposed high-level explanation is actually valid. We introduce a benchmark of ten complex systems spanning both discrete and continuous state spaces, as well as static and dynamical regimes, each equipped with consensual ground-truth causal explanations and invalid contrastive conditions. Within a unified causal abstraction framework, we systematically evaluate over thirty candidate metrics drawn from observational, functional, information-theoretic, and causal families. Our results show that only the latter reliably discriminates valid from invalid abstractions, and only when incorporating faithfulness testing over unmapped variables. Building on these findings, we introduce the Causal Abstraction Error (CAE), a continuous validity metric with an explicit faithfulness test, which passes all discrimination tests across every system and can converge with as few as 30 sampled interventions. We offer it as a general-purpose metric for the discovery and validation of high-level explanations.

items.title: Researchers propose entropy-regularized probabilistic gates for sparse model discovery in federated learning with scarce data, improving performance under data and client heterogeneity [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Entropy-Regularized Probabilistic Gates for Sparse Model Discovery in Scarce-Data Federated Learning
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced entropy-regularized probabilistic gates to improve sparse model discovery in federated learning, particularly when data is scarce and heterogeneous across clients. This approach maintains uncertainty during sparse model optimization by preventing premature commitment to specific sparse configurations, enhancing generalization in high-dimensional, small-sample settings.

The study evaluates the method's effectiveness under varying data and client participation heterogeneity, demonstrating consistent improvements over existing techniques like federated iterative hard thresholding and pruning after dense federated averaging. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets show better statistical performance on test data and more accurate recovery of sparse model structures.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00275v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a distributed machine learning (ML) paradigm with collaboration among multiple clients without sharing data. FL is challenging under data heterogeneity and partial client participation. Learning sparse models is useful for communication and computational efficiency in FL, but it is especially difficult in the small-sample high-dimensional regime (d >> N) where optimization can yield parameter configurations that fail to generalize to unseen test data. While magnitude-based pruning doesn't account for uncertainty exploration in the parameter space, a formulation with probabilistic gates and an L0 constraint allows sampling from competing sparse configurations during training. In this work, we study entropy regularization of gate distributions as a mechanism to maintain uncertainty in sparse federated optimization by preventing early commitment to sparse support. We examine its impact under data heterogeneity, client participation heterogeneity, and sparsity. Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks show consistent improvements over federated iterative hard thresholding (Fed-IHT) and pruning after dense federated averaging (FedAvg) training, both in statistical performance on test data and in sparsity recovery accuracy.

items.title: Researchers introduce a four-stage diagnostic to test large language models' physics reasoning across three parallel physics frameworks, revealing low pass rates and weaknesses in self-review and judge reliability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Testing Frontier Large Language Models' Physics Literacy in Parallel Physical Worlds
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a four-stage diagnostic test to evaluate large language models' (LLMs) ability to reason within unfamiliar physics frameworks. This test assesses induction, formulation, prediction, and review across three distinct physics worlds: a single-equation counterfactual world, Aristotelian mechanics, and a four-domain counterfactual world called Decay World. When applied to models including Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5.5, and Gemini 3.1 Pro, the pass rates were low, with the Decay World yielding no passes, highlighting challenges in genuine physics reasoning beyond pattern recall.

The study revealed a notable asymmetry where models rarely predicted incorrect directions of change but often miscalculated quantitative ratios by reverting to standard physics relations. Additionally, the reliability of LLM-based judges varied across frameworks, and the models' self-review processes were weak, frequently failing to identify their own errors. The researchers have made all prompts, responses, verdicts, and audit records publicly available to support further investigation and transparency.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00276v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Current large-language-model (LLM) physics benchmarks are usually scored by answer accuracy, which cannot distinguish genuine reasoning from recall of familiar problem patterns and reveals little about where a model's reasoning breaks down. We introduce an auditable four-stage diagnostic that evaluates whether an LLM can reason inside an unfamiliar physics framework through induction, formulation, prediction, and review. The diagnostic combines locked pre-registrations, fresh sessions between stages, dual-LLM judging, and a human-audit pathway, and we apply it to three parallel physics worlds: a single-equation counterfactual world ($F=mv$), a historical framework (Aristotelian mechanics), and a four-domain counterfactual world (Decay World). Across Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5.5, and Gemini 3.1 Pro, the three worlds yield composite PASS rates are 6/15, 6/15, and 0/15 respectively (content $\land$ structural for $F=mv$ and Aristotelian, content axis only for Decay World where the structural axis is out of scope). The most pointed empirical pattern is a qualitative-versus-quantitative asymmetry: in Decay World, models almost never predict the wrong direction of change, but frequently compute the wrong ratio by slipping back to standard-physics relations. The protocol also surfaces two methodology findings: LLM-judge reliability does not transfer across frameworks, and Stage 4 self-review is weak in every framework, with the model's own review wrongly reporting no earlier error in at least two-thirds of the trials that actually contained one. We release the full prompts, responses, verdicts, and audit records.

items.title: Researchers expand empirical study of bias-reliability tradeoff in LLM evaluation across 11 evaluator-agent conditions, confirming coupling suppresses strategy diversity and releasing benchmark dataset [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Mapping the Evaluation Frontier: An Empirical Survey of the Bias-Reliability Tradeoff Across Eleven Evaluator-Agent Conditions
items.summary:
Researchers have expanded the empirical study of the bias-reliability tradeoff in large language model (LLM) evaluation systems by analyzing 11 evaluator-agent conditions. Their findings confirm that evaluator coupling, strategy diversity, and measurement reliability cannot all be optimized simultaneously at a fixed sample size. Specifically, conditions with low evaluator coupling show high measurement noise, while those with strong coupling achieve low noise, indicating a tradeoff between these factors. The study also observed that evaluator coupling suppresses strategy diversity, supported by a strong negative correlation between these variables.

The research included measurements of evaluator coupling and strategy diversity across all conditions, with reliability assessed in a subset with sufficient data. Notably, some conditions involving the GPT-4o API exhibited unique patterns attributed to version changes. The study found no conditions that combined low evaluator coupling with low measurement noise, reinforcing the tradeoff hypothesis. To support further research and comparison, the authors have released a standardized benchmark dataset containing all per-condition metrics.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00304v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The bias-reliability tradeoff conjectures that LLM evaluation systems are constrained in (gamma, H, CV) space, where evaluator coupling (gamma), strategy diversity (H), and small-sample measurement reliability (CV(N)) cannot be simultaneously optimized at fixed sample size N. Prior evidence rests on n=5 conditions with complete metrics from a single study. We expand the empirical base to 11 conditions, measuring gamma and H for all 11 (nine with valid weight vectors) and CV(N=5) for seven with sufficient seeds (N >= 5). Five conditions provide the complete (gamma, H, CV) triple. The data confirm the trade-off: conditions with low evaluator coupling (gamma < 0.2) exhibit high measurement noise (CV(N=5) > 1.0), while conditions with strong coupling (gamma > 0.9) achieve low noise (CV(N=5) < 0.16). The correlation r(H, gamma) = -0.989 (n=5, excluding GPT-4o conditions) confirms that evaluator coupling suppresses strategy diversity. Four GPT-4o conditions show gamma=0.000 and H=1.000 across all seeds -- a pattern we attribute to version drift in the June 2026 GPT-4o API. No condition occupies the region {gamma < 0.2, CV(N=5) < 0.3}. We release all per-condition metrics as a standardized benchmark dataset for evaluator comparison.

items.title: Researchers introduce K-Inverse-RFM, a modified Recursive Feature Machine that improves learning on noisy, imbalanced mathematical tasks to match or exceed neural network performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: K-Inverse-RFM: A Modified RFM that Bridges the Gap to Neural Networks for Data-Corrupted Mathematical Tasks
items.summary:
Researchers have developed K-Inverse-RFM, a modified version of Recursive Feature Machines (RFMs), to enhance learning performance on mathematical tasks affected by noisy, imbalanced, or corrupted data. While RFMs typically replicate the feature learning dynamics of Feedforward Neural Networks (FNNs), they have underperformed in certain challenging scenarios. The new approach applies a transformation to training labels, enabling RFMs to match or even surpass the performance of neural networks in these difficult conditions.

This advancement addresses the limitations of RFMs in handling complex data representations and class imbalances by promoting more effective learning. The modification is simple yet powerful, allowing kernel machines to close the gap with neural networks and improve robustness in data-corrupted mathematical problem settings.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00329v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recursive Feature Machines (RFMs) are a class of kernel machines that utilize the Average Gradient Outer Product (AGOP) as a mechanism for feature learning. They have been shown to effectively replicate the learning dynamics and feature representations of Feedforward Neural Networks (FNNs) across various settings. However, despite comparable capacity for feature learning and the similarities in the features they acquire, RFMs exhibit significantly lower performance than neural networks in certain data-corrupted scenarios. In this work, we investigate these limitations in mathematical problems. As a solution, we introduce a remarkably effective transformation applied to the training labels which promotes learning in noisy, complexly represented, and class-imbalanced data. This simple yet powerful adjustment enables RFMs to close the performance gap with FNNs and, in some cases, even surpass them.

items.title: Researchers propose DiscoLoop, a looping architecture combining discrete embeddings and continuous hidden states to improve multi-hop reasoning accuracy and efficiency in language models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: DiscoLoop: Looping Discrete Embeddings and Continuous Hidden States for Multi-hop Reasoning
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced DiscoLoop, a novel looping architecture that combines discrete embeddings with continuous hidden states to enhance multi-hop reasoning in language models. This approach addresses limitations in standard Transformers, which struggle to retain and utilize information across multiple reasoning steps within a single forward pass. DiscoLoop improves accuracy and efficiency by maintaining both discrete and continuous representations during recurrence, enabling better alignment and generalization in tasks requiring multi-step inference.

The study highlights that traditional non-recurrent Transformers face a depth-local storage problem, where earlier learned facts become inaccessible in later reasoning stages. While Looped Transformers partially mitigate this by reusing memory, they still fall short due to representational misalignment. DiscoLoop overcomes this by integrating a discrete embedding channel alongside the continuous hidden state, achieving near-perfect accuracy with fewer training steps on symbolic and synthetic multi-hop reasoning tasks. When applied to real-world pretraining, DiscoLoop demonstrated lower training loss and superior benchmark performance compared to existing looped-transformer models, indicating its potential for practical language modeling applications.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00341v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models achieve strong performance on many reasoning tasks when allowed to externalize intermediate steps as Chain-of-Thought (CoT). However, many questions require the model to internalize the multi-step reasoning within a single forward pass before generating the answer. We study this challenge through two-hop reasoning, a representative task where the model must compose multiple pieces of parametric knowledge within a single forward pass. Standard non-recurrent Transformers suffer from a depth-local storage problem: facts learned in earlier layers are unavailable where second-hop retrieval happens. We found that Looped Transformers mitigate this issue by reusing the same memory, but still generalize imperfectly. We show that the remaining bottleneck is representational. In the two-hop reasoning task, the first loop often makes the correct bridge entity nearly perfectly decodable, yet the corresponding hidden state remains poorly aligned with the bridge token embedding. Surprisingly, an easy training-free realignment intervention nearly closes the generalization gap. Building upon this insight, we propose DiscoLoop, a looping architecture whose recurrence carries both a discrete embedding channel and a continuous hidden-state channel. DiscoLoop achieves near-perfect accuracy with substantially fewer training steps across symbolic and synthetic-language multi-hop reasoning tasks. When applied to real-world pretraining, DiscoLoop attains lower training loss and stronger benchmark performance than looped-transformer baselines, suggesting that the mixed-channel design transfers to practical language modeling.

items.title: arXiv: Systematization of knowledge on mobile on-device AI security covering attack and defense landscapes and identifying research gaps [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SoK: Attack and Defense Landscape of Mobile On-device AI Systems
items.summary:
A new paper presents the first comprehensive systematization of knowledge on the security of mobile on-device AI (MoAI) systems, which run AI models locally on mobile devices instead of relying on cloud services. This approach offers benefits like privacy preservation, low latency, and offline functionality but also introduces unique security risks due to local AI model storage. The study outlines the key security principles, maps the current attack and defense landscapes, and identifies gaps in existing research.

The authors highlight unresolved challenges in both attacking and defending MoAI systems and suggest promising directions for future investigation. Their work establishes a foundational framework to better understand and secure MoAI systems, supporting the development of safer mobile AI applications. Additional resources related to this research are available on GitHub.

items.originalTitle: When AI meets quantum information: A comprehensive review
items.summary:
The article reviews the rapid co-evolution of artificial intelligence (AI) and quantum information (QI), highlighting how AI is increasingly used to learn, design, control, and verify quantum systems, while QI introduces new computational models and learning challenges for AI. It surveys recent advances in applying AI to quantum tasks such as extracting information from limited measurements, discovering quantum algorithms, stabilizing hardware, and automating workflows. Conversely, it explores how quantum computation and quantum-inspired structures enhance AI through speedups, improved expressivity, and novel neural network designs.

The review also addresses challenges in reproducibility, scalability, hardware realism, and the integration of theory and experiment. It emphasizes that future progress will rely on closer collaboration between theoretical research, experimental efforts, and hybrid quantum-classical systems to fully realize the potential of combining AI and quantum information.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00365v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and quantum information (QI) are rapidly co-evolving. AI is becoming a practical tool for learning, designing, controlling, and verifying quantum systems, while QI offers new computational models, representational structures, and learning-theoretic questions for AI. This survey reviews the interface from both directions. In the AI for QI direction, we organize recent progress around the central tasks of extracting information from limited measurements, training and discovering quantum algorithms, stabilizing noisy hardware, automating experimental and programming workflows, and extending learning-based methods to sensing and networking. In the QI for AI direction, we examine how quantum computation and quantum-inspired structures affect learning through algorithmic speedups, expressivity, trainability, generalization, neural-network design, and tensor-network representations. We close by identifying cross-cutting challenges in reproducibility, scalability, hardware realism, and co-design, arguing that progress will depend on tighter integration of theory, experiment, and hybrid quantum--classical systems.

items.title: Researchers propose GenDa framework to improve data efficiency and generalizability in unsupervised reinforcement learning skill policies [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Learning Generalizable Skill Policy with Data-Efficient Unsupervised RL
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced GenDa, a new framework designed to enhance unsupervised reinforcement learning (URL) by improving data efficiency and generalizability in skill-conditioned policies. GenDa addresses key limitations in current URL methods, such as non-stationary skill semantics and weak generalization, by implementing a skill relabeling mechanism and a Complementary Information Bottleneck (CIB) that focuses on ego-centric features to maintain robustness across different tasks.

The framework's skill relabeling mechanism helps mitigate non-stationarity, significantly boosting data efficiency during pre-training. Meanwhile, the CIB encourages the learned policies to be resilient to distribution shifts, enhancing their applicability to downstream control tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that GenDa improves the scalability of URL with superior generalizability and data efficiency compared to existing approaches. The researchers have made their code and demonstration videos publicly available for further exploration.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00392v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Unsupervised Reinforcement Learning (URL) aims to pre-train scalable, skill-conditioned policies without extrinsic rewards, serving as a foundation for downstream control tasks. Despite recent progress, we argue that current off-policy URL methods are limited by two critical, overlooked bottlenecks: (1) non-stationary skill semantics and (2) brittle generalization. To address these challenges, we propose GenDa (Generalizable Data-efficient Agent), a unified framework for robust unsupervised reinforcement learning. First, we introduce a skill relabeling mechanism to mitigate non-stationarity and significantly improve data efficiency for pre-training. Second, we propose a Complementary Information Bottleneck (CIB), encouraging the learned skill policy to focus on ego-centric features and become robust to distribution shifts for downstream tasks. Through various experiments, we demonstrate that GenDa significantly enhances the scalability of URL with superior generalizability and data efficiency. Our code and videos are available at https://ihatebroccoli.github.io/official-GenDa.

items.title: Researchers identify semantic collapse causing utility loss in safety-aligned text-to-image diffusion models and propose SAGE to restore structured utility while maintaining safety [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Illusion of High Utility in Safety Alignment of Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
items.summary:
Researchers have identified a phenomenon called semantic collapse in safety-aligned text-to-image diffusion models, which leads to a loss of detailed semantic accuracy despite maintaining high scores on broad utility metrics. This collapse involves a contraction and distortion in the text-encoder's embedding space, causing significant drops in the models' ability to accurately represent objects, attributes, and relationships in generated images. To address this, the team proposed StructureAware Geometric Regularization (SAGE), a new safety alignment method that preserves the embedding structure and improves semantic fidelity while maintaining safety and competitive overall utility.

The study highlights that previous evaluations relying on coarse metrics like FID and CLIPScore overlooked fine-grained semantic errors, creating an illusion of high utility in safety-aligned models. By using a structured evaluation framework called TIFA, the researchers demonstrated the shortcomings of existing approaches and showed that SAGE enhances semantic faithfulness by 5% over prior methods. Their approach balances safety and utility more effectively, and the source code and trained models have been made publicly available for further research and development.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00402v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Safety alignment of text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models aims to suppress harmful generations while preserving utility on benign prompts. Recent methods often appear to deliver high safety with high utility, but this conclusion rests largely on coarse global utility metrics (e.g., FID, CLIPScore) that are insensitive to fine-grained semantic correctness, creating an illusion of high utility. We show that when utility is measured with structured evaluation, this illusion breaks: on TIFA (Text-to-Image Faithfulness evaluation with Question Answering), safety-aligned models suffer substantial drops in semantic fidelity, including failures in object counts, attributes, and relationships. To diagnose the source of this gap, we analyze the text-encoder prompt embedding space and uncover semantic collapse, a contraction of embedding spread coupled with distortion of inter-prompt similarity structure, which strongly correlates with structured utility loss. Guided by this insight, we propose StructureAware Geometric Regularization (SAGE), a safety alignment objective that explicitly preserves embedding spread and inter-prompt relational structure during adaptation. Our method restores structured utility (TIFA +5.0% over prior state-of-the-art) while maintaining strong safety performance and competitive coarse-grained utility scores. Our source code and trained models are available at https://adeelyousaf.github.io/SAGE_ECCV26_Project_Page/.

items.title: Researchers introduce spectral effective-rank entropy to measure and control critic complexity in actor-critic reinforcement learning across TD3 and PPO algorithms [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Gauging, Measuring, and Controlling Critic Complexity in Actor-Critic Reinforcement Learning
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced a new method to measure and control the complexity of critics in actor-critic reinforcement learning algorithms, specifically TD3 and PPO. They use spectral effective-rank entropy, which summarizes the singular-value distributions of critic weight matrices, to assess critic model complexity. Their experiments show that critic complexity can be tracked throughout training and is linked to training behavior, though this relationship varies across different algorithms, tasks, and hyperparameters.

The study also evaluates a direct intervention by adding a spectral-entropy penalty to the critic loss, which effectively adjusts the critic complexity. While this control mechanism reliably changes the targeted spectral quantity, its impact on performance varies depending on the task, indicating that complexity control effects are context-dependent rather than universally beneficial.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00452v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Actor-critic methods depend on learned critics, but critic quality is often evaluated only indirectly through return, temporal-difference error, or value loss. Critic complexity is introduced as an additional diagnostic and intervention dimension for actor-critic reinforcement learning. The analysis uses spectral effective-rank entropy, a rank-like summary of the singular-value distributions of critic weight matrices, to assess critic model complexity. Across TD3 and PPO experiments, critic complexity is tracked together with return and Monte Carlo value-estimation bias. The results show that critic complexity is measurable throughout training and is systematically associated with training behavior, while also making clear that the relationship is heterogeneous across algorithms, tasks, and hyperparameters. A direct complexity-control intervention is then evaluated by adding a spectral-entropy penalty to the critic loss. This intervention reliably changes the targeted spectral quantity, demonstrating that critic complexity can be controlled rather than only observed. Return effects are treated as task-dependent evidence rather than as a general performance claim, because overall complexity-control results vary.

items.title: Researchers develop deep neural network and ensemble machine learning model to predict lethal outcomes and identify key biomarkers in acute myocardial infarction for faster diagnosis [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Predicting Lethal Outcome (Cause) And Understanding Key Biomarkers Linked With Acute Myocardial Infarction Using Deep Artificial Neural Network And Ensemble Of Machine Learning Methodologies
items.summary:
Researchers have developed an automated model using deep neural networks and ensemble machine learning techniques to predict lethal outcomes and identify key biomarkers associated with acute myocardial infarction (MI), commonly known as a heart attack. This model aims to improve the speed and accuracy of MI diagnosis, which is critical for timely treatment and better patient outcomes. The approach integrates data preprocessing, feature selection, and a combination of algorithms including Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Light-GBM, Bagging SVM, and an artificial neural network to enhance predictive performance.

The study addresses the challenges of current diagnostic methods that rely heavily on physician experience and patient history, which can be time-consuming and inconsistent. By handling missing and imbalanced data with advanced techniques like SVMSMOTE and ADASYN, the model identifies the most relevant clinical variables and evaluates its effectiveness using precision, recall, and other metrics. This development has the potential to assist clinicians in making faster, more reliable decisions and could lead to more affordable and accessible MI diagnosis in clinical settings.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00472v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cardiovascular disease is still one of the main causes of death around the world. Acute myocardial infarction (MI), or heart attack, claims millions of lives each year. MI happens when blood flow to the coronary arteries is blocked or reduced, which causes permanent damage to the heart muscle. Without treatment, this can lead to cardiac arrest, where the heart stops pumping blood to the organs, resulting in organ failure and death. Even survivors often face serious problems like heart failure, pulmonary edema, and asystole. Research shows that 5 to 10 percent of survivors die within the first year after an MI, and nearly half need to be hospitalized again. Early thrombolytic treatment leads to better outcomes, so there is a clear need for faster and more accurate ways to diagnose MI. Right now, doctors usually review patient history and use their own experience to find the causes of MI. This process takes a lot of time and can be inconsistent. Detecting MI accurately and quickly can help patients take better care of themselves and prevent fatal events. In this study, we introduce an automated model to predict deadly outcomes of MI and help doctors understand important biomarkers linked to its complications. This approach aims to make diagnosis clearer, faster, and more affordable. The process includes preparing the data, filling in missing values, and handling imbalanced data using SVMSMOTE, ADASYN, and class-weighted methods. We use wrapper and embedded feature selection to find the most important variables, then scale the features for consistency. The model combines Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Light-GBM, and Bagging SVM, and is further improved with an artificial neural network to increase accuracy. We evaluate all models using precision, recall, and other key measures to find the best option for clinical use.

items.title: Researchers introduce PAPA, a method for online personalized active preference alignment that fine-tunes diffusion models using real-time user feedback without requiring large-scale preference data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: PAPA: Online Personalized Active Preference Alignment
items.summary:
Researchers have developed PAPA, a new method for online personalized active preference alignment that fine-tunes diffusion models using real-time user feedback without needing large-scale preference data. This approach addresses challenges in personalized recommender systems by directly optimizing diffusion models to better match individual user preferences, framed as a reinforcement learning problem but without requiring a parameterized reward model.

PAPA draws on variational inference principles to efficiently align preferences and has been validated through extensive experiments across various tasks. The team also introduced EPAPA, an enhanced fine-tuning strategy that reduces computational costs and speeds up the process, making the method more practical for real-world applications. The researchers have made their code publicly available to support further development and deployment.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00486v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion models are highly effective at modeling complex data distributions, including images and text. However, in applications like personalized recommender systems, the objective often shifts to modeling specific regions of the distribution that maximize user preferences-initially unknown but gradually uncovered through interactive feedback. This can naturally be framed as a reinforcement learning problem, where the goal is to fine-tune a diffusion model to maximize a reward function based on preferences. However, the main challenge lies in learning a parameterized reward model, which typically requires large-scale preference data-something that is often not feasible in practice. In this work, we introduce Personalized Active Preference Alignment PAPA, a novel method that bypasses the requirement for a parametrized reward model by directly optimizing the diffusion model using real-time user feedback. PAPA enables feedback-efficient preference alignment, drawing inspiration from the variational inference framework. We demonstrate PAPA's effectiveness through extensive experiments and ablation studies across diverse class-conditioned and fine-grained alignment tasks. Additionally, based on theoretical insights, we propose an enhanced fine-tuning strategy, referred to as EPAPA, that requires less computational budget and accelerates the fine-tuning process, further boosting PAPA's suitability for real-world deployment. Our code is made publicly available at https://github.com/NasikNafi/papa.

items.title: Researchers propose Active-GRPO, an adaptive imitation and self-improving reasoning method for molecular optimization that surpasses reference-guided policy optimization on TOMG-Bench MOLOPT benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Active-GRPO: Adaptive Imitation and Self-Improving Reasoning for Molecular Optimization
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Active-GRPO, an adaptive imitation and self-improving reasoning method designed to enhance molecular optimization. This approach addresses limitations in existing training methods by allowing the policy to dynamically choose when to imitate reference data and when to reinforce its own discoveries, continuously upgrading its reference points. Active-GRPO outperforms previous techniques on the TOMG-Bench MOLOPT benchmarks, showing significant improvements in key molecular properties such as LogP, MR, and QED.

Active-GRPO operates through two mechanisms: active imitate-reinforce, which switches between imitation learning and reinforcement learning based on performance comparisons, and active referencing, which updates the reference with the best policy-generated candidates over time. This strategy overcomes the performance ceiling imposed by weak or misaligned references in prior methods, resulting in more robust and efficient training for molecular optimization tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00531v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scientific reasoning is an increasingly important capability of large language models, yet improving the robustness and efficiency of training such reasoning remains a key open challenge. We study this problem in instruction-based molecular optimization, where answer-only supervised fine-tuning (SFT) collapses multi-step reasoning and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) suffers from sparse feedback. Reference-guided Policy Optimization mitigates both by anchoring policy updates to dataset-provided references, but its effectiveness is tightly coupled to reference quality: weak or misaligned references impose a performance ceiling. To overcome this ceiling, we propose active reasoning, a paradigm in which the policy actively decides, on a per-instance basis, when to imitate a reference and when to reinforce its own discoveries, while continuously upgrading what it imitates. We instantiate this paradigm as Active Group Relative Policy Optimization (Active-GRPO), realized through two coupled mechanisms: active imitate-reinforce and active referencing. The former performs imitation learning when the reference still outperforms the policy's own candidates, and shifts to self-improvement via reinforcement learning once the policy has generated molecules that surpass the reference. The latter continuously upgrades the reference itself by replacing it with the best policy-generated candidate discovered so far, progressively raising the imitation target and ensuring that reference guidance remains informative-rather than restrictive-throughout training. Across TOMG-Bench MOLOPT, Active-GRPO improves average SRxSim from 0.0959 for GRPO and 0.1665 for RePO to 0.1773 under matched three-seed evaluation, with statistically significant gains on LogP, MR, and QED.
