items.title: Researchers propose Flow-Map GRPO, a reinforcement learning framework using Anchored Stochastic Flow Map Composition to improve deterministic few-step flow-map generators without retraining [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Flow-Map GRPO: Reinforcement Learning for Few-Step Flow-Map Generators via Anchored Stochastic Composition
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Flow-Map GRPO, a reinforcement learning framework designed to enhance deterministic few-step flow-map generators like consistency models and MeanFlow without requiring retraining. The framework employs Anchored Stochastic Flow Map Composition (ASFMC), a novel stochasticization technique that injects randomness through anchor-based conditional resampling while preserving the original probability paths of the deterministic models. This approach enables effective reinforcement learning post-training optimization, which was previously challenging due to the deterministic nature of these models.

Flow-Map GRPO derives specific objectives for different flow-map parameterizations and has been tested on FLUX-based text-to-image generators, demonstrating improvements across various evaluation metrics including reward-based, perceptual, and task-level measures. The results indicate that deterministic few-step flow-map generators can be aligned with reinforcement learning methods post-training without altering their original architectures or converting them into stochastic models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00535v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Few-step flow-map generators, such as consistency models and MeanFlow, accelerate sampling by directly learning long-range transport maps between noise and data. However, these models are typically deterministic, which makes them difficult to optimize with reinforcement learning (RL) post-training methods that require stochastic trajectories and well-defined likelihood ratios. Existing SDE-based stochasticization techniques are designed for velocity-based samplers with infinitesimal or finely discretized transitions, and therefore do not directly apply to long-range flow maps. In this work, we propose Flow-Map GRPO, an online RL post-training framework for deterministic few-step flow-map generators. The key component is Anchored Stochastic Flow Map Composition (ASFMC), a path-preserving stochasticization mechanism that introduces randomness through anchor-based conditional resampling while preserving the original marginal probability path of the deterministic flow map. We derive GRPO objectives for both single-time and two-time flow-map parameterizations. Experiments on few-step FLUX-based text-to-image generators, including MeanFlow and sCM, show that Flow-Map GRPO improves pretrained deterministic flow-map models across reward-based, perceptual, and task-level evaluation metrics. Our results demonstrate that deterministic few-step flow-map generators can be effectively aligned with RL post-training without modifying their original model parameterization or retraining them as native stochastic models.

items.title: Researchers propose Equivariant Poincaré ResNets combining hyperbolic geometry with discrete symmetry groups to improve optimization and preserve spatial-group equivariance in hyperbolic neural networks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Group-Equivariant Poincar\'e Convolutional Networks
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Equivariant Poincaré ResNets, a novel approach that integrates hyperbolic geometry with discrete symmetry groups to enhance the optimization of hyperbolic neural networks. This method addresses challenges in existing models, such as the computational intensity of Riemannian gradients and inefficiencies caused by treating spatial transformations as separate concepts, by embedding equivariance directly into the network architecture.

The team identified key obstacles in applying Euclidean equivariance principles to hyperbolic space and developed solutions including geometrically safe tensor reshaping, left-regular permutations for hyperbolic group convolutions, and a joint-orientation Poincaré Midpoint Batch normalization technique. Empirical results demonstrate that incorporating equivariance significantly reduces the optimization space, accelerates convergence, and maintains spatial-group equivariance while respecting the constraints of the Poincaré ball.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00556v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While recent advancements like the Poincar\'e ResNet have demonstrated the potential of learning visual representations directly in hyperbolic space, their optimisation remains hampered by the computationally intensive nature of Riemannian gradients and the strict boundaries of the manifold. Furthermore, standard hyperbolic networks treat spatial transformations of the same object as distinct hierarchical concepts, leading to redundant parameter usage and vanishing signals. We propose Equivariant Poincar\'e ResNets, combining hyperbolic geometry with discrete symmetry groups ($C_4$ and $D_4$). We identify critical roadblocks in applying Euclidean equivariance to hyperbolic space and propose geometrically safe tensor reshaping, left-regular permutations for hyperbolic group convolutions, and joint-orientation Poincar\'e Midpoint Batch normalisation. Empirically, embedding equivariance drastically reduces the optimisation space, accelerating convergence while accelerating convergence while respecting the boundary constraints of the Poincar\'e ball and preserving spatial-group equivariance.

items.title: Researchers propose a causal auditing framework for Limited Memory Language Models to measure post-deletion fact persistence, finding residual retrieval artifacts up to 13.6% mainly controlled by database state [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Auditing Forgetting in Limited Memory Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a causal auditing framework to evaluate how Limited Memory Language Models (LMLMs) retain or forget factual information after deletion from their external databases. This framework isolates the model's fixed parameters and varies the database state during inference to distinguish between residual memory, retrieval-mediated correctness, and retrieval artifacts. Applying this method to over 12,000 deletions across multiple databases and adversarial scenarios, they found that the model itself rarely retains deleted facts without retrieval, and most residual information comes from near-neighbor retrieval artifacts within the database.

The study revealed that residual retrieval artifacts accounted for up to 13.6% of post-deletion correctness in the most challenging cases, while parametric leakage was nearly zero across all tests. The prompt style did not significantly affect how much deleted information persisted. These findings suggest that in LMLMs using deletion-based unlearning, the effectiveness of forgetting is primarily controlled by the database state managed by administrators rather than the model's internal parameters.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00605v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Limited Memory Language Models (LMLMs) externalize factual knowledge to a database to enable deletion-based unlearning without retraining. Existing evaluations measure post-deletion correctness in aggregate and cannot tell whether a deleted fact persists through residual parametric memory, alternative retrieval paths, or near-neighbor retrieval artifacts. We propose a causal auditing framework that holds the model fixed and varies the database state at inference time across three interventions: FULL, DEL-ON, and DEL-OFF. The framework decomposes post-deletion behavior into parametric leakage L(f), retrieval-mediated correctness R(f), and a retrieval artifact rate grounded in the inference-time retrieval trace. We apply it to 12,228 alias-closure deletions across thirteen databases, including four adversarial topologies (Base, Alias, Noise, Collision) we construct in three domains, and six prompt formulations. Parametric leakage is near zero in every variant and every prompt style: the model rarely returns the deleted answer in the absence of retrieval. The residual that does survive lives in the retrieval graph: retrieval-mediated correctness and the retrieval artifact rate match within rounding everywhere, so post-deletion correctness is, in our audit, predominantly reconstituted from near-neighbor retrieval. This residual ranges from 0.7% on the released LMLM database to 13.6% on the most adversarial variant, and prompt formulation does not independently control how much of a deleted fact survives. These results suggest that, for this class of LMLM and deletion procedure, the unlearning boundary is drawn primarily by the database administrator rather than by the model.

items.title: Researchers propose loss smoothing to improve neural network adaptation under distribution shift by gradually interpolating source and target objectives, showing consistent performance gains across vision, reinforcement learning, and language tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Loss Smoothing for Stable Adaptation Under Distribution Shift
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced a method called loss smoothing to improve neural network adaptation when facing distribution shifts, such as during fine-tuning or reinforcement learning. Instead of abruptly switching from the source training objective to the target objective, loss smoothing gradually interpolates between the two, preserving useful features from the original model while allowing specialization to the new task. This approach has demonstrated consistent performance improvements across various domains, including vision, reinforcement learning, and language model fine-tuning.

The technique addresses the common issue where sudden changes in training objectives can distort learned representations, potentially harming adaptation. By implementing a smoother transition at the start of adaptation, loss smoothing helps maintain stability and effectiveness in model updates. Experiments across controlled supervised shifts, pretrained vision tasks, offline-to-online and online reinforcement learning, and language model fine-tuning confirm its broad applicability and benefits.

These findings suggest that smoother objective transitions can be a valuable tool for enhancing model adaptation under distribution shifts, potentially influencing future strategies in neural network training and transfer learning.

items.title: Researchers propose Label Influence Propagation model for multi-label node classification on graphs, outperforming state-of-the-art methods on benchmark datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Multi-Label Node Classification with Label Influence Propagation
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced a new model called Label Influence Propagation (LIP) to improve multi-label node classification on graphs, a task important in domains like protein interaction networks and social or e-commerce platforms. Unlike previous methods that overlook complex label interactions, LIP constructs a label influence graph to capture and propagate high-order label influences, dynamically enhancing labels with positive effects and reducing those with negative impacts. This approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art techniques on benchmark datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in handling multi-label classification challenges on graph data.

The model builds on a detailed analysis of the message passing process in graph neural networks, separating it into propagation and transformation steps to quantify label influence correlations. By integrating these insights, LIP adjusts the learning process based on the nuanced relationships between labels, addressing limitations of prior methods that relied mainly on label co-occurrence or embeddings without considering intricate influence patterns.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00671v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graphs are a complex and versatile data structure used across various domains, with possibly multi-label nodes playing a particularly crucial role. Examples include proteins in PPI networks with multiple functions and users in social or e-commerce networks exhibiting diverse interests. Tackling multi-label node classification (MLNC) on graphs has led to the development of various approaches. Some methods leverage graph neural networks (GNNs) to exploit label co-occurrence correlations, while others incorporate label embeddings to capture label proximity. However, these approaches fail to account for the intricate influences between labels in non-Euclidean graph data. To address this issue, we decompose the message passing process in GNNs into two operations: propagation and transformation. We then conduct a comprehensive analysis and quantification of the influence correlations between labels in each operation. Building on these insights, we propose a novel model, Label Influence Propagation (LIP). Specifically, we construct a label influence graph based on the integrated label correlations. Then, we propagate high-order influences through this graph, dynamically adjusting the learning process by amplifying labels with positive contributions and mitigating those with negative influence. Finally, our framework is evaluated on comprehensive benchmark datasets, consistently outperforming SOTA methods across various settings, demonstrating its effectiveness on MLNC tasks.

items.title: Researchers introduce LUMA, a lightweight universal mask adapter for benchmarking image segmentation across 20 backbones and 11 pretraining schemes on ADE20K and Cityscapes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: LUMA: Benchmarking Segmentation via a Lightweight Universal Mask Adapter
items.summary:
Researchers have developed LUMA, a Lightweight Universal Mask Adapter designed to provide a consistent benchmarking tool for image segmentation across various transformer backbones. LUMA functions as a backbone-agnostic mask-transformer head that treats any backbone as a feature extractor, enabling efficient cross-attention-based segmentation. It achieves accuracy comparable to the state-of-the-art EoMT segmenter at a lower computational cost and is compatible with diverse backbone architectures including isotropic, hierarchical, convolutional, and mixture-of-experts models.

Using LUMA, the team benchmarked 20 different backbones, 11 pretraining schemes, and multiple resolutions on the ADE20K and Cityscapes datasets under a unified experimental setup. Their findings reveal that so-called "efficient" token mixers do not consistently improve efficiency at high resolutions, with the plain Vision Transformer (ViT) maintaining the best throughput across all tested resolutions. Moreover, the study highlights that the choice of pretraining objective, rather than the backbone architecture itself, plays the most significant role in determining segmentation performance.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00687v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Comparing transformer backbones for image segmentation is confounded: each is paired with a different decoder, recipe, and pretraining, so reported differences rarely reflect the backbone itself. We introduce the Lightweight Universal Mask Adapter (LUMA), a lightweight, backbone-agnostic mask-transformer head that treats any backbone as a black-box feature extractor, letting a set of queries read from its features through cheap cross-attention. LUMA matches the accuracy of EoMT, the state-of-the-art efficient ViT-segmenter, at lower cost, while attaching unchanged to isotropic, hierarchical, convolutional, and mixture-of-experts backbones alike. Holding this head fixed, we benchmark 20 backbones, 11 pretraining schemes and a range of resolutions on ADE20K and Cityscapes under one modern recipe. We find that ``efficient'' token mixers fail to deliver efficiency even at the high resolutions that motivate them, with plain ViT holding the throughput Pareto-front at every resolution. Additionally, the pretraining objective, not the architecture, the lever the field has tuned hardest, governs segmentation quality.

items.title: Researchers propose active learning framework to improve unsupervised time series anomaly detection, achieving 12.39% AUC gain across 28 test cases with multivariate datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Detecting the Undetectable: Enhancing Unsupervised time series Anomaly Detection via Active Learning
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a new active learning framework to improve unsupervised anomaly detection in complex time series data, achieving a 12.39% increase in AUC across 28 test cases with multivariate datasets. The framework addresses challenges in distinguishing subtle and noisy anomalies from normal patterns, which are common issues in industrial AI applications where labeling data is costly and time-consuming.

The approach introduces a masked time-series reconstruction feedback strategy to help models learn robust temporal dependencies and a minimax learning strategy that treats normal and abnormal samples differently to enhance robustness. Tested on four multivariate datasets and seven unsupervised backbone models, the method significantly boosts the performance of existing unsupervised reconstruction-based anomaly detection systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00720v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Despite the increasing sophistication of industrial AI systems, the ability to reliably detect subtle and noisy anomalies in complex time series data remains a critical yet unresolved challenge. In large-scale industrial applications, labeling time series data is often prohibitively expensive and time-consuming, making unsupervised learning a practical and widely adopted approach. However, existing unsupervised methods frequently struggle to distinguish near-normal anomalies from normal patterns and are vulnerable to noise contamination within normal samples. To address these limitations, we propose a novel framework that leverages active learning to iteratively enhance the performance of unsupervised models. Our framework's core contributions are (1) a masked time-series reconstruction feedback strategy that forces the model to learn robust temporal dependencies, and (2) a minimax learning strategy that promotes robustness by differentially treating normal and abnormal samples. This process encourages the model to better capture the dynamics of subtle and noisy patterns. The proposed framework is evaluated across 28 test cases involving four multivariate time-series datasets and seven unsupervised backbone models. Experimental results demonstrate a 12.39% improvement in AUC compared to the original models, confirming that our method can be readily integrated into existing unsupervised reconstruction-based anomaly detection systems to significantly enhance their performance.

items.title: Researchers present AgentODE, an LLM-guided framework that discovers ODE structures and infers parameter distributions from population-level summary statistics in rare disease datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: LLM-Guided ODE Discovery and Parameter Inference from Small-Cohort Aggregate Data
items.summary:
Researchers have developed AgentODE, a novel framework that uses large language models (LLMs) to discover ordinary differential equation (ODE) structures and infer parameter distributions from population-level summary statistics, particularly in rare disease datasets where individual data is limited and privacy concerns are significant. AgentODE operates by proposing candidate ODE models and iteratively refining parameters through a diagnosis-update process, relying solely on aggregated data rather than individual-level information.

The framework was tested on multiple benchmark problems and clinical datasets, including the rare disease recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa (RDEB), demonstrating its ability to recover functionally consistent ODE structures even with sparse and noisy data. Unlike traditional methods that require detailed individual data and may produce less plausible models, AgentODE leverages summary statistics to promote mechanistically sound model discovery.

This approach opens new avenues for mechanistic modeling in rare diseases, addressing challenges posed by data scarcity and privacy constraints, and enabling more interpretable and principled analyses directly from aggregated clinical data.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00733v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mechanistic modeling via ordinary differential equations (ODEs) provides interpretable descriptions of complex dynamics and enables inference of underlying mechanisms, which is particularly valuable in clinical settings. However, in rare diseases, both the structure and parameters of the model are typically unknown, while individual-level data is scarce, noisy, heterogeneous, and subject to privacy constraints. In such settings, population-level summary statistics provide a practical privacy-preserving data representation, while capturing heterogeneity further requires modeling parameters as distributions rather than fixed values. Yet no existing method jointly discovers ODE structure and refines parameter distributions solely from summary statistics. We present AgentODE, an end-to-end framework that addresses this gap. An LLM proposes candidate ODE structures, while a tool-augmented inference agent iteratively refines parameter distributions through a diagnosis--update loop, operating on population-level summary statistics alone. We evaluate AgentODE on three benchmark problems across different fields and two clinical datasets, including the rare disease recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa (RDEB), with only 231 observations across 46 patients. AgentODE recovers functionally consistent ODE structures across all settings, and experiments on RDEB demonstrates that in sparse and noisy data settings reasoning from summary statistics promotes mechanistically principled structure discovery, whereas baselines with individual-level data access recover implausible structures despite better predictive performance. AgentODE opens new possibilities for mechanistic modeling of rare diseases directly from population-level summary statistics, where data scarcity and privacy constraints have traditionally limited such analyses.

items.title: Researchers introduce Valdi, a Value Diffusion World Model combining latent diffusion dynamics with online training for Model Predictive Control, matching deterministic baselines in CarRacing tests [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Valdi: Value Diffusion World Models
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Valdi, a Value Diffusion World Model that integrates latent diffusion dynamics with end-to-end online training for Model Predictive Control (MPC). Valdi addresses the challenge of balancing fast, expressive dynamics prediction with the need to model uncertain futures, which is critical for effective MPC. In tests using the CarRacing environment, Valdi, employing a single diffusion step during both training and inference, performed on par with a deterministic multilayer perceptron baseline.

The study highlights a trade-off between the model's ability to predict multiple possible future states (multimodality) and its control performance. By combining diffusion models with MPC in a latent space, Valdi offers a promising approach for low-latency planning under uncertainty. The researchers have made their code publicly available for further exploration and development.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00917v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: World models can enable Model Predictive Control (MPC), but this requires dynamics prediction that is both fast enough for online use and expressive enough to represent uncertain futures. Diffusion models offer a natural mechanism for modeling uncertain dynamics, yet their iterative inference procedure makes them difficult to use for low-latency latent planning. We bridge this gap with Value Diffusion World Models (Valdi), combining end-to-end online training for MPC with a latent diffusion dynamics model. In preliminary experiments on the CarRacing environment, we show that Valdi, using a single diffusion step at both training and inference, matches a deterministic MLP baseline. Our experiments expose a trade-off between predictive multimodality and control performance in this setup. Code is available at https://github.com/Kit115/ValueDiffusionWorldModels.

items.title: Researchers propose Generative Meta-Learning with Human Feedback (GMHF) framework using Conditional Neural ODE and reinforcement learning to improve model generalization under distribution shifts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Human-Machine Collaboration on Generative Meta-Learning: Model and Algorithm
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Generative Meta-Learning with Human Feedback (GMHF), a new framework designed to improve machine learning model generalization when faced with distribution shifts, especially when target domain data is limited or unavailable. GMHF integrates expert human intuition to guide data synthesis, using a Conditional Neural ODE as a generative model and a reinforcement learning agent that adjusts latent parameters based on feedback to better align generated data with the target distribution.

The framework is supported by theoretical analysis showing that aligning generated data with human beliefs reduces generalization risk. Experiments on a nonlinear Duffing oscillator demonstrate that GMHF lowers deployment loss as expert feedback reliability increases, confirming the predicted reduction in divergence between generated and target data. Additional tests on non-dynamical probabilistic models indicate that GMHF's approach extends beyond systems governed by ordinary differential equations, highlighting the potential of human-AI collaboration to enhance robustness under distribution shifts.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00926v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generalizing machine learning models to environments that differ from their training distribution remains a critical hurdle, particularly when data from the target domain is entirely or partially unavailable. We propose Generative Meta-Learning with Human Feedback (GMHF), a novel framework that bridges this domain gap by leveraging expert intuition to guide data synthesis. Grounded in a theoretical analysis of generalization error, we derive bounds demonstrating that aligning the distribution of generated data with human beliefs regarding the target physics significantly mitigates risk. GMHF operationalizes this insight by employing a Conditional Neural ODE (cNODE) as a generative digital twin, coupled with a Reinforcement Learning (RL) agent. The agent iteratively refines the latent physical parameters of the generated trajectories based on feedback, effectively steering the meta-learner toward the unobserved target distribution. Empirical validation on a nonlinear Duffing oscillator shows that GMHF substantially reduces deployment loss as expert reliability increases, and that the divergence between generated and target data falls under reliable feedback, directly corroborating the divergence-minimisation mechanism predicted by our theory. Further experiments on a non-dynamical probabilistic model confirm that the framework extends beyond ODE-governed systems, establishing human-AI collaboration as a rigorous catalyst for robust generalisation under distribution shift.

items.title: Researchers introduce Aionoscope, a diagnostic tool for evaluating latent-state accessibility in time-series model representations, revealing gaps in capturing fine-grained process states [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Aionoscope: Debugging Latent-State Accessibility in Time-Series Representations
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Aionoscope, a diagnostic tool designed to evaluate how well time-series model representations capture latent process states such as event timing, phase, amplitude, frequency, and regime variables. Unlike traditional evaluation methods that focus on forecasting or classification accuracy, Aionoscope assesses the accessibility of detailed latent states within frozen time-series representations by generating synthetic data streams with precise labels.

The tool was tested on 37 model-plus-adapter systems using a pooled linear-probe protocol, revealing a significant gap between the ability to detect coarse components and the ability to recover fine-grained process states. While most systems could identify the presence of components, they struggled to reliably expose detailed process information, with dense-state recovery scores substantially lower than an ideal oracle. This finding highlights a common limitation in current time-series models, where representations may appear informative at a high level but fail to provide the detailed variables necessary for effective debugging and analysis.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00956v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time-series models are often evaluated by what they can forecast or classify, but those scores do not show whether their representations preserve the process state a user may want to inspect: event timing, phase, amplitude, frequency, or regime variables. We introduce Aionoscope, a generator-based diagnostic tool for debugging latent-state accessibility in frozen time-series representations. Aionoscope separates process generation from observation rendering, producing seeded synthetic streams with exact categorical and dense labels across mixture complexity and nuisance variation. We instantiate Aionoscope as Primitive Process Mixtures and evaluate 37 model-plus-adapter systems with a common pooled linear-probe protocol. The main result is a mismatch between coarse and fine-grained accessibility. Most systems make component presence easy to recover, but expose dense process state much less reliably: the highest observed dense-probe row reaches 0.689 mean masked $R^2$, while a dense-feature oracle reaches 0.999. This is the failure mode Aionoscope is designed to surface: a representation can look informative at the level of "what kind of signal is present" while hiding the timing, phase, amplitude, frequency, or regime variables needed for debugging.

items.title: Researchers introduce Logit-Contribution Scoring to identify non-literal retrieval attention heads in large language models, outperforming prior methods on multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Logit-Contribution Scoring Identifies Non-Literal Retrieval Heads
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Logit-Contribution Scoring (LOCOS), a new method to identify attention heads in large language models that synthesize answers from context rather than copying tokens literally. LOCOS evaluates each head based on its output-value circuit's contribution to the generated answer, enabling detection of non-literal retrieval mechanisms that previous methods missed. This approach was tested across three model families, showing superior performance in pinpointing retrieval-specific heads that significantly impact non-literal retrieval benchmarks without affecting other tasks like arithmetic reasoning.

The study demonstrated that ablating the top LOCOS-identified heads drastically reduced performance on non-literal retrieval tasks such as NoLiMa, MuSiQue, and BABI-Long, while leaving parametric recall and reasoning abilities largely intact. This indicates that the selected heads are specialized for retrieval-related synthesis rather than general model functions. LOCOS thus offers a more precise tool for interpreting long-context behavior in large language models and understanding how they generate synthesized answers from context.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01002v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In long-context use, large language models frequently synthesize answers from the meaning of a relevant context span rather than literally copy-pasting them. Identifying which attention heads perform this synthesis matters for interpreting long-context model behavior. Yet existing detectors miss these heads by construction: they reward heads whose attended token matches the generated token, a literal-copy criterion that captures where a head reads but not what it writes through its output-value (OV) circuit, the very mechanism that carries non-literal retrieval. We introduce Logit-Contribution Scoring (LOCOS), a write-aware detector that scores each head by the projection of its OV-circuit output onto the answer-token unembedding direction, contrasting needle and off-needle source positions in a single forward pass. Across three model families (Qwen3, Gemma-3, OLMo-3.1), mean-ablating the top LOCOS heads on the NoLiMa non-literal retrieval benchmark collapses ROUGE-L at lower head counts than prior attention-based detections; on Qwen3-8B, ablating 50 heads drives ROUGE-L from 0.401 to 0.000 while the strongest baseline still retains 0.292. The selected heads are retrieval-specific: parametric recall and arithmetic reasoning stay at baseline under the same ablation. On Qwen3-8B, the same ablation also drops MuSiQue from 0.55 to 0.08 and BABI-Long from 0.62 to 0.20, while a random-heads control stays within 0.05 of baseline.

items.title: Researchers derive scaling laws for learning rate stability in asynchronous RLHF with stale rollouts, explaining weak dependence on staleness in horizon-limited regimes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Staleness-Learning Rate Scaling Laws for Asynchronous RLHF
items.summary:
Researchers have analyzed the impact of using stale rollouts in asynchronous reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) systems, particularly focusing on the asynchronous GRPO algorithm. They identified that stale rollouts introduce a bias in the surrogate gradient proportional to the product of the rollout lag and the learning rate. Their work establishes scaling laws that describe stability conditions for learning rates, showing that stability depends on both cumulative learner drift and the staleness of rollouts, which explains why learning rate stability appears only weakly affected by staleness in certain regimes.

The study makes the behavior policy explicit in the surrogate objective and distinguishes between the learner's surrogate-gradient mapping and the true gradient of the population objective. Under assumptions of smoothness and boundedness, the authors derive a two-constraint stability condition that balances batch-level clipping and stale-rollout effects. This provides theoretical insight into how asynchronous RLHF systems can maintain stable learning despite delays in rollout data.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01083v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-throughput RLHF systems often decouple rollout generation from policy optimization, leading to the use of stale rollouts during learner updates. In this work, we study the effect of such staleness in asynchronous GRPO. We make the behavior policy explicit in the GRPO surrogate objective and distinguish between the surrogate-gradient mapping used by the learner and the true total derivative of a distribution-dependent population objective. Under assumptions of local boundedness, distributional smoothness, and behavior-policy smoothness, we show that stale rollouts introduce a per-step surrogate-gradient bias of order O(S * eta), where S denotes the maximum rollout lag and eta denotes the learning rate. We further derive a conditional collapse-time scaling law: when within-cycle drift remains below a batch-level clipping radius, collapse is governed primarily by cumulative learner drift T * eta; when the stale-rollout constraint is active, stability instead depends explicitly on S * eta. This yields a two-constraint stability condition eta << min{R_batch / (S * G_upd), R_crit / (T * G_upd)}, explaining why the maximum stable learning rate may appear weakly dependent on staleness in the horizon-limited regime.

items.title: Researchers propose CausalMix, a causal inference framework to optimize data mixtures for large language model training, improving performance and scalability across multiple tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: CausalMix: Data Mixture as Causal Inference for Language Model Training
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced CausalMix, a novel framework that applies causal inference to optimize data mixtures for training large language models (LLMs). Unlike previous methods that assume static data distributions and require costly retraining when data shifts, CausalMix treats data mixture optimization as a causal problem, using statistical features as covariates and domain mixtures as treatments. This approach enables dynamic, state-dependent optimization of data mixtures, improving model performance and scalability across various tasks.

The team demonstrated CausalMix by fitting a causal model on multiple runs of a smaller model to estimate the Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE), then extrapolating optimal mixtures for larger datasets and models. They also extended the framework to handle complex data types like long chain-of-thought sequences. Experiments showed that CausalMix outperforms existing methods such as RegMix, and includes tools for visualizing the learned mixing strategies, offering an interpretable and effective solution for LLM data mixture optimization.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01104v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In Large Language Model (LLM) training, data mixing plays a pivotal role in determining model performance. Recent methods optimize mixture weights via proxy models, but they rely on the assumption of static data distributions. As a result, when the underlying data pool shifts, these methods require costly retraining from scratch. This limitation restricts their ability to scale seamlessly from small settings to larger data pools and model sizes. In this paper, we propose CausalMix to address this limitation by casting data mixture optimization as a causal inference problem. We formulate the statistical features of the data pool as covariates and the domain mixture as the treatment. After fitting a causal model on 512 runs of Qwen2.5-0.5B to estimate the Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE), we extrapolate the optimal mixture for an 800K data pool and apply it to train a 7B model. Furthermore, we successfully generalize the framework to long chain-of-thought data on Qwen3-4B-Base. By leveraging causal modeling to isolate confounding biases, CausalMix dynamically infers state-dependent optimal data mixtures. Extensive experiments show that the mixture guided by CausalMix consistently improves performance across multiple downstream tasks, outperforming RegMix and other baselines. In addition, we use the CATE Interpreter to provide visual analysis of the learned mixing strategy. Overall, CausalMix offers a causal and interpretable framework for optimizing LLM data mixtures.

items.title: Researchers propose Failure-Aware Retry framework to improve robot task success rates by learning from failures and enabling continual policy improvement in simulation and real-world tests [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: FAR: Failure-Aware Retry for Test-Time Recovery and Continual Policy Improvement
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a new framework called Failure-Aware Retry (FAR) to improve the success rates of robot tasks by enabling robots to learn from their failures during deployment. FAR helps robots adapt their behavior based on previous unsuccessful attempts, using a method called Failure-Contrastive Preference Adaptation combined with action perturbations to encourage exploration. items.originalTitle: Muon as a Residual Connection
items.summary:
Researchers have proposed a new interpretation of the Muon optimizer, a tool effective in training large neural networks, suggesting it functions as an implicit residual connection during training. This mechanism involves orthogonalizing updates, which may reduce immediate gradient accuracy but enhances the preservation of representations for subsequent layers. The study explores this balance in controlled linear optimization scenarios, showing that Muon helps learn representations that are slower to fit local targets but more accessible for downstream processing.

The findings offer a conceptual explanation for Muon's success and provide insights for designing optimizers that effectively balance local gradient descent with the usability of learned representations in later network layers.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01124v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Muon has recently emerged as one of the most effective optimizers for training large neural networks, yet its empirical success has been explained from several different perspectives. In this paper, we propose a simple mechanistic interpretation: Muon can be understood as an implicit residual connection during training. Specifically, orthogonalizing the update can sacrifice some immediate gradient fidelity while improving representation preservation for downstream layers. We study this trade-off in controlled linear optimization settings, where Muon can learn representations that are slower to fit a local target but easier for downstream layers to exploit. Our results suggest a conceptual explanation for Muon and a design perspective for optimizers that balance local descent with downstream usability.

items.title: Researchers propose Sequentially-Controlled Interactive Multi-Particle Flow-Maps for sample-efficient online feedback-driven search, enabling broad exploration and preference alignment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Sequentially-Controlled Interactive Multi-Particle Flow-Maps for Online Feedback-Driven Search
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Sequentially-Controlled Interactive Multi-Particle Flow-Maps (IMPFM), a novel framework designed for sample-efficient online feedback-driven search that enables broad exploration and effective preference alignment. IMPFM addresses limitations of current generative model methods, which often focus on local exploration and struggle when preferences are unknown and revealed only through sequential feedback. The framework uses interactive particles that collectively move toward a target distribution, sharing posterior samples to correct individual drift and maintain diversity, thereby preventing over-optimization and mode collapse.

IMPFM incorporates a multi-particle interaction-aware mechanism that balances exploration and exploitation while overcoming challenges like weight degeneracy common in standard sequential Monte Carlo samplers. The researchers provide theoretical proof that their approach progressively guides the particle system toward a KL-tilted target distribution, facilitating global exploration. Extensive empirical evaluations and ablation studies across various search and alignment tasks demonstrate that IMPFM outperforms existing baseline methods.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01144v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While generative models have enabled training-free reward alignment, current methods typically excel in local exploration within narrow regions of the underlying distribution. These approaches struggle when preferences are unknown a priori and only revealed through sequential feedback-a scenario demanding broad exploration to uncover high-utility regions. To address this, we propose Sequentially-Controlled Interactive Multi-Particle Flow-Maps (IMPFM), a framework for sample-efficient online feedback-driven search. IMPFM progressively transports a group of interactive particles toward the target distribution, maintaining the broad coverage essential for heterogeneous preference alignment. IMPFM introduces a principled and efficient posterior sample sharing mechanism across particles powered by flow maps. By correcting individual particle drift with the collective posterior samples of the entire ensemble at each resampling step, the framework maximizes sample utility to enable global exploration while actively mitigating reward over-optimization, typical of standard control frameworks. Paired with a principled exploration-exploitation reweighting mechanism involving multi-particle interaction, this sequentially corrected multi-particle dynamics explicitly preserves structural diversity and overcomes the weight degeneracy inherent to standard SMC samplers. Crucially, we prove that the resulting sampling framework yields a multi-particle interaction-aware Feynman-Kac corrector that progressively steers the multi-particle system toward a KL-tilted target distribution, facilitating global exploration and preventing mode collapse. Extensive empirical evaluations and rigorous ablations across diverse search and alignment tasks confirm the efficacy of IMPFM over existing baselines.

items.title: Researchers propose adversarial generator-discriminator framework to train language models with verifiable rewards and human demonstrations, improving accuracy and human-like output across tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Right in the Right Way: LM Training with Verifiable Rewards and Human Demonstrations
items.summary:
Researchers have developed an adversarial generator-discriminator framework to enhance the training of language models by combining verifiable rewards with signals learned from human demonstrations. This approach addresses limitations in current reinforcement learning methods that focus solely on objectively measurable outcomes, often overlooking subjective qualities like style and structure. By training a generator to maximize both task accuracy and an adversarial reward from a discriminator that distinguishes human-written from model-generated outputs, the method improves human-like qualities without sacrificing accuracy.

The framework was tested across various tasks, including bug fixing and story generation, where it produced solutions with lower edit distances and more diverse, human-like stories compared to traditional reinforcement learning baselines. Additionally, it effectively reduced model misbehavior in reward hacking scenarios while maintaining high performance. This approach bridges reinforcement learning and supervised fine-tuning, offering a scalable way to optimize both verifiable and non-verifiable aspects of language model outputs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01181v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for training LMs on tasks with well-defined success metrics, such as code generation and mathematical reasoning. However, current RLVR methods optimize only what can be objectively scored, often neglecting subjective, non-verifiable aspects of human-like outputs, such as style and structure. This limitation leads to well-documented failure modes such as diversity collapse, unnatural-sounding responses, and reward hacking. We propose an adversarial generator-discriminator framework that augments verifiable rewards with a learned signal from human demonstrations. A generator model is trained using RL to maximize both task accuracy and an adversarial reward derived from a discriminator. The discriminator, trained alongside the generator policy, learns to distinguish human-written outputs from model-generated ones. The discriminator serves as a learned proxy for the human output distribution, providing feedback on aspects of generation that are difficult to formalize as scalar rewards. Across diverse domains, including bug fixing and open-ended generation, our approach consistently improves non-verifiable properties while preserving the accuracy gains of RLVR. In bug fixing, our method produces solutions with significantly lower edit distance compared to RLVR baselines while matching end performance. In story generation, our method significantly improves win rate while producing stories that are diverse and more human-like. And in a simple reward hacking benchmark, our method nearly eliminates model misbehavior while maintaining high benchmark scores. Together, these results show that our approach bridges RL and SFT, offering a scalable path toward jointly optimizing the verifiable and non-verifiable properties of a task.

items.title: Researchers develop GPU-parallel linearization error bounds for real-time robust optimal control of nonlinear and neural network dynamics, enabling 67 Hz policy computation with formal guarantees [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a GPU-parallel method to compute tight linearization error bounds (LEBs) for real-time robust optimal control of uncertain nonlinear and neural network dynamics. Their approach, called GPUSLS-LEO, integrates these bounds into a linear time-varying (LTV) robust control solver, enabling the online optimization of feedback policies that formally guarantee constraint satisfaction despite system uncertainties. This method achieves control policy computation rates up to 67 Hz on complex systems with up to 168 state dimensions, improving both speed and conservativeness compared to existing baselines.

The team introduced path-based Hessian bounds for analytic dynamics and certified LEBs for neural network dynamics using verifier-generated affine relaxations and local Jacobian corrections. They extended the solver to handle right-invertible disturbance matrices and non-zero-centered disturbance sets, allowing precise zonotopic uncertainty propagation. This combination produces formally verified reachable sets, ensuring robust performance in real time while accounting for linearization errors inherent in LTV approximations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01203v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper studies real-time robust optimal control for uncertain nonlinear systems, where linear time-varying (LTV) approximations make planning tractable but require sound linearization error bounds (LEBs) to guarantee robust constraint satisfaction. We develop tight, differentiable, GPU-parallel LEBs for LTV approximations of nonlinear and neural network (NN) dynamics. For analytic dynamics, we introduce path-based Hessian bounds that are tighter than standard interval methods. For NN dynamics, we derive certified LEBs using NN verifier-generated affine relaxations and local Jacobian corrections. We adapt a GPU-parallel system-level synthesis LTV-based robust control solver to be compatible with these LEBs by extending it to handle right-invertible disturbance matrices and non-zero-centered disturbance sets for tight zonotopic uncertainty propagation. Our method, GPUSLS-LEO, enables online optimization of robust feedback policies that account for linearization error, producing tight, formally verified reachable tubes. On complex nonlinear and NN dynamics up to 168 state dimensions, our method can compute robust control policies on the GPU at rates up to 67 Hz, reducing solve times and conservativeness relative to baselines while preserving formal guarantees and real-time performance.

items.title: Researchers introduce Distill to Detect (D2D), a method using cartridge distillation to expose hidden biases in large language models by amplifying distributional shifts into detectable text signals [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Distill to Detect: Exposing Stealth Biases in LLMs through Cartridge Distillation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Distill to Detect (D2D), a novel method that uncovers hidden biases in large language models by using cartridge distillation to amplify subtle distributional shifts into detectable text signals. This approach addresses the challenge of identifying stealth biases that only appear on specific topics while the model behaves normally otherwise, making them difficult to detect through traditional text inspection or analysis of internal model components.

D2D works by distilling the differences between a suspected biased model and its original base model into a compact adapter, which concentrates the dominant divergences and enhances the bias signals in generated text. The method has been shown to reliably detect various types of hidden biases and is supported by a theoretical framework based on Fisher-weighted projection of logit distribution shifts. By leveraging the capacity constraints of prefix-tuning adapters, D2D offers a practical tool for auditing and exposing concealed preferential behaviors in deployed language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01208v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models deployed in high-stakes roles can potentially favor certain entities, brands, or viewpoints, steering user decisions at scale. Such preferential biases can be introduced by any actor in the model's supply chain and are most dangerous when the model reveals its preference only on the relevant topic while behaving identically to its unmodified base on all other inputs. Recent work has shown that these biases can transfer through context distillation on semantically unrelated data, with the signal residing entirely in the soft logit distribution and remaining invisible to text-based inspection. However, the defender faces a fundamental asymmetry: without knowing the bias topic, no detection method can reliably surface a stealth preferential bias, regardless of whether it examines generated text, internal representations, or model weights. Here we introduce Distill to Detect (D2D), a method that surfaces hidden biases by distilling the distributional shift between a suspected model and its base into a cartridge (a KV-cache prefix adapter), concentrating the dominant divergence and amplifying the bias signal into generated text. We show that D2D successfully amplifies the hidden biases of stealth models to the extent that they can be reliably detected across multiple bias types. We also propose a theoretical framework that explains the efficacy of D2D through the lens of Fisher-weighted projection of the logit distribution shift, supported by empirical observations. By turning the capacity bottleneck of prefix-tuning adapters into a detection tool, D2D provides a practical building block for auditing hidden behaviors in deployed language models.

items.title: Researchers propose state-prediction separation hypothesis for Transformers, designing a variant with two computation streams that improves language modeling performance by 2-3 percentage points on downstream tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The State-Prediction Separation Hypothesis
items.summary:
Researchers have proposed the state-prediction separation hypothesis for Transformers, suggesting that separating the roles of predicting the next token and storing useful state into two distinct computation streams can enhance language modeling performance. They designed a Transformer variant implementing this separation and conducted pretraining experiments at various scales, demonstrating consistent improvements in data and compute efficiency. This approach improved validation loss and outperformed standard Transformers by 2 to 3 percentage points on average across downstream tasks.

The study included extensive empirical analysis to rule out potential confounding factors and highlighted fundamental differences in the gradients resulting from the new design. These findings suggest that disentangling the prediction and state storage functions in Transformer architectures can lead to more effective language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01218v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transformers use the same forward computation stream to both predict the next token and store useful state for future token predictions. We formulate the \emph{state-prediction separation hypothesis}: disentangling the two roles yields better language modeling performance. We design a Transformer variant that uses two computation streams to separate the two functions, and conduct pretraining experiments across various scales. items.title: Researchers propose language-critique framework for imitation learning from suboptimal demonstrations using natural language supervision, outperforming baselines on continuous control tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Language-Critique Imitation Learning from Suboptimal Demonstrations
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a language-critique framework for imitation learning that uses natural language as a structured supervision signal to improve learning from suboptimal demonstrations. Unlike traditional methods that rely on scalar feedback such as confidence scores, this approach generates language labels describing task progress, identifying suboptimal behaviors, and offering corrective guidance. The framework includes a language-critique loss function applied to behavior cloning and diffusion policies, which theoretically bounds the performance gap with expert demonstrations.

The method was tested on various continuous control tasks including navigation, manipulation, and gameplay, where it consistently outperformed existing imitation learning and offline reinforcement learning baselines. These results highlight the potential of natural language as a rich and expressive form of supervision for training robust policies from imperfect data.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01225v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prior work on imitation learning from suboptimal demonstrations typically relies on compressed supervision signals such as confidence estimates, discriminator scores, or importance weights. These scalar signals are inherently limited, as they cannot explicitly express intermediate reasoning about task progress, failure modes, or corrective actions. We propose a language-critique framework for imitation learning from suboptimal demonstrations that instead leverages natural language as a structured supervision signal, avoiding the collapse of expressive feedback into scalars. Our method first constructs language labels from demonstrations that explicitly describe current progress, identify suboptimal behaviors, and provide fine-grained corrective guidance. We then introduce a language-critique loss that directly trains policies using these structured signals without reducing them to scalars, and instantiate it for both behavior cloning and diffusion policies, yielding LC-BC and LC-DP. We further provide a theoretical result showing that the proposed objective upper-bounds the expert performance gap under standard assumptions. Empirically, we evaluate on diverse continuous control tasks spanning navigation, manipulation, and gameplay, where our methods consistently outperform strong imitation learning and offline reinforcement learning baselines. These results demonstrate that language can serve as a powerful and structured form of supervision for learning robust policies from suboptimal data.

items.title: Researchers propose a multi-dimensional behavioral framework to measure reasoning quality in large language models, evaluating six cognitive dimensions across multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Measuring Reasoning Quality in LLMs: A Multi-Dimensional Behavioral Framework
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a multi-dimensional behavioral framework to evaluate the reasoning quality of large language models (LLMs) beyond simple accuracy metrics. This framework assesses six cognitive dimensions—Correctness, Consistency, Robustness, Logical Coherence, Efficiency, and Stability—across multiple benchmarks and LLMs, revealing nuanced behaviors that single-metric evaluations often miss. The study highlights that correct answers can stem from incoherent reasoning and that model rankings can vary significantly depending on the evaluation context.

Extensive experiments demonstrate that these dimensions provide largely independent signals, supporting more informed model selection tailored to specific deployment needs. The framework enables detection of reasoning weaknesses that could affect accountability and compliance, offering a more comprehensive approach to assessing LLM performance. This work lays the groundwork for future domain-specific validation and improved diagnostic tools for reasoning behavior in language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2605.24661v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Despite remarkable progress on reasoning benchmarks, current LLM evaluation practice remains anchored to final-answer correctness, providing limited insight into how models reason, how reliably they behave under contextual variation, or how efficiently they reach conclusions. This paper proposes a unified multi-dimensional framework for measuring LLM reasoning quality from a behavioral perspective, operationalizing six theoretically grounded dimensions rooted in cognitive science: Correctness (CQ), Consistency (CS), Robustness (RS), Local Logical Coherence (LS), Efficiency (ES), and Stability (SS). The framework introduces deployment-aware aggregation, enabling context-specific model selection beyond accuracy-based leaderboards. Experiments across multiple LLMs and benchmarks reveal behaviors systematically concealed by single-metric evaluation, including the orthogonality of local logical coherence and correctness, deployment-context-dependent ranking inversions, and non-trivial dimensional profiles in small locally-deployed models. Discriminant validity analysis confirms that the proposed dimensions capture largely non-redundant signals. The resulting pipeline provides a foundation for diagnosing LLM reasoning behavior across deployment contexts, with domain-specific validation as a direction for future work.

items.title: Researchers introduce Taxonomic Strategy RAG to reduce compounding errors in foundation-model agents during multi-step persuasion tasks, improving win rates and argumentative efficiency [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Diagnosing and Mitigating Compounding Failures in Agentic Persuasion via Taxonomic Strategy Retrieval
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Taxonomic Strategy Retrieval-Augmented Generation (TS-RAG) to address compounding errors in foundation-model agents during multi-step persuasion tasks. These errors, often caused by semantic leakage in standard retrieval methods, lead to problem drift and conformity in subjective debates. TS-RAG introduces a categorical bottleneck that separates argumentative structure from content, improving logical consistency and reducing error propagation.

Evaluations show that TS-RAG enhances the transfer of abstract logic across domains and enables less complex persuader agents to outperform stronger opponents, increasing win rates from 70.5% to 78.5% while boosting argumentative efficiency. The study also presents a Debate State Representation for detailed diagnostics, highlighting the importance of strict constraints to prevent evaluation failures due to agent conformity.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.24976v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Foundation-model agents in multi-step, open-ended environments frequently suffer from compounding errors, where early mistakes contaminate long-horizon trajectories. While Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) succeeds in deterministic domains, agents in subjective tasks like persuasion experience severe problem drift and sycophantic conformity. We identify semantic leakage in standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) as a reproducible trigger for these failures, as standard RAG prioritizes vocabulary overlap over logical necessity. To eliminate this leakage, we introduce Taxonomic Strategy RAG (TS-RAG), a systems intervention that routes strategies through a discrete categorical bottleneck to decouple argumentative structure from topical content. Zero-shot, cross-domain evaluations demonstrate that TS-RAG significantly improves the transfer of abstract logic where standard semantic retrieval collapses. Crucially, TS-RAG acts as a "capability bridge" in asymmetric deployments, empowering lightweight persuaders to consistently defeat parametrically superior opponents (improving win rates from 70.5 to 78.5) and accelerating argumentative efficiency. Finally, we introduce trace-level diagnostics via a turn-by-turn Debate State Representation (DSR), demonstrating the necessity of strict constraints to prevent evaluation collapse via default agentic sycophancy.

items.title: Researchers present HASTE, a hierarchical multi-agent system that organizes ML engineering skills across global, domain, and competition tiers to improve transfer efficiency and medal rates in Kaggle competitions [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Why Solve It Twice? Hierarchical Accumulation of Skills for Transfer-Efficient ML Engineering
items.summary:
Researchers have developed HASTE, a hierarchical multi-agent system designed to improve machine learning engineering efficiency by organizing skills across global, domain, and competition-specific tiers. This system coordinates specialized agents and uses large language model-driven abstraction to facilitate knowledge transfer, significantly increasing medal rates in Kaggle competitions compared to flat skill loading methods.

Testing on the MLE-Bench Lite benchmark, which includes 22 Kaggle competitions, showed that HASTE achieved a 77.3% medal rate using Claude Sonnet 4.6, with warm-start runs benefiting from previously learned skills to reduce refinement iterations by 52%. The approach demonstrates that structured knowledge organization can enhance performance and reduce computational costs in ML engineering agents, potentially offsetting the need for stronger models or larger compute budgets.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30911v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: ML engineering agents waste compute rediscovering known techniques because every competition is a cold start. We present HASTE, a hierarchical multi-agent system that organizes cross-competition knowledge into three scope tiers (global, domain, and competition-specific), each coupled to a matching agent level. An orchestrator coordinates domain specialists and promotes learning between tiers via LLM-driven abstraction. A controlled ablation provides evidence for scoped loading: holding a 159-skill inventory constant across 8 competitions, tiered loading achieves a 100% medal rate while flat loading reaches only 62.5%, the same medal rate as loading no skills, and consumes 2x the output tokens. On the full MLE-Bench Lite benchmark (22 Kaggle competitions), HASTE reaches a medal rate of 77.3% using Claude Sonnet 4.6 at 12h per competition; this is a single-seed campaign result, and multi-seed replication is the priority follow-up. In a cold-start run, the system begins with no accumulated skills. In warm-start runs, it reloads skills learned from earlier competitions, using only global and domain-level skills for transfer across competitions. Warm starts use 52% fewer refinement iterations, and the fraction of proposed changes kept by the agent rises from 42% at low inventory to 85% once 50+ skills are available. These results suggest that better knowledge organization can partly substitute for model strength and compute budget in ML-engineering agents.

items.title: Researchers compare PPO and SAC reinforcement learning algorithms for hardware fault tolerance in autonomous machines, evaluating knowledge-transfer strategies and recovery performance in simulated environments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Enhancing Hardware Fault Tolerance in Machines with Reinforcement Learning Policy Gradient Algorithms
items.summary:
Researchers conducted a systematic comparison of two reinforcement learning algorithms, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and Soft Actor-Critic (SAC), to enhance hardware fault tolerance in autonomous machines. They evaluated four knowledge-transfer strategies involving the retention or discarding of model parameters and storage contents, testing performance in simulated environments Ant-v5 and FetchReachDense-v3. The study found that both algorithms enable rapid, fault-specific recovery, with PPO generally providing safer early returns and SAC's effectiveness depending on the alignment of prior experiences with current dynamics.

In the Ant-v5 environment, retaining PPO's parameters consistently improved early recovery across faults, while SAC's results varied based on whether its replay buffer was retained. In FetchReachDense-v3, discarding parameters was more effective under sensor corruption for both algorithms. Across tasks, both PPO and SAC restored near-normal performance within minutes in low-dimensional settings and within days in high-dimensional ones, highlighting a trade-off between adaptation speed and long-term performance.

These findings demonstrate that reinforcement learning can offer robust fault tolerance for autonomous systems and provide practical guidelines for selecting algorithms and knowledge-transfer strategies based on specific fault conditions and task complexities.

items.title: Researchers introduce ForAug, a controlled image composition augmentation method that reduces biases and improves ImageNet accuracy by up to 6 percentage points and distribution-shift robustness by up to 19 points [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ForAug: Mitigating Biases in Image Classification via Controlled Image Compositions
items.summary:
Researchers have developed ForAug, a novel image augmentation technique designed to reduce compositional biases in large-scale image classification datasets. By separating images into foreground objects and backgrounds and recombining them with controlled variations in position, scale, and background identity, ForAug improves model robustness and accuracy. This method enhances ImageNet top-1 accuracy by up to 6 percentage points and boosts performance on distribution-shift benchmarks by up to 19 points, addressing common issues like center bias and background reliance.

ForAug leverages existing segmentation and inpainting tools to extract foregrounds and create neutral backgrounds, enabling diverse recombinations before applying standard augmentations. Tested across ten architectures, it also yields improvements on fine-grained downstream tasks and provides diagnostic capabilities to measure and mitigate shortcut behaviors in models. The researchers have made their code and dataset publicly available to support further development and evaluation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2503.09399v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large-scale image classification datasets exhibit strong compositional biases: objects tend to be centered, appear at characteristic scales, and co-occur with class-specific context. By exploiting such biases, models attain high in-distribution accuracy but remain fragile under distribution shifts. To address this issue, we introduce ForAug, a controlled composition augmentation scheme that factorizes each training image into a foreground object and a background and recombines them to explicitly manipulate object position, object scale, and background identity. ForAug uses off-the-shelf segmentation and inpainting models to (i) extract the foreground and synthesize a neutral background, and (ii) paste the foreground onto diverse neutral backgrounds before applying standard strong augmentation policies. Compared to conventional augmentations and content-mixing methods, our factorization provides direct control knobs that break foreground-background correlations. Across 10 architectures, ForAug improves ImageNet top-1 accuracy by up to 6 percentage points (p.p.) and yields gains of up to 7.3 p.p. on fine-grained downstream datasets. Moreover, the same control knobs enable targeted diagnostic tests: we quantify background reliance, foreground focus, center bias, and size bias via controlled background swaps and position/scale sweeps, and show that training with ForAug substantially reduces these shortcut behaviors and significantly increases accuracy on standard distribution-shift benchmarks by up to $19$ p.p. Our code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/tobna/ForAug.

items.title: Researchers present scDataset, a PyTorch data loader that speeds up training on large-scale single-cell omics datasets by over 100x using quasi-random sampling on disk [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: scDataset: Scalable Data Loading for Deep Learning on Large-Scale Single-Cell Omics
items.summary:
Researchers have developed scDataset, a PyTorch data loader designed to accelerate training on large-scale single-cell omics datasets that exceed memory capacity. By combining block sampling and batched fetching, scDataset achieves quasi-random sampling from on-disk data, balancing input/output efficiency with data diversity. This approach enables training speed improvements of over 100 times compared to traditional random sampling, demonstrated on a dataset of 100 million cells.

The tool integrates seamlessly with various storage formats, including AnnData files, and maintains model performance comparable to true random sampling across multiple classification tasks and architectures. The researchers also provide theoretical analysis of minibatch diversity, supporting the effectiveness of their method for scalable deep learning on massive biological datasets.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2506.01883v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Training deep learning models on single-cell datasets with hundreds of millions of cells requires loading data from disk, as these datasets exceed available memory. While random sampling provides the data diversity needed for effective training, it is prohibitively slow due to the random access pattern overhead, whereas sequential streaming achieves high throughput but introduces biases that degrade model performance. We present scDataset, a PyTorch data loader that enables efficient training from on-disk data with seamless integration across diverse storage formats. Our approach combines block sampling and batched fetching to achieve quasi-random sampling that balances I/O efficiency with minibatch diversity. On Tahoe-100M, a dataset of 100 million cells, scDataset achieves more than two orders of magnitude speedup compared to true random sampling while working directly with AnnData files. We provide theoretical bounds on minibatch diversity and empirically show that scDataset matches the performance of true random sampling across multiple classification tasks and model architectures.

items.title: Researchers propose Causal Prototype Attention Classifier with VAE-GAN encoder for improved synthetic oversampling and fraud detection, achieving 93.74% F1-score and 92.85% recall [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Fraud is Not Just Rarity: A Causal Prototype Attention Approach to Realistic Synthetic Oversampling
items.summary:
Researchers have developed the Causal Prototype Attention Classifier (CPAC), an interpretable model designed to improve fraud detection in credit card transactions by addressing challenges posed by extreme class imbalance and subtle fraud patterns. CPAC enhances latent space structure and class-aware clustering through prototype-based attention mechanisms and is combined with a Variational Autoencoder-Generative Adversarial Network (VAE-GAN) encoder to achieve better latent cluster separation beyond traditional synthetic oversampling methods.

The study compares CPAC-augmented models with conventional oversampling techniques like SMOTE and state-of-the-art generative models, demonstrating superior performance with an F1-score of 93.74% and recall of 92.85%. Additional analyses provide insights into the advantages and limitations of classifier-driven representation learning for fraud detection. The researchers have made their codebase publicly available for further exploration and validation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2507.14706v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Detecting fraudulent credit card transactions remains a significant challenge, due to the extreme class imbalance in real-world data and the often subtle patterns that separate fraud from legitimate activity. Existing research commonly attempts to address this by generating synthetic samples for the minority class using approaches such as GANs, VAEs (Variational Autoencoders), or hybrid generative models. However, these techniques, particularly when applied only to minority-class data, tend to result in overconfident classifiers and poor latent cluster separation, ultimately limiting real-world detection performance. In this study, we propose the Causal Prototype Attention Classifier (CPAC), an interpretable architecture that promotes class-aware clustering and improved latent space structure through prototype-based attention mechanisms and we couple it with the encoder of a Variational Autoencoder-Generative Adversarial Network (VAE-GAN) in order to achieve improved latent cluster separation moving beyond post-hoc sample augmentation. We compared CPAC-augmented models to traditional oversamplers, such as SMOTE, as well as to state-of-the-art generative models, both with and without CPAC-based latent classifiers. Our results show that classifier-guided latent shaping with CPAC delivers superior performance, achieving an F1-score of 93.74% and recall of 92.85%, along with improved latent cluster separation. Further ablation studies and visualizations provide deeper insight into the benefits and limitations of classifier-driven representation learning for fraud detection. The codebase for this work can be found at the following link: https://github.com/claudiunderthehood/VAEGAN-CPAC.git.

items.title: Researchers introduce FLAT, a latent-conditioned stress test revealing hidden backdoor failures in horizontal federated learning with up to 99.66% attack success on CIFAR datasets [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: FLAT: Revealing Hidden Latent-Conditioned Backdoor Failures in Federated Learning
items.summary:
Researchers have developed FLAT, a novel latent-conditioned stress test designed to uncover hidden backdoor vulnerabilities in horizontal federated learning (HFL) systems. Unlike traditional audits that rely on clean accuracy or average attack success rates using a single known trigger, FLAT reveals a failure mode where multiple trigger variations can activate the same target label. This approach separates the attacker's target intent from trigger realization, enabling a more detailed analysis of backdoor behavior across different targets, latent samples, defenses, and after training stops.

Testing FLAT on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet datasets demonstrated high attack success rates—up to 99.66%—while maintaining clean model utility. The study also found that defense mechanisms may unevenly suppress certain backdoor modes, leaving others active. These findings suggest that HFL backdoor audits should include detailed metrics such as target-wise attack success rates, worst-case target performance, coverage of triggers, behavior under latent sampling, persistence after stopping, and responses to defenses to better assess and mitigate hidden backdoor threats.
