items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00155v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study runtime human oversight of an AI agent when private information runs in both directions: the human privately knows her reward function, while the AI privately knows the quality of the action it proposes. This is the kind of asymmetry that arises naturally when an autonomous robot or software agent has inspected a situation its human supervisor cannot directly assess. Building on Cooperative Inverse Reinforcement Learning (CIRL) and the Oversight Game, we introduce a contextual-bandit team game with two-sided asymmetric information and a play/ask/trust/oversee interface. The bandit structure removes physical state transitions and thereby yields exact one-shot characterizations that would remain conjectural in the full POMDP setting, though the common belief remains a dynamically controlled state across rounds. We give two one-shot characterizations, a team optimum and a behaviorally natural myopic rule, whose gap is a slab of avoidable harm: a region in which the AI privately knows the proposed action is harmful and shutdown would help, yet a myopic human, trusting her prior, declines to oversee. We show this gap is the price of non-credible oversight communication, and give a partial analysis of how it resolves dynamically over repeated rounds through passive learning and active signaling with a one-period-lagged oversight response.

items.title: Study introduces Epistemic AI Literacy framework to analyze student-GenAI co-programming interactions, finding 78.8% rely on non-mastery aims and unreliable epistemic strategies [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Constructing Epistemic AI Literacy: Detecting Epistemic Aims and Processes in Student-AI Co-Programming
items.summary:
A new study introduces the Epistemic AI Literacy (EAIL) framework to analyze how students interact with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) during co-programming tasks. The research examines students' epistemic aims and processes, such as query construction, output evaluation, and problem-solving regulation, revealing that 78.8% of interactions rely on non-mastery-oriented aims and less reliable strategies like outsourcing and verification-seeking. Only 11.1% of interactions demonstrated high epistemic engagement, combining mastery-oriented aims with advanced strategies like epistemic justification.

Using a large dataset of human-AI co-programming dialogues, the study operationalizes dimensions of epistemic aims and processes based on the AIR framework, highlighting the dynamic nature of AI literacy as an epistemic phenomenon emerging through human-AI interaction. The findings suggest a widespread lack of effective epistemic engagement among students when working with GenAI, underscoring the need for educational approaches that foster more reliable and mastery-focused epistemic strategies in AI-supported learning environments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00211v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Epistemic thinking plays a central role in students' learning processes when applying generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), particularly in programming contexts where learners must construct queries, evaluate and validate AI-generated outputs, and regulate problem-solving strategies. This study introduces the conceptual framework of Epistemic AI Literacy (EAIL), reframing AI literacy as a process-oriented epistemic phenomenon that emerges through dynamic human-AI interactions across different domains. Drawing on the AIR (epistemic aims, ideals and reliable epistemic processes) framework, this study examines how epistemic aims and epistemic processes are enacted in GenAI-supported co-programming activities and explores scalable approaches for operationalizing these constructs in interaction data. Using a large dialogue dataset of human-AI co-programming, this study identifies observable dimensions of epistemic aims (i.e., mastery-oriented aims) and epistemic processes (i.e., outsourcing, explanation seeking, verification seeking, prompt monitoring, and epistemic justification). The results reveal a prevalent lack of EAIL, with 78.8% of student-GenAI interactions relying on non-mastery-oriented aims and less reliable epistemic strategies like outsourcing and verification-seeking. Conversely, only 11.1% of interactions showed high epistemic engagement, where mastery-oriented aims were coupled with advanced epistemic strategies like epistemic justification in a more reliable epistemic process.

items.title: Researchers find memory architecture influences language emergence in LLM agents more than channel capacity, with persistent notebooks improving coordination in signaling games [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: From Signals to Structure: How Memory Architecture Drives Language Emergence in LLM Agents
items.summary:
Researchers investigated how two agents develop a shared language from scratch using Lewis signaling games, focusing on the impact of memory architecture versus channel capacity in large language model (LLM) agents. Their study of five memory architectures revealed that memory design plays a more critical role than channel capacity in achieving reliable coordination. Agents equipped with a persistent private notebook, which externalizes learned conventions, outperformed stateless agents by maintaining stable communication even as vocabulary size increased, reaching a coordination reliability of approximately 0.867 at higher channel capacities.

The study found that stateless agents performed best at moderate channel capacities but deteriorated as the vocabulary expanded beyond what their limited context windows could handle. Contrary to predictions based on information bottleneck theory, which suggested an optimal channel capacity matching the number of objects, the researchers observed that this bottleneck point was a vulnerability, and having surplus capacity generally improved performance. Their findings emphasize that both memory architecture and channel capacity must be considered together to understand how stable communication systems and languages emerge from interaction history.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00233v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How do two agents invent a shared language from scratch? In a Lewis signaling game, a sender and receiver must coordinate on a code using only their interaction history. We study five memory architectures across varying channel configurations with LLM agents and find that memory architecture matters more than channel capacity. Agents with a persistent private notebook benefit from surplus channel capacity and avoid the high-capacity collapse seen in stateless agents, achieving the most reliable coordination ($0.867 \pm 0.023$ at capacity = 25). Stateless agents peak at moderate capacity and then degrade as the vocabulary grows beyond what a rolling context window can track The notebook externalizes learned conventions, freeing agents from having to re-derive codes each round. An information bottleneck-inspired argument predicts an optimal capacity equal to the number of objects. Instead, the bottleneck (capacity = 8) proves to be a fragility point, and surplus capacity is generally better. We show that channel capacity alone cannot predict coordination; memory architecture determines whether agents turn interaction history into stable conventions, and both dimensions are needed to understand how signals become language.

items.title: Researchers introduce Mnemosyne, an open-source runtime implementing Agentic Transaction Processing to validate and repair AI-generated workflows with safety guarantees and under 6% overhead [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Mnemosyne: Agentic Transaction Processing for Validating and Repairing AI-generated Workflows
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Mnemosyne, an open-source runtime that implements Agentic Transaction Processing (ATP) to validate and repair AI-generated workflows with safety guarantees and minimal overhead. ATP treats AI-generated actions as untrusted proposals that must pass deterministic checks against a defined constraint set before being committed, ensuring correctness regardless of the proposing agent's reliability. Mnemosyne features an append-only transition log, state projection, dependency-safe compensation, and active commitment records, and it enforces four key safety properties along with a bounded reactive repair protocol.

The system was tested against nine falsification scenarios, successfully rejecting invalid actions while admitting valid ones, with less than 6% overhead for projection and validation. Its localized repair protocol significantly reduces the number of operations needed for corrections compared to global recomputation. Mnemosyne is available as an open-source project, providing a practical tool for enhancing the reliability and safety of AI-generated workflows.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00269v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLMs, solvers, and agent teams increasingly generate workflow actions, repairs, and plans, but a generated action may be syntactically valid yet stale, infeasible, conflicting, or destructive of the evidence that triggered a repair. We introduce Agentic Transaction Processing (ATP), a transaction model that treats generated actions as untrusted proposals until they pass deterministic admission under a declared, executable constraint set C. The principle is two-sided: a proposal is not truth, and no proposal foresees every disruption: anything may propose, but only the runtime admits and commits, and when an unforeseen disruption strikes it repairs reactively within bounds rather than trusting a fresh proposal. Relative to C, committed-state correctness becomes independent of the competence, honesty, or learning of the proposing layer. We realize ATP in Mnemosyne, a runtime with an append-only transition log, effective-state projection, dependency-safe compensation, and active commitment records, and prove four safety properties relative to C (authority separation, serial-equivalent generative admission, evidence-preserving repair, and obligation containment) together with a bounded-reactive-repair guarantee for its localized repair protocol (LCRP). A reproducible artifact rejects the targeted violations across nine falsification tests while still admitting valid work, at under 6% projection-and-validation overhead, and bounded local repair edits an order of magnitude fewer operations than global recompute. Mnemosyne is open source: https://github.com/eyuchang/Mnemosyne/tree/arxiv-atp-rq1-rq9b-r8-v2.

items.title: Researchers develop gear-based managed autonomy system for single- and multi-agent cyber-physical systems, achieving 99.6% anomaly detection and formal safety certification in robotic assembly tests [ ~ ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: Managed Autonomy at Runtime: Gear-Based Safety and Governance for Single- and Multi-Agent Cyber-Physical Systems
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a gear-based managed autonomy system called \system{} that enhances safety and governance for both single- and multi-agent cyber-physical systems. This discrete-time control system integrates five execution gears with utility-gated dispatch and event-driven fallback to address common failure modes such as safety violations, behavioral instability, and error state continuity loss. The system demonstrates monotonic stability and execution safety for single agents and provides distributed safety guarantees, including zero collisions, for multi-agent setups.

The approach applies the \smart{} managed-autonomy lifecycle to map runtime evidence into governance states and uses consensus gating, swarm-level analysis, and per-agent gear authority to maintain stability. Evaluated on a three-agent UR5 robotic assembly cell with fault data from the NIST robot arm accuracy dataset, the system achieved a 99.6% anomaly detection rate, significantly outperforming the single-agent baseline, and reduced detection latency by 3.5 times. It also provides a formal safety certificate for the physical workspace, separating action control from autonomy governance through its execution gears.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00334v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous agents, whether LLM-driven software agents or robotic physical agents, face a common class of failure modes when operating without continuous human oversight: safety violations from unverified actions, behavioral instability from unconstrained loops, and continuity loss from unhandled error states. We develop \system{}, a discrete-time control system that combines five execution gears (\Gobs{}, \Gsug{}, \Gplan{}, \Gexec{}, \Gint{}) with utility-gated dispatch and event-driven fallback. For the single-agent case, we prove monotonic stability, execution safety, eventual stabilization, fallback completeness, and equivalence to a gear-constrained Markov decision process. For multi-agent cyber-physical systems (CPS), we apply the established \smart{} managed-autonomy lifecycle and map runtime evidence into its four governance states (\Stable{}/\Meta{}/\Assisted{}/\Regulated{}). Consensus gating, swarm-level Lyapunov analysis, per-agent gear authority, and rendezvous control provide distributed safety and stability guarantees, including zero collision under the stated assumptions. We evaluate the resulting runtime on a three-agent UR5 robotic assembly cell using fault magnitudes calibrated from the NIST \emph{Degradation Measurement of Robot Arm Position Accuracy} dataset across 10,000 Monte Carlo episodes. It achieves a 99.6\% anomaly detection rate versus 2.1\% for the single-agent baseline, reduces detection latency by $3.5\times$, and supplies a formal physical-workspace safety certificate. The execution gears act as micro-level permissions beneath the \smart{} runtime governance states, separating action control from autonomy governance.

items.title: Researchers propose SPIRE framework to learn latent design intents for personalized slide generation via structural denoising and multi-agent reinforcement learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Personalization as Inverse Planning: Learning Latent Design Intents for Agentic Slide Generation via Structural Denoising
items.summary: Researchers have introduced SPIRE, a new framework designed to improve personalized slide generation by learning latent design intents through structural denoising and multi-agent reinforcement learning. This approach addresses the limitations of current AI methods that rely heavily on predefined templates or detailed user instructions, which often fail to capture fine-grained, page-level design preferences. SPIRE formulates slide personalization as an inverse planning problem and enables two agents to collaboratively refine slide designs without requiring knowledge of the specific tools used to create them.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00407v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Slide design requires personalizing both deck themes and page layouts. Yet, current AI agent-based methods struggle with fine-grained, page-level design. Solely relying on prespecified templates or user verbose instructions, they fail to capture latent design intents, leaving Page-level Slide Personalization (PSP) unresolved. To close this gap, this work formulates PSP as an inverse planning problem. We propose to learn a design intent without assuming any knowledge of the specific executing tools (e.g., PowerPoint, Beamer) being used. However, relinquishing control over these tools makes the problem intractable to optimize end-to-end. To overcome this, we propose SPIRE, a principled framework to solve PSP approximately. By intentionally corrupting the visual structures of clean slides, SPIRE creates a verifiable task to denoise the corruption, whereby two agents learn to collaboratively refine executable designs via reinforcement learning (RL). We present a proof that structural denoising is a consistent surrogate for PSP, and that the multi-agent formulation strictly reduces policy gradient variance in RL. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of SPIRE.

items.title: Researchers introduce PHREEQC-MCQ-200 benchmark with 200 questions to evaluate tool-augmented AI agents on aqueous-geochemistry simulations, revealing accuracy gains and regressions across model types [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: PHREEQC-MCQ-200: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Tool-Augmented Scientific Simulator Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have developed PHREEQC-MCQ-200, a benchmark consisting of 200 multiple-choice questions designed to evaluate AI agents augmented with scientific tools on aqueous-geochemistry simulations. The benchmark tests agents' abilities to create simulator inputs, run the PHREEQC software, analyze outputs, and provide accurate answers. Results show that access to the simulator generally improves accuracy across various AI models, but also reveals cases where tool use causes performance regressions that average accuracy metrics can obscure.

The study highlights the importance of how AI agents access and interpret simulator outputs, noting that interfaces like a table-of-contents can reduce computational costs and enhance accuracy for advanced models, while hindering mid-tier models that struggle with structured data. The researchers emphasize that evaluating scientific AI agents should go beyond overall accuracy to include detailed diagnostics such as item-level retention, sensitivity to output access methods, and points of failure in the computational process.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00436v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly connected to scientific software, yet it remains unclear when tool access makes scientific computation more reliable rather than merely more complex. We introduce PHREEQC-MCQ-200, a benchmark for evaluating tool-augmented agents on deterministic aqueous-geochemistry simulations. The benchmark contains 200 multiple-choice questions derived from 21 validated PHREEQC scenarios, requiring agents to construct simulator inputs, execute PHREEQC, inspect structured outputs, and commit to final answers. Across multiple frontier and mid-tier model families, simulator access substantially improves aggregate accuracy, confirming that grounded execution is necessary for many scientific-computation tasks. However, the gains are not monotonic: tool-augmented agents also lose items they answered correctly without tools, revealing regressions that average accuracy alone hides. We further show that output-access protocol matters. A table-of-contents interface can reduce token cost while preserving or improving accuracy for stronger models, but it degrades performance for mid-tier models that cannot reliably navigate structured simulator outputs. PHREEQC-MCQ-200 therefore frames scientific tool use as an end-to-end diagnostic problem rather than a simple tool-calling capability. We argue that evaluations of scientific agents should report not only accuracy, but also item-level retention, output-access sensitivity, trajectory failures, and where the computation chain breaks.

items.title: Researchers present Agri-SAGE, a simulation-grounded multi-agent LLM framework integrating APSIM biophysical simulation for context-aware agricultural advisory generation, outperforming static guidelines in a 10-year retrospective study [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Agri-SAGE: Simulation-Grounded Multi-Agent LLM for Context-Aware Agricultural Advisory Generation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Agri-SAGE, a novel framework that combines multi-agent large language models (LLMs) with APSIM biophysical simulation to generate context-aware agricultural advisories. This approach addresses the limitations of static agronomic guidelines, which lack responsiveness to in-season variability, and previous LLM-based systems that may produce recommendations lacking physiological validity. Agri-SAGE integrates retrieval-grounded reasoning with simulation to both generate and validate agronomic advice, improving decision-making in agriculture.

The framework was evaluated using three reasoning methods—Plan-and-Solve, Tree of Thoughts, and Reflexion—over a retrospective 10-year analysis. All methods outperformed traditional static Package-of-Practice baselines, with Tree of Thoughts achieving the highest peak yields. Reflexion offered similar agronomic results while reducing computational costs by utilizing cross-seasonal episodic memory, demonstrating efficient and effective advisory generation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00454v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agricultural advisory systems face a fundamental tension: static agronomic guidelines offer consistent, evidence-based recommendations, yet remain blind to in-season variability and dynamic uncertainties. Recent advisory systems powered by LLMs are liable for a different risk of generating recommendations that are agronomically credible but physiologically unconvincing. Agri-SAGE is a closed-loop framework designed to resolve the above two limitations by integrating retrieval-grounded multi-agent LLM reasoning with APSIM-based biophysical simulation, to generate and validate agronomic advisories. To assess this framework, we evaluate three reasoning approaches, namely Plan-and-Solve, Tree of Thoughts, and Reflexion, over a 10-year retrospective analysis. All three significantly outperform static PoP (Package-of-Practice) baselines, with Tree of Thoughts achieving impressive peak yields. At the same time, Reflexion achieves comparable agronomic outcomes at substantially lower computational cost by leveraging cross-seasonal episodic memory.

items.title: Researchers present MuSix, a multi-scale mixture of world models framework for embodied agents that improves reasoning and adaptation in evolving environments, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Multi-scale Mixture of World Models for Embodied Agents in Evolving Environments
items.summary:
Researchers have developed MuSix, a multi-scale mixture of world models framework designed for embodied agents operating in dynamic real-world environments. MuSix addresses challenges in multi-scale reasoning and knowledge adaptation by introducing a scale-aware routing mechanism and scale-dependent update policies, enabling agents to better handle situational novelty and varying rates of knowledge obsolescence. This approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in experiments on benchmarks such as EmbodiedBench and HAZARD.

MuSix employs a two-stage routing process inspired by Construal Level Theory, where a meta-router assigns weights over a continuous scale space based on experiential distance, followed by base routers selecting appropriate world models within the chosen scale. The framework also incorporates scale-dependent forgetting rates to allow rapid updating of low-scale knowledge while preserving high-scale abstractions, with gated inter-scale transfer ensuring coherence across the hierarchy.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00457v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Embodied agents operating in the real world require multi-scale reasoning and knowledge adaptation as conditions change. We identify two challenges in applying Mixture of Experts (MoE) to this setting: routing lacks an explicit notion of scale, preventing targeted updates at specific scales, and a uniform update policy cannot accommodate the different rates at which knowledge at each scale becomes outdated. We present MuSix, a framework that addresses both challenges through scale-aware world model mixture and evolution. A two-stage routing mechanism grounds scale selection in experiential distance, a measure of situational novelty inspired by Construal Level Theory: a meta-router first maps this quantity to a weight over continuous scale space, then per-scale base routers select world models within the identified scale. For adaptation, scale-dependent forgetting rates allow low-scale knowledge to refresh rapidly while high-scale abstractions persist, and gated inter-scale transfer maintains coherence across the hierarchy. Experiments on EmbodiedBench and HAZARD show that MuSix improves over state-of-the-art baselines on multi-scale reasoning and dynamic adaptation.

items.title: Researchers define AI-native games by runtime generative AI as core gameplay, analyze 53 examples, and propose a taxonomy and roadmap for design, evaluation, and safety [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AI Native Games: A Survey and Roadmap
items.summary:
Researchers have defined AI-native games as those in which runtime generative AI is essential to the core gameplay loop, meaning that removing or replacing the AI would fundamentally alter the game's play. They analyzed 53 publicly available AI-native games and prototypes, distinguishing these from AI-augmented games and other AI-assisted content by this criterion. The study introduces a dual-axis taxonomy categorizing games by player-facing type and the dominant AI mechanic that makes generative AI indispensable.

The analysis found that most AI-native games focus on language-driven designs such as narrative adventures and generative storytelling, while other categories like multi-agent simulation and generative construction are less common. The researchers emphasize that a key design challenge is maintaining stable gameplay despite the semantic openness of AI-generated content, relying on consistent goals, rules, and player agency. They conclude with a roadmap addressing controllable generation, AI mechanics, multimodal systems, evaluation, safety, and regulation in AI-native game design.

They analyzed 53 publicly available AI-native games and prototypes, distinguishing these from AI-augmented games and other AI-assisted content by this criterion. The study introduces a dual-axis taxonomy categorizing games by player-facing type and the dominant AI mechanic that makes generative AI indispensable.

The analysis found that most AI-native games focus on language-driven designs such as narrative adventures and generative storytelling, while other categories like multi-agent simulation and generative construction are less common. The researchers emphasize that a key design challenge is maintaining stable gameplay despite the semantic openness of AI-generated content, relying on consistent goals, rules, and player agency. They conclude with a roadmap addressing controllable generation, AI mechanics, multimodal systems, evaluation, safety, and regulation in AI-native game design.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00527v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative AI now enables games to produce dialogue, quests, characters, images, and worlds at runtime. Yet generation alone does not make a game AI-native, nor does it guarantee playability. This paper defines AI-native games by whether runtime generative AI is constitutive of the core loop: if the AI component were removed or trivially replaced, the central form of play would collapse or become fundamentally different. This counterfactual criterion separates AI-native games from AI-augmented games, boundary artifacts, chatbots, tavern-style role-play, procedural content generation, and AI-assisted production. Using this definition, we screen candidate artifacts and analyze 53 publicly available AI-native games and prototypes. We introduce a dual-axis G/N taxonomy: the G-axis captures player-facing game type, while the N-axis captures the dominant AI mechanic that makes generative AI indispensable to play. The corpus is concentrated around language-forward designs, especially narrative adventure, epistemic interaction, and generative narrative, while categories such as semantic adjudication, multi-agent simulation, generative construction, and relationship/companion play remain less represented. We argue that the central design problem is organizing semantic openness into stable gameplay. AI-native design depends on mechanical invariants: goals, rules, state, feedback, pacing, and player agency that make open-ended AI outputs interpretable and consequential. We conclude with a roadmap for controllable generation, AI-as-mechanic design, multimodal and multi-agent systems, inference economics, evaluation, safety, and regulation.

items.title: Researchers introduce HARC, a fine-tuning method coupling harmfulness and refusal directions in LLMs to improve safety alignment and robustness across multiple model families and scales [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: HARC: Coupling Harmfulness and Refusal Directions for Robust Safety Alignment
items.summary:
Researchers have developed HARC, a fine-tuning method designed to enhance the safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) by coupling harmfulness and refusal directions within the models. This approach addresses vulnerabilities that allow jailbreaks by targeting the internal representations of harmful content and refusal signals at both prompt and response token positions. HARC confines its intervention to the harmfulness-refusal subspace, preserving the model's overall capabilities while improving robustness against safety breaches.

The study reveals that jailbreak attacks manipulate either the refusal or harmfulness directions before token generation, with different attack types occupying distinct regions in this subspace. Notably, models can recognize harmful content during generation even if they fail to detect it at the prompt stage. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HARC outperforms six baseline safety methods across multiple model families and scales without requiring architecture-specific adjustments, achieving a strong balance between robustness, capability, and usability.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00572v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding how aligned LLMs internally represent safety is critical for diagnosing alignment vulnerabilities, as it explains why jailbreaks succeed and informs the design of robust alignment strategies. Prior work shows that aligned LLMs encode harmfulness and refusal as separable directions in the residual stream at prompt-side token positions. We show that jailbreaks succeed at prompt encoding by suppressing either the refusal or harmfulness direction before any token is generated, with distinct attack classes occupying separable regions of the harmfulness-refusal plane. Extending the analysis to response-token positions, we find that the model recognizes harmful content while it is generating that content, even when it failed to recognize the input as harmful at the prompt side. Motivated by our findings, we introduce HARC (Harmfulness-And-Refusal Coupling), a fine-tuning method that pairs the two directions across both prompt and response positions. Since the intervention is confined to the harmfulness-refusal subspace, it leaves the rest of the residual stream intact and does not degrade general capability or inflate over-refusal. Across extensive experiments, HARC achieves the strongest robustness-capability-usability trade-off among six baselines spanning the major training-time and inference-time safety methods. The harmfulness and refusal directions at prompt and response positions transfer across the five model families and two scales we tested without architecture-specific tuning.

items.title: Researchers introduce AGI Maze, a lightweight benchmark framework for testing world-modeling capabilities of language model agents in partially observable, stateful environments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AGI Maze as a Benchmark Framework for World-Modeling Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have developed AGI Maze, a lightweight benchmark framework designed to test the world-modeling capabilities of language model agents in environments that are partially observable and stateful. Unlike traditional large language models (LLMs) that predict the next token based on static context, AGI Maze challenges agents to build and use persistent representations of the environment through grid-based maze tasks with varying difficulty levels. Initial tests show that standard LLMs struggle to internally represent these mazes during inference, highlighting limitations in their reasoning abilities in dynamic settings.

The framework avoids high-dimensional sensory inputs and focuses on requiring agents to maintain memory and form structured hypotheses about hidden states. A baseline agent using message history as working memory showed some performance improvement but still failed to reliably solve even small mazes within a reasonable step budget. This suggests that current LLM architectures may need enhancements to effectively handle tasks involving persistent world state representation and reasoning in complex, partially observable environments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00627v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are powerful pattern-completion systems, but their default operating mode - predicting the next token from a static context - does not reliably produce persistent, manipulable representations of an external world. Many tasks that look like "reasoning" in text become substantially harder once the environment is partially observable, stateful, and requires memory and structured hypotheses about hidden state. AGI Maze is a lightweight framework for building such environments without requiring high-dimensional sensory inputs. It provides a family of grid-based maze tasks with a clean API and multiple difficulty regimes. The goal is to create benchmarks where agents must learn and use world state representations, not just infer a local rule over readily provided observations. We provide an initial evaluation of several vanilla LLMs on simple mazes showing that they fail to represent mazes internally at LLM inference time. We also introduce a baseline agent, which is allowed to use its message history as a working memory to construct descriptions of observations at agentic runtime. Although this can improve performance, it is still insufficient for an LLM agent to reliably solve even small mazes within a step budget that is more than enough for humans.

items.title: Researchers present Self-GC, a self-governing context system for long-horizon LLM agents that manages lifecycle of context objects and reduces input tokens by up to 20% in production [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Self-GC: Self-Governing Context for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Self-GC, a self-governing context system designed for long-horizon large language model (LLM) agents to manage the lifecycle of context objects more effectively. Unlike traditional methods that rely on heuristics or summaries to handle accumulated data such as tool results and user constraints, Self-GC treats these elements as indexed objects and uses a side-channel planner to optimize folding, masking, and pruning actions. This approach significantly reduces input tokens while preserving the integrity of future continuations.

In testing, Self-GC pruned nearly 44% of prefix tokens on a challenging dataset with minimal impact on subsequent outputs, outperforming heuristic baselines. In a larger production-derived suite, it achieved no-impact rates above 91%, compared to 77% to 87% for existing methods. Deployment in a production environment demonstrated daytime input token reductions of 10% to 15%, with peaks near 20%, highlighting the system's efficiency in runtime context management as opposed to post hoc text cleanup.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00692v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents accumulate tool results, files, plans, and user constraints that are too structured to be treated as a disposable text suffix. Current systems mostly rely on in-run heuristics such as chronological pruning and tool-output masking, or on final self-summary near a context limit. Heuristics are cheap but blind to future dependencies; summaries preserve narrative state but often hide exact evidence, locators, and editable artifacts. We present Self-GC, where GC denotes self-governing context while deliberately echoing garbage collection: the system does not merely reclaim unused tokens, but governs the lifecycle of agent context objects. Self-GC turns user turns, tool spans, and skill state into indexed objects; asks a side-channel planner to propose fold, mask, and prune actions; and lets the harness enforce recoverable sidecars, safe commit boundaries, and cache-aware commit. On a 33-session Hard Set, Self-GC prunes 43.95% of prefix tokens while leaving 84.85% of future continuations unaffected, compared with no-impact rates of 54.55% to 69.70% for heuristic baselines. On a 332-session production-derived suite, three planner backbones reach no-impact rates of 91.27% to 94.58%, while baselines remain at 77.71% to 87.46%. In production, an online account-level split reduces daytime average input tokens by 10% to 15%, with peak reductions near 20%. These results point to context management as runtime lifecycle control over indexed, recoverable objects rather than post hoc text cleanup.

items.title: Researchers present SEA architecture for self-evolving agents with anytime-valid certificates that confine self-modification and provide auditable guarantees on a frozen base model [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Self-Evolving Agents with Anytime-Valid Certificates
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced SEA, a novel architecture designed for self-evolving agents that addresses the challenge of self-modification in learning systems. SEA confines changes to a small steering adapter and a versioned harness around a frozen base model, allowing modifications only through an anytime-valid gate that issues auditable certificates within a fixed error budget. This approach ensures that self-modifications are controlled and verifiable, maintaining the integrity of the base model's behavior.

The architecture incorporates five loop controllers and verifier-in-the-loop mechanisms, such as best-of-N selection and self-repair, which provide dense, grader-free feedback derived solely from the task text. Evaluations on a 52-instance benchmark across four base models demonstrated that SEA improves performance by selecting among existing behaviors without regressions, with notable gains on strong base models. While results are based on single runs of costly evaluations, future work aims to address variability and optimize algorithm selection per task.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00871v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-evolving agents violate the assumption behind most learning-theoretic guarantees: the data, evaluator, components, and hypothesis space are produced by the policy being updated. We present \textbf{SEA}, an architecture that confines self-modification to a small steering adapter and a versioned harness around a \emph{frozen} base model and admits each modification only through an anytime-valid gate that emits an auditable certificate against a fixed error budget. Five loop controllers compose published guarantees; because such gates can only \emph{select} among behaviors the frozen base already produces, five verifier-in-the-loop mechanisms -- best-of-$N$, micro-step search, self-authored reproduction oracles, search-layer control, and self-repair -- supply the dense, grader-free signal the gates require, computed from the issue text alone. On a $52$-instance SWE-bench Verified subset across four base models, base capability is the dominant, confound-free effect, and on two strong base models a deliberate no-op-composite control isolates the suite's contribution at $+4$ and $+5$ (\textsc{Glm}~5.2 $24\to28$; \textsc{Gpt} $29\to34$, the $65\%$ best), with event logs confirming that its mechanisms fire and prevent regressions. Results are single-run on expensive evaluations; confirming run-to-run variance and adapting the per-task algorithm mix are future work.

items.title: Researchers show divergent AI performance metrics affect whether frontier capabilities concentrate among wealthy actors or spread through smaller models, influencing policy decisions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Two AI Metrics Diverged: Will it Make All the Difference?
items.summary:
Researchers have examined how different AI performance metrics influence whether advanced AI capabilities remain concentrated among wealthy developers or become accessible through smaller, less resource-intensive models. Their study shows that while some metrics indicate a narrowing performance gap between frontier and modest models, others reveal an ever-growing lead for frontier models. The distinction hinges on whether the metrics are bounded or unbounded, which affects how capabilities like software engineering or synthetic biology might spread or concentrate.

The team provides mathematical conditions to classify performance metrics and highlights that many commonly used bounded metrics have closely related unbounded counterparts. This distinction is crucial for policy decisions, as bounded metrics suggest capabilities will diffuse broadly, whereas unbounded metrics imply concentration among a few actors with substantial resources. Understanding which metric best captures a domain's capabilities is essential for shaping effective AI governance and access strategies.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00913v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As exponential compute scaling continues, will the capabilities of frontier AI models outstrip what is accessible to developers on a small fixed budget? Or will capabilities converge, with "meek models inheriting the earth"? Building on Gundlach et al. (2025b), we show that the answer depends on how we value and measure AI capabilities. We discuss conventional performance measures and show that, while validation loss shows a shrinking gap, on other metrics frontier models grow their lead forever. Conversely, if that capability is instead bounded, frontier-level capabilities proliferate through meek models into the hands of the many.

items.title: Researchers present Bayesian uncertainty propagation framework for Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipelines, evaluated on multi-hop question answering datasets StrategyQA and HotpotQA using GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4.1-Nano [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Bayesian Uncertainty Propagation for Agentic RAG Pipelines: A Proof-of-Concept Study on Multi-Hop Question Answering
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a Bayesian uncertainty propagation framework for Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems to estimate potential failures in multi-stage reasoning pipelines. This framework integrates uncertainty signals from planner, evaluator, and generator stages, which are combined through a Bayesian Network to assess system-level uncertainty and identify possible failure points. The approach was tested on multi-hop question answering datasets StrategyQA and HotpotQA using GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4.1-Nano models, demonstrating improved uncertainty estimation especially in HotpotQA where uncertainty accumulates across reasoning steps.

The evaluation employed metrics such as AUROC, AUARC, Expected Calibration Error, and Brier Score to measure discrimination, selective prediction, and calibration. Results indicated that Bayesian propagation effectively captures uncertainty in complex reasoning tasks, though limitations were noted in StrategyQA due to miscalibration and unreliable upstream signals. This study suggests that Bayesian uncertainty propagation is a promising preliminary method for monitoring Agentic RAG systems, with further validation needed in practical applications like Offshore Wind maintenance decision support.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00972v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Trustworthy deployment of Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems requires mechanisms for estimating when multi-stage reasoning pipelines may fail. Results show that Bayesian propagation is more effective on HotpotQA, where uncertainty accumulates across multi-hop reasoning stages, while StrategyQA exposes limitations caused by miscalibration and unreliable upstream signals. The study positions Bayesian uncertainty propagation as a promising but preliminary mechanism for monitoring Agentic RAG systems, with future validation required in industrial domains such as Offshore Wind (OSW) maintenance decision support.

items.title: Researchers release PedNStream, an open-source Python simulator for scalable macroscopic pedestrian network flow with built-in control interfaces and validated large-scale performance
items.originalTitle: PedNStream: Scalable Network Flow Simulation for Pedestrian Traffic Management
items.summary:
Researchers have developed PedNStream, an open-source Python simulator designed for scalable macroscopic pedestrian network flow. The tool is based on the Link Transmission Model and incorporates stochastic dynamics to capture variability in pedestrian movement. It features a utility-based route choice model and built-in interfaces for control interventions such as gating and route guidance, making it suitable for large-scale crowd management and feedback-based control scenarios.

The simulator was evaluated through synthetic scenarios that tested key pedestrian flow mechanisms like queue formation and congestion dissipation, as well as real-network experiments that confirmed its consistency with observed pedestrian counts. A closed-loop case study demonstrated its capability for controller integration, and runtime analysis showed its scalability, establishing PedNStream as an efficient and practical platform for pedestrian network simulation and control.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01021v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large-scale crowd management requires pedestrian simulations that are both computationally efficient and compatible with feedback-based control. However, most open-source tools are either microscopic or not designed for network-scale closed-loop evaluation. This paper presents PedNStream (Pedestrian Network Flow Simulation), an open-source, Python-native simulator for macroscopic pedestrian network loading based on the Link Transmission Model (LTM). The framework extends LTM-based pedestrian models by incorporating stochastic link dynamics that capture diffusion and activity-induced variability, and replaces dynamic user equilibrium route choice with a utility-based formulation suited to uncertain, intervention-driven settings. PedNStream is implemented as a modular framework with built-in controller interfaces for interventions such as gating, flow separation, and route guidance. We evaluate the framework in a staged manner. Synthetic scenarios verify key mechanisms, including queue formation, spillback, congestion dissipation, and adaptive rerouting. Real-network experiments assess large-scale behavior and consistency with observed pedestrian counts. A closed-loop case study demonstrates controller integration, and a runtime analysis quantifies scalability. These results establish PedNStream as an efficient and practical testbed for large-scale pedestrian network simulation and control.

items.title: Researchers present an automated multi-agent LLM pipeline that generates and verifies reaction classification rules, expanding taxonomy from 68 to 14,073 classes and classifying 97.7% of unseen reactions [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Agentic generation of verifiable rules for deterministic, self-expanding reaction classification
items.summary:
Researchers have developed an automated multi-agent system using large language models (LLMs) to classify chemical reactions and generate corresponding classification rules. Applied to 665,901 US patent reactions, this pipeline expanded a traditional reaction taxonomy from 68 to 14,073 classes without human intervention and achieved classification of 97.7% of unseen reactions, matching the performance of leading proprietary classifiers while providing finer chemical resolution.

The system operates through a verification loop that tests each generated rule against the reaction corpus, ensuring reliability. By combining this approach with a lightweight fingerprint classifier, the method adapts to new chemistries beyond its training data, creating a dynamic and self-expanding reactivity database. This work demonstrates a scalable route to transforming generative models into dependable symbolic systems for chemical synthesis planning.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01061v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computer-assisted synthesis planning breaks target molecules into accessible precursors using large libraries of reaction rules that assign each transformation a deterministic, interpretable label. But chemistry is long-tailed, making manual encoding intractable, and existing tools rely on fixed rulesets that cannot adapt to new chemistries. Here we present a fully automated pipeline in which a multi-agent framework of large language models (LLMs) classifies reactions and writes the rules themselves across 665,901 US patent reactions, generating each rule under a verification loop that tests it against the corpus. It expands a standard taxonomy from 68 to 14,073 classes without human curation. With a lightweight fingerprint classifier, it classifies 97.7\% of unseen reactions, matching a leading proprietary classifier while resolving chemistry more finely and extending on demand to chemistry outside its training distribution. The result is a living reactivity database and a general route to turning generative models into reliable, self-expanding symbolic systems.

items.title: Researchers formalize OpenAgent problem to study LLM agent generalization failures in dynamic tool use environments and propose Perturbation-Augmented Fine-Tuning to improve robustness [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Can Agents Generalize to the Open World? Unveiling the Fragility of Static Training in Tool Use
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced the OpenAgent problem to study the challenges Large Language Model (LLM) agents face when generalizing in dynamic, real-world environments involving tool use. They formalize this setting by characterizing distributional shifts across queries, actions, observations, and domains, and create a controlled sandbox environment to systematically analyze these shifts across four levels: Perception, Interaction, Reasoning, and Internalization. Their experiments reveal that agents trained with Supervised Fine-Tuning and Reinforcement Learning experience significant performance drops under such open environmental changes.

To address these generalization issues, the team proposes Perturbation-Augmented Fine-Tuning, a method that introduces controlled disturbances during training to improve agent robustness and adaptability. This approach aims to enhance the practical utility of LLM agents in realistic, evolving scenarios. The researchers plan to release their code publicly to support further development in this area.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01084v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While Large Language Model (LLM) agents demonstrate proficiency in static benchmarks, their deployment in real-world scenarios is hindered by the dynamic nature of user queries, tool sets, and interaction dynamics. To address this generalization gap, we formalize OpenAgent (Tool-Use Agent in Open-World), a problem setting characterized by distributional shifts across query, action, observation, and domain dimensions. To systematically diagnose its impact, we construct a controlled sandbox environment where we define fine-grained environmental shifts across a four-tier hierarchy, Perception, Interaction, Reasoning, and Internalization, and conduct a comprehensive series of experiments. Our analysis yields a series of key insights, demonstrating that agents trained via both Supervised Fine-Tuning(SFT) and Reinforcement Learning suffer from varying degrees of performance degradation when confronting open environmental shifts. Building on these insights, we propose Perturbation-Augmented Fine-Tuning, a disturbance-based intervention strategy for SFT that lays the foundation for enhancing agent robustness and utility in realistic environments. Our code will be released at: https://github. com/LAMDA-NeSy/OpenAgent.

items.title: Researchers demonstrate a two-step method using constraint programming and task status dependencies to optimize resource utilization in autonomous laboratories for metal-organic framework synthesis [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Optimal Resource Utilization for Autonomous Laboratory Orchestrators
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a two-step approach to optimize resource utilization in autonomous laboratories conducting metal-organic framework synthesis. The method first employs constraint programming to generate optimal schedules that minimize total experiment time while respecting hardware limitations and capacities. Then, a system of task status dependencies ensures the robust execution of these schedules, effectively managing multiple instruments with varying capacities and throughputs.

This approach addresses the challenge of planning and executing experimental tasks in real-world settings where hardware constraints complicate resource management. By integrating scheduling optimization with task dependency tracking, the system enhances the efficiency and reliability of autonomous laboratory operations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01188v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In autonomous laboratories, AI agents suggest the next batch of experiments to do. However, planning and executing those tasks taking full advantage of the available resources is a completely different question. This can be challenging when dealing with real-world hardware constraints, especially so when there are multiple instruments with different capacities and throughputs. Here we demonstrate a 2-step method to address resource utilization for our autonomous platform for metal-organic framework synthesis. First, we use constraint programming to find optimal schedules. This finds schedules that minimizes the total time while still satisfying the limitations and capacities of the hardware. Secondly, we use a system of status dependencies for each task, which allows for the robust execution of the optimal schedules.

items.title: AutoMem framework automates memory management as a trainable skill in LLMs, doubling to quadrupling performance on long-horizon tasks across three games with a 32B parameter model [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AutoMem: Automated Learning of Memory as a Cognitive Skill
items.summary:
Researchers have developed AutoMem, a framework that treats memory management in large language models (LLMs) as a trainable skill, significantly enhancing performance on long-horizon tasks. By integrating file-system operations as memory actions alongside task actions, the model autonomously manages its memory, improving both the structure supporting memory and the model's proficiency in using it. This approach doubled to quadrupled performance in three procedurally generated games using a 32-billion parameter model, achieving results comparable to leading systems like Claude Opus 4.5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro Thinking.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01224v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Memory expertise is a learned skill: knowing what to encode, when to retrieve, and how to organize knowledge--a capacity known in cognitive science as metamemory. We bring this perspective to LLMs by treating memory management as a trainable skill. We promote file-system operations to first-class memory actions alongside task actions, letting the model itself decide how to manage its memory. This memory skill improves along two axes: the structure that supports it (prompts, file schemas, action vocabulary), and the proficiency of the model exercising it. Both axes resist manual optimization: episodes in long-horizon tasks run for thousands of steps, and a single memory mistake can hide long before it surfaces, making human review of full trajectories impractical. We introduce AutoMem, a framework that automates both axes. In the first loop, a strong LLM reviews complete agent trajectories and iteratively revises the memory structure that shapes how the agent interacts with its memory files. In the second loop, the agent's own good memory decisions are identified from many episodes and used as training signal to sharpen the model's memory proficiency directly. Across three procedurally generated long-horizon games (Crafter, MiniHack, and NetHack), optimizing memory alone--without modifying the model's task-action behavior--improved the base agent's performance ~2x-4x, bringing a 32B open-weight model competitive with frontier systems such as Claude Opus 4.5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro Thinking. Our results show that memory management is an independently learnable skill, and a high-leverage objective yielding large gains on long-horizon tasks.

items.title: UltraFlux introduces data-model co-design for native 4K text-to-image generation across diverse aspect ratios, outperforming open-source baselines on fidelity and aesthetics [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: UltraFlux: Data-Model Co-Design for High-quality Native 4K Text-to-Image Generation across Diverse Aspect Ratios
items.summary:
UltraFlux is a new approach to text-to-image generation that achieves high-quality native 4K resolution across various aspect ratios by addressing interconnected challenges in positional encoding, VAE compression, and optimization. Developed using a data-model co-design strategy, UltraFlux is trained on a large, diverse 4K image dataset with bilingual captions and metadata to enable resolution- and aspect ratio-aware sampling. The model integrates advanced techniques including Resonance 2D RoPE positional encoding, a non-adversarial VAE post-training scheme, an SNR-aware Huber Wavelet objective, and a stage-wise aesthetic curriculum learning method to enhance detail preservation and stability.

UltraFlux demonstrates superior performance compared to strong open-source baselines on fidelity, aesthetics, and alignment metrics in multi-aspect ratio 4K settings, and with a large language model prompt refiner, it matches or exceeds the proprietary Seedream 4.0 model. This advancement represents a significant step forward in generating high-resolution, visually appealing images that generalize well across different formats.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2511.18050v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Diffusion transformers have recently delivered strong text-to-image generation around 1K resolution, but we show that extending them to native 4K across diverse aspect ratios exposes a tightly coupled failure mode spanning positional encoding, VAE compression, and optimization. Tackling any of these factors in isolation leaves substantial quality on the table. We therefore take a data-model co-design view and introduce UltraFlux, a Flux-based DiT trained natively at 4K on MultiAspect-4K-1M, a 1M-image 4K corpus with controlled multi-AR coverage, bilingual captions, and rich VLM/IQA metadata for resolution- and AR-aware sampling. On the model side, UltraFlux couples (i) Resonance 2D RoPE with YaRN for training-window-, frequency-, and AR-aware positional encoding at 4K; (ii) a simple, non-adversarial VAE post-training scheme that improves 4K reconstruction fidelity; (iii) an SNR-Aware Huber Wavelet objective that rebalances gradients across timesteps and frequency bands; and (iv) a Stage-wise Aesthetic Curriculum Learning strategy that concentrates high-aesthetic supervision on high-noise steps governed by the model prior. Together, these components yield a stable, detail-preserving 4K DiT that generalizes across wide, square, and tall ARs. On the Aesthetic-Eval at 4096 benchmark and multi-AR 4K settings, UltraFlux consistently outperforms strong open-source baselines across fidelity, aesthetic, and alignment metrics, and-with a LLM prompt refiner-matches or surpasses the proprietary Seedream 4.0.

items.title: Researchers evaluate Qwen- and Gemma-based LLMs for extracting RDF triples from conversational data to build Personal Knowledge Graphs for recommendation systems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: From "Strings" to "Things" for Personal Knowledge Graphs: Evaluating LLM Triple Extraction for Recommendation Systems
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a reproducible pipeline that uses lightweight Large Language Models (LLMs) based on Qwen and Gemma to extract structured RDF triples from unstructured conversational data. This approach aims to build Personal Knowledge Graphs (PKGs) that model user preferences while preserving privacy. The study evaluates these models on their ability to generate RDF-compliant triples linked to Wikidata identifiers and assesses the quality of the extracted data in supporting recommendation systems.

The evaluation focused on both the semantic accuracy of the triple extraction and the effectiveness of the resulting PKGs in downstream recommendation tasks. Results showed that some models achieved strong performance in extracting meaningful triples, which correlated with improved recommendation outcomes, demonstrating the potential of LLMs for constructing PKGs from conversational inputs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00003v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Personal Knowledge Graphs (PKGs) offer a privacy-preserving framework for modeling user preferences, yet constructing them from unstructured, decentralized conversational data remains a challenge. This paper bridges the gap between conversational "strings" and semantic "things" by presenting a reproducible pipeline for extracting structured user-preference triples using lightweight Large Language Models. We evaluate Qwen- and Gemma-based models on their ability to extract RDF-compliant triples linked to Wikidata identifiers from conversational data for PKG construction. Our evaluation assesses both the semantic extraction fidelity and the utility of the resulting graphs in a downstream recommendation task. We found that certain models performed well and had proportionally high downstream performance relative to their triple extraction performance.

items.title: Researchers present Topological Void Analysis, a mathematical framework identifying unexplored innovation opportunities in high-dimensional knowledge spaces, applied to 140,000 documents generating over 2,100 invention candidates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Topological Void Analysis A Mathematical Framework for Systematic Technical Innovation Discovery in Knowledge Spaces
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Topological Void Analysis (TVA), a mathematical framework designed to identify unexplored innovation opportunities within complex, high-dimensional knowledge spaces. TVA defines topological voids as specific triads of concepts that are semantically related yet occupy unfilled regions in a hybrid embedding space, indicating potential areas for novel invention. Applying this method to approximately 140,000 documents, the team generated over 2,100 invention candidates across 96 target areas, with a high rate of quality validation through automated filtering and expert review.

The framework operates by ensuring that concept pairs are both relevant to a domain anchor and sufficiently distinct to avoid obvious or unrelated combinations, while also sharing a sparse lexical connection. This approach allows TVA to uncover non-obvious connections that traditional keyword or citation-based methods might miss. Case studies demonstrate its effectiveness in surfacing innovative links rather than merely obvious related pairs, suggesting TVA's potential to systematically guide technical innovation discovery in dense research fields.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00005v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Identifying where to innovate in a dense technical domain - such as operating systems or hardware/software co-design - is fundamentally a search problem in a high-dimensional knowledge space. Existing approaches rely on keyword search, citation proximity, or human intuition, none of which formalise the notion of an unexplored region that is simultaneously relevant to a target goal and absent from prior art. We present Topological Void Analysis (TVA), a mathematical framework that defines topological voids as triads (A, B, C) in a dense-sparse hybrid embedding space. A void requires three conditions: (i) both concepts A and B are semantically cohesive with domain anchor C; (ii) their pairwise similarity falls within a calibrated marginality band - avoiding both obvious combinations and unrelated noise; and (iii) they share a sparse lexical bridge while the geodesic midpoint on the embedding hypersphere is unoccupied. Applied to ~140k indexed documents, TVA generates 2,128 invention candidates across 96 targets; 90% survive automated quality filtering, yielding 191 REVISE and 1 APPROVE verdict from four-specialist adversarial review (0.05% end-to-end). Two case studies demonstrate the framework surfaces non-obvious connective tissue rather than merely obvious related pairs.

items.title: Researchers challenge cross-regime co-reference assumption in LLM individuation, proposing regime-indexed identity units based on experiments with Qwen3-4B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Persona Without Substrate: Regime-Dependence and the LLM Individuation Problem
items.summary: Researchers challenge the common assumption in large language model (LLM) individuation that the same representational direction corresponds to the same content across different regimes such as prompt-conditioning, fine-tuning, and inference-time steering. Through experiments on Qwen3-4B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2, they identify inconsistencies including non-collinearity of vectors, stronger displacement by fictional personas, biased mixtures influenced by training history, and asymmetric compositional behaviors that undermine this assumption. They propose a new framework called regime-indexed individuation, where identity is defined by a combination of representational vehicle and regime rather than by the vehicle alone. This approach reinterprets previous theoretical positions as describing distinct regime-specific objects rather than competing for a single referent, offering a revised perspective on LLM representation and individuation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00006v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Beckmann & Butlin's (2026) ontological framework for the LLM individuation problem inherits an unargued cross-regime co-reference assumption from the persona-vectors literature: that the same direction picks out the same content under prompt-conditioning, gradient-descent fine-tuning, and inference-time steering. We present four empirical wedges from persona-topology experiments on Qwen3-4B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 - non-collinearity of prompt-extracted vectors and fine-tune basins; fictional personas displacing the model along real-anchor directions more strongly than real anchors do; contradictory-valenced mixtures biased toward a training-history-determined attractor; and asymmetric compositional algebra under inference-time arithmetic versus fine-tune-time chimera training - that jointly undermine the assumption. We propose regime-indexed individuation: the identity unit for representational content is a (vehicle, regime) pair, not a vehicle alone. Under this framework, Beckmann & Butlin's three candidate positions describe three different regime-internal objects rather than competing for the same referent; the same diagnosis applies to Mollo & Milli\`ere, Chalmers, and Cerullo.

items.title: Researchers present BaRA, a BFS-and-Reflection web data collection agent that outperforms existing LLM-based agents on link discovery and multimodal extraction across synthetic and public websites [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: BaRA: BFS-and-Reflection Web Data Collection Agent
items.summary:
Researchers have developed BaRA, a web data collection agent that combines bounded breadth-first search (BFS) traversal with history-based self-reflection to improve site-level data collection under fixed interaction limits. BaRA addresses common issues faced by large language model (LLM)-based web agents, such as missing relevant pages and incomplete multimodal outputs, by enhancing link discovery and extraction of downloadable media.

The team evaluated BaRA on 50 synthetic websites with known reference sets and on three public sites with complex or dynamic layouts. BaRA outperformed existing methods including Pure LLM, SeeAct-Vision, and Browser-use, particularly excelling in recovering valid downloadable images and videos. The researchers have made their code publicly available for further use and development.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00007v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based web agents reduce manual scripting for web data collection, yet on live websites, they often miss relevant pages, return incomplete multimodal outputs, or return media URLs that are not directly downloadable. We present BFS-and-Reflection Agent (BaRA), a framework for site-level collection under a fixed interaction budget. The framework combines bounded breadth-first search (BFS) traversal with history-based self-reflection. We evaluate BaRA on 50 synthetic websites with ground-truth reference sets. We additionally test on three public websites with cluttered or dynamic layouts. BaRA outperforms Pure LLM, SeeAct-Vision, and Browser-use on link discovery and downloadable multimodal extraction, with the largest gains in download-valid image and video recovery. Our code is available at https://github.com/MLAI-Yonsei/BaRA-Agent.

items.title: Researchers propose SchemaRAG, a retrieval-augmented generation framework that dynamically reduces large schemas for LLM-driven structured information extraction, improving accuracy by 8.8% and cutting latency and token costs by nearly half [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SchemaRAG: Dynamic Large Schema Reduction for LLM-driven Structured Information Extraction
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced SchemaRAG, a retrieval-augmented generation framework designed to improve structured information extraction from unstructured text using large language models (LLMs). SchemaRAG addresses challenges posed by large and complex target schemas by dynamically pruning the output schema space, which reduces prompt size and mitigates issues like increased cost, latency, and context length limits. This approach enhances extraction accuracy while optimizing resource use.

The framework leverages schema metadata and few-shot examples to selectively reduce the schema during extraction tasks. Evaluations on healthcare and e-commerce datasets demonstrate that SchemaRAG achieves up to an 8.8% improvement in micro-F1 score, alongside a 47% reduction in latency and a 48% decrease in token costs. These results highlight SchemaRAG's effectiveness and practicality for handling large-schema extraction tasks with LLMs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00008v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Extracting structured data from unstructured text using large language models (LLMs) becomes challenging when target schemas are large and complex. In such cases, including the full schema in the prompt increases cost and latency, risks lost-in-the-middle performance degradation, and can exceed context length limits. We propose SchemaRAG, a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework that dynamically prunes the output schema space for schema-conditioned information extraction tasks by leveraging schema metadata and few-shot examples when available. We evaluate SchemaRAG on real-world healthcare and e-commerce datasets. Our results show that SchemaRAG can achieve up to an 8.8% increase in micro-F1, a 47% reduction in latency, and a 48% reduction in token costs, demonstrating its practicality for large-schema extraction.

items.title: Researchers propose Loom, a three-layer assisted writing framework that controls narrative intent and rendering density to improve creative writing fidelity and descriptive intensity [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Controllable Narrative Rendering for Enhanced Assisted Writing
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Loom, a three-layer assisted writing framework designed to enhance creative writing by balancing narrative fidelity and descriptive intensity. Loom addresses a common issue in large language models where writing assistance either results in overly safe, superficial edits or uncontrolled plot expansions. By separating the generation of perceptual content from syntactic insertion, Loom maintains the original story structure while improving descriptive detail.

The framework is based on a narratological distinction between story and discourse and uses an intent-centered semiotic chain-of-thought to precisely control narrative intent and rendering density. Evaluations using both automated metrics and human assessments show that Loom outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, achieving higher overall quality with significant improvements in factual accuracy and descriptive richness.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00009v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Despite the remarkable proficiency of large language models (LLMs) in basic writing assistance, their utility in creative writing is fundamentally hindered by a persistent binary failure. This issue manifests as an oscillation between safe, surface-level editing, referred to as remedial polishing, and destructive, uncontrolled plot expansion. This dilemma defines a critical trade-off between narrative fidelity and descriptive intensity. We propose Loom, an assisted writing framework grounded in the narratological distinction between story and discourse. Loom employs a three-layer pipeline that operationalizes an intent-centered semiotic chain-of-thought to enforce precise control over narrative intent and rendering density. This architecture separates the generation of perceptual material from syntactic insertion, ensuring that enhancement occurs without violating the original event structure. Our comprehensive evaluation, which includes LLM-based metrics and human assessment, demonstrates that Loom successfully resolves this fundamental tension. Loom achieves the highest overall quality score, yielding substantial gains in factual integrity and descriptive intensity compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

items.title: Researchers propose a multi-objective framework to automatically optimize prompts for LLM-based user simulators in conversational recommender systems, improving behavioral alignment and addressing bias and data issues [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Prompt Optimization for User Simulation in Conversational Recommender Systems: A Multi-Objective Framework
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a multi-objective framework to automatically optimize prompts for large language model (LLM)-based user simulators in conversational recommender systems (CRSs). This approach aims to improve behavioral alignment with human interaction patterns while addressing challenges such as systematic positive bias, data leakage, and limited behavioral diversity that affect existing methods. The framework also reduces reliance on manual prompt engineering, which typically requires extensive domain expertise.

Conversational recommender systems enable users to actively express preferences and adapt recommendations in real time, but evaluating these systems through human studies is costly and time-consuming. Additionally, obtaining CRS interaction data for training is difficult due to privacy concerns. LLM-based user simulators offer a promising solution by generating synthetic user interactions for both evaluation and training, and the proposed framework enhances their effectiveness across diverse prompt settings.

Experimental results demonstrate that this automated prompt optimization framework outperforms baseline methods in producing user simulations that better reflect real human behaviors, potentially advancing the development and assessment of more accurate and reliable conversational recommender systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00010v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Conversational recommender systems (CRSs) are a core component of next-generation intelligent recommender systems because they enable users to actively elicit preferences, clarify intentions, and adapt recommendations in real time. However, there are two key obstacles in the CRS domain: evaluation and access to training data. Evaluating CRSs through real human studies is more critical than for traditional recommender systems, yet such studies are both costly and time-consuming. Moreover, CRS interaction data are often difficult to obtain for model training due to privacy concerns. Large language model (LLM)-based user simulators have shown promise in addressing both challenges by generating synthetic user interactions for evaluation and training. However, existing approaches suffer from systematic positive bias, data leakage, and limited behavioral diversity, and they rely on brittle manual prompt engineering that requires extensive domain expertise. In this paper, we propose a framework to automatically optimize prompts for LLM-based user simulators in CRSs, simultaneously mitigating these issues. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves improved behavioral alignment with human interaction patterns compared to baseline methods across diverse prompt settings.

items.title: Researchers present SkillSelect-Serve, a budget-controllable and QoS-aware framework for skill service recommendation and composition in small LLM agents, improving utility over fixed top-k methods in tests with 35,353 skills [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SkillSelect-Serve: Budget-Controllable and QoS-Aware Skill Service Recommendation and Composition for Small LLM Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have developed SkillSelect-Serve, a new framework designed to improve skill service recommendation and composition for small large language model (LLM) agents. Unlike traditional methods that return fixed top-k skill lists, SkillSelect-Serve offers budget control and quality of service (QoS) awareness by representing skills as structured services with detailed attributes such as dependencies, costs, risks, and QoS metrics. The framework translates natural language tasks into structured requirements and retrieves candidate services from a large registry, optimizing selection through dual-granularity utility modeling to balance coverage, redundancy, cost, and risk.

Testing SkillSelect-Serve on a dataset of 35,353 skills and 586 task queries demonstrated consistent improvements in bundle recall and mean utility compared to fixed top-k retrieval methods. This approach enhances the efficiency and effectiveness of skill selection in LLM agents, potentially advancing their capability to handle complex tasks within specified resource constraints.
