items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00011v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reusable skill libraries are becoming important infrastructure for large language model (LLM) agents, yet existing selection methods often treat skills as retrievable documents and return fixed top-k lists. This paper presents SkillSelect-Serve, a budget-controllable and QoS-aware framework that formulates agent skill selection as Skill Service Recommendation and Composition. SkillSelect-Serve represents raw skills as structured Skill Services with functional descriptions, dependencies, context cost, risk, and QoS-related attributes. A local Micro-Agent Requirement Planner converts natural-language tasks into structured service requirements, while a shared discovery backbone retrieves candidate services from a large registry. The framework then performs dual-granularity utility modeling with skill-level marginal suitability estimation and bundle-level calibration for coverage, redundancy, cost, and risk trade-offs. Experiments on 35,353 skills and 586 task queries show that SkillSelect-Serve consistently improves same-budget bundle recall and mean utility over fixed top-k retrieval baselines.

items.title: Researchers propose PRA-RAG, a provably robust aggregation algorithm for Retrieval-Augmented Generation that reduces poisoning attack success to 1% while maintaining 71% accuracy across benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: PRA-RAG: Provably Robust Aggregation in Retrieval-Augmented Generation against Retrieval Corruption
items.summary:
Researchers have developed PRA-RAG, a provably robust aggregation algorithm designed to enhance the security of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems against poisoning attacks. These attacks manipulate retrieved texts to mislead Large Language Models (LLMs), which RAG uses to supplement external knowledge. PRA-RAG reduces the success rate of such attacks to 1% while maintaining 71% accuracy across various benchmarks, outperforming existing defense methods.

PRA-RAG works by sampling multiple combinations of retrieved texts and leveraging geometric structures in the embedding space to identify a robust subset for stable aggregation. The researchers provide theoretical bounds on the maximum impact of poisoned content and introduce a quantitative measure of RAG's robustness. Experiments across different RAG architectures demonstrate the effectiveness of PRA-RAG in defending against retrieval corruption without compromising model performance.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00012v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enhances Large Language Models (LLMs) by incorporating external knowledge, effectively mitigating their inherent knowledge limitations. However, RAG remains vulnerable to poisoning attacks that manipulate retrieved texts to mislead model outputs. Existing defense mechanisms often lack theoretical robustness guarantees and perform unreliably when the LLM has limited knowledge of the retrieved content. In this work, we propose PRA-RAG, a provably robust retrieval aggregation algorithm designed to defend against poisoning attacks on retrieved texts. PRA-RAG samples multiple combinations of retrieved texts and utilizes geometric structures in the embedding space to identify a robust subset, from which a stable aggregated representation is derived. We provide theoretical bounds on the maximum impact of poisoned retrieved content and establish a quantitative measure of RAG's robustness. Experiments across multiple benchmarks and RAG architectures demonstrate that PRA-RAG reduces the attack success rate to as low as 1% while maintaining an accuracy of 71%, significantly outperforming representative state-of-the-art methods.

items.summary:

GRACE-RAG shifts structural reasoning from the generative phase to a structured retrieval layer, which helps resolve ambiguities offline and supports deployment on lightweight, self-hosted models tailored to specific institutional vocabularies. This approach enhances evidence synthesis by up to 20% in quality, particularly in domains with dense entities and heterogeneous documents.

Tests conducted with models of varying sizes, including Mistral 24B, GPT OSS 120B, and Gemini 2.5 Flash, demonstrated consistent improvements in completeness, depth, and anticipatory coverage. The findings suggest that the retrieval architecture plays a more critical role in structural quality than model scale, enabling reduced computational demands and latency without relying on proprietary systems.

items.title: Researchers propose an AI-based framework using large language models for automated compliance checks of multi-apartment floor plans under Australian building regulations [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Towards an automated AI-based framework for floor plan compliance checks for residential buildings
items.summary:
Researchers have proposed an AI-based framework to automate compliance checks of multi-apartment floor plans against Australian building regulations aimed at improving residents' well-being. The framework uses a Large Language Model (LLM) within a Rule Engine to translate textual building codes into executable rules, while a Data Extraction Engine processes floor plan images into structured building graphs. These graphs are then assessed by a Compliance Check Engine using the LLM-generated rules, enabling scalable and consistent evaluation of design features such as daylight access, ventilation, privacy, and space efficiency.

This approach addresses challenges in current manual compliance checking, which is time-consuming and limited in scalability, as well as the fragmented nature of existing automated methods that typically focus on single apartments. By providing a unified, transparent system for multi-unit compliance assessment, the framework supports efficient enforcement of apartment design standards and promotes healthier, higher-density urban development across jurisdictions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00015v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: To improve residents' well-being in Australia's urban areas, governments have introduced policy reforms such as SEPP65, BADS, and SPP7.3 to enhance apartment design quality. These regulations require precise geometric and spatial analysis to evaluate health-related features, including daylight access, natural ventilation, privacy, and space efficiency. However, compliance checking remains challenging due to its manual, time-intensive nature. Additionally, evolving policies limit scalability for large-scale assessments across thousands of apartments. Existing automated floor plan analysis methods are fragmented and typically focus on single apartments, lacking a unified framework for multi-unit compliance checking. This article explores current advancements in automated floor plan analysis, particularly AI-driven approaches, and highlights key challenges in their practical adoption. To address these gaps, a conceptual framework is proposed for automated compliance checking in multi-apartment buildings. A Large Language Model (LLM) is used within a Rule Engine to convert textual building codes into executable, explainable rules. A Data Extraction Engine segments floor plan images into elements such as walls, rooms, fixtures, text, and symbols, and transforms them into a structured building graph with topological relationships. This structured representation is then evaluated by a Compliance Check Engine, which leverages LLM-generated rules for assessment. The proposed framework offers a scalable, consistent, and transparent approach to automated compliance checking across jurisdictions, supporting efficient enforcement of apartment design standards and promoting healthier, higher-density urban development.

items.title: Researchers present Libra, a self-evolving framework that optimizes information retrieval environments using mutable catalogs and LLM-driven loops, improving code localization accuracy across 12 repositories [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Libra: Training the Environment for Agentic Information Retrieval
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Libra, a self-evolving framework designed to optimize information retrieval environments by introducing mutable catalogs—hierarchical Markdown files that serve as navigable indices—within code repositories. Libra operates through an LLM-driven loop where synthetic queries are generated, attempts are made to resolve them by navigating the catalogs, and the catalogs are rewritten in response to failures, leading to continuous improvements in code localization accuracy across 12 software engineering repositories.

Evaluations show that this approach yields logarithmic gains in localization performance, and these improvements transfer effectively across different large language models and problem sets without additional training. The study also demonstrates that a minimalist coding agent using Libra-optimized catalogs outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, highlighting the potential of environment-focused optimization in agentic information retrieval systems. The code and datasets are publicly available for further research and development.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00016v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Information localization within massive repositories is a cornerstone of agentic LLM systems. While synthetic data-driven optimization has proven successful in training LLMs, little attention has been paid to optimizing the agent's working environment (the repository itself) in a data-driven manner. To bridge this gap, we present Libra, a self-evolving framework that introduces mutable "catalogs" (hierarchical Markdown files serving as navigable indices) into the repository. Libra runs an LLM-driven optimization loop where a Prompter generates synthetic queries, a frozen Solver attempts to resolve them by navigating the catalogs, and a Healer rewrites the catalogs in response to the Solver's localization failures. Evaluations across 12 SWE-bench Lite repositories demonstrate that this environmental healing yields continual, logarithmic improvements in code localization accuracy. Furthermore, these environmental improvements transfer zero-shot across different LLMs and problem sets. Although the focus of this paper is to study the general behavior of such a system, we also demonstrate that a minimalist coding agent equipped with Libra-optimized catalogs outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/salesforce-misc/Libra and data at https://huggingface.co/datasets/Salesforce/Libra.

items.title: Researchers propose Profile-guided Personalized Retrieval Optimization to improve user-aware memory retrieval in long-term conversational agents, showing gains on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Learning User-Aware Recall: Personalized Retrieval in Long-Term Conversational Memory
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Profile-guided Personalized Retrieval Optimization (PPRO), a new framework designed to enhance memory retrieval in long-term conversational agents by making it user-aware and optimizable. PPRO constructs episodic and semantic memory banks from dialogue histories and creates a user profile that guides memory ranking, accounting for individual user attributes and preferences. The approach also includes training a query rewriter using Group Relative Policy Optimization to improve retrieval and answer quality without altering the memory banks or answer model.

Experiments on the LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S benchmarks demonstrate that PPRO consistently outperforms both training-free and training-based memory retrieval systems. Ablation studies confirm that the combination of profile-guided ranking and retrieval-oriented query rewriting significantly contributes to the improved performance, highlighting the importance of retrieval optimization in personalized long-term memory use for conversational agents.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00017v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Long-term conversational agents are expected to remember past interactions, but memory is useful only when the right evidence is recalled for the right user. Existing memory-augmented LLM agents have made progress in building compact memory banks, yet retrieval is still often driven by query-centered similarity or fixed ranking rules, leaving user-conditioned relevance underexplored.To address this gap, we propose Profile-guided Personalized Retrieval Optimization (PPRO), a retrieval-centric framework that makes memory retrieval both user-aware and optimizable.PPRO builds episodic and semantic memory banks from dialogue histories and derives a user profile from accumulated memories.The profile serves as an explicit personalized prior in memory ranking, allowing retrieval to account for stable user attributes, preferences, and relationships.PPRO further trains a query rewriter with Group Relative Policy Optimization, using both evidence retrieval quality and downstream answer quality as feedback while keeping the memory banks and answer model fixed.Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S show consistent gains over training-free memory systems and training-based baselines.Ablation studies further show that both profile-guided ranking and retrieval-oriented rewriting contribute substantially to performance, highlighting retrieval optimization as a key factor in personalized long-term memory use.

items.title: Researchers evaluate deployment of LLM-based text-to-911 translation system in emergencies, identify misconceptions, and offer recommendations for development and deployment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: LLMs in the Real World: Evaluating "AI" in Emergency Contexts
items.summary:
Researchers have evaluated the deployment of a large language model (LLM)-based text-to-911 translation system designed to assist emergency communications in 55 languages when direct calls to operators are difficult. The study highlights common misconceptions about such technologies and provides concrete recommendations and best practices for stakeholders involved in the development and deployment process. The authors emphasize the importance of addressing simpler, often overlooked problems alongside more complex scientific challenges.

The paper serves as a call to action for the research community to better communicate their findings to the public, using the case study to illustrate the real-world stakes of deploying AI-driven emergency translation tools. It underscores the need for careful consideration at every stage to ensure these systems are effective and reliable in critical situations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00019v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper offers a call to action. We urge our colleagues in the research community to play a greater role in the articulation of our findings to the public. To illustrate the stakes we present a case study on the initial stages of an LLM-based machine translation application's deployment in a real-world context: a text-2-911 system advertising capabilities in 55 languages for use in emergencies in which it may be difficult to call operators directly. We identify a number of common misconceptions about technologies such as these, concluding with a set of concrete recommendations and best practices for stakeholders at every stage of the development and deployment pipeline. While the advancement of scientific research often lies in solving the "hard" problems, we argue it is often the "easy" ones -- problems for which the latest technology is often unnecessary -- that are most overlooked.

items.title: Researchers propose using Top-k Sparse Autoencoders to disentangle dense sentence embeddings into human-interpretable concepts, enabling steerable retrieval without retraining models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Aligning Sentence Embeddings to Human Concepts via Sparse Autoencoders
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a method to make dense sentence embeddings, commonly used in Retrieval-Augmented Generation systems, more interpretable by disentangling them into human-understandable concepts using Top-k Sparse Autoencoders. This approach reveals that the resulting features correspond to semantic, syntactic, and pragmatic categories, enabling clearer alignment between retrieval processes and human intent.

The team also introduced an activation steering mechanism that allows users to adjust specific latent features to re-rank search results according to their preferences without needing to retrain the underlying model. This technique offers a promising path toward more transparent and controllable neural information retrieval systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00023v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Dense sentence embeddings are fundamental to modern Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems but suffer from a lack of interpretability due to feature superposition. This opacity hinders the alignment of retrieval processes with human intent, as the entangled representations are difficult to analyze or control. In this work, we propose a method to disentangle the dense representations of sentence transformers (e.g., E5) into human-interpretable concepts using Top-k Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs). items.title: Researchers develop FLYNN, a recurrent neural network based on fruit fly brain connectome, achieving robust robot navigation with superior tolerance to sensory loss and out-of-distribution data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: FLYNN: Robust Neural Network for Robot Navigation using Fly Brain Topology
items.summary:
Researchers have developed FLYNN, a recurrent neural network modeled directly on the synaptic connectome of the fruit fly brain, to improve robot navigation. Trained for vision-based navigation in a simulated environment, FLYNN matches the performance of modern hand-crafted networks but shows greater robustness to sensory loss and out-of-distribution data without additional training. Notably, it maintained functionality even with complete vision loss, a scenario where traditional networks failed despite training with camera dropout.

Analysis of FLYNN's internal states revealed a high degree of representational modularity, which may contribute to its resilience. This work suggests that designing artificial agents based on biological brain topologies could lead to more robust and adaptable systems capable of handling unexpected challenges in real-world environments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00025v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While deep learning models achieve state-of-the-art performance in complex tasks, they remain brittle when faced with new environments or sensory deprivation. In contrast, biological systems exhibit remarkable tolerance to these challenges. We address this vulnerability by developing a recurrent neural network (RNN) whose architecture is directly derived from the synaptic-resolution brain connectome of the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster. We demonstrate the feasibility of training the fly connectome neural network (FLYNN) to perform vision-based navigation in MuJoCo, achieving performance comparable to modern hand-crafted networks of similar parameter counts. Crucially, FLYNN exhibits superior resistance to out-of-distribution (OOD) data and tolerance to sensory loss without further training. It remained functional even under total vision loss while hand-crafted networks largely failed, even when specifically trained with camera dropout. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) of the internal state of FLYNN suggests that it exhibits a particularly high degree of representational modularity, which might be related to its robustness. Our work provides a new direction for designing resilient artificial agents following the topology of biological brains.

items.title: Researchers propose memory-native non-terrestrial networks with dual-memory architecture to optimize embodied intelligence connectivity, outperforming stateless NTN and terrestrial methods in satellite experiments [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Memory-Native Non-Terrestrial Networks for Embodied Intelligence
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced a memory-native non-terrestrial network (MemNTN) paradigm designed to enhance connectivity for embodied intelligence (EI) systems, such as robots operating in remote environments. This approach uses a dual-memory architecture that separates physical memory, representing the current state of the world, from digital memory, which stores historical network data. By leveraging long-term contextual information, MemNTN enables more efficient decision-making across multiple network layers compared to traditional memoryless NTN protocols.

The team developed mechanisms for memory acquisition, compression, valuation, updating, and utilization to support this architecture. Experiments involving satellite embodied question answering (SEQA) demonstrated that MemNTN significantly outperforms conventional stateless NTN and terrestrial network methods, highlighting its potential to improve communication and resource use in dynamic, resource-constrained, and topology-varying environments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00029v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) provide ubiquitous connectivity for embodied intelligence (EI), enabling robots in wilderness to leverage cloud resources or report critical information to remote centers. However, the synergy is nontrivial due to the highly-dynamic, resource-constrained, topology-varying, and task-oriented environment. Existing memoryless NTN protocols become inefficient, since the decisions are driven by local channel conditions and instantaneous service demands. To address these limitations, this paper proposes the memory-native NTN (MemNTN) paradigm that leverages long-horizon contexts for memory augmented system optimization. To realize this paradigm shift, we establish a dual-memory architecture that distinguishes between physical memory representing the state of the world and digital memory encoding historical network experience. We develop memory acquisition, compression, valuation, update, and utilization mechanisms that facilitate cross-layer, memory-native decision-making, spanning from the physical and access layers up to the network and application layers. Experiments in satellite embodied question answering (SEQA) demonstrate that the proposed MemNTN significantly outperforms conventional stateless NTN and terrestrial approaches.

items.title: Researchers present CHORD framework using contact wrench guidance from human demonstrations for scalable dexterous robot manipulation, achieving over 82% success on 1,831 benchmark tasks and real-world transfer [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Learning Dexterous Manipulation Using Contact Wrench Guidance From Human Demonstration
items.summary:
Researchers have developed CHORD, a new framework that uses contact wrench guidance derived from human demonstrations to improve dexterous robot manipulation. By representing motions through the forces and torques applied to objects, CHORD enables reinforcement learning to scale effectively for complex, contact-rich tasks. The framework was tested on a large benchmark of 1,831 tasks, achieving over 82% success, and also demonstrated strong generalization to whole-body manipulation and real-world applications.

The team introduced a comprehensive simulation benchmark with thousands of bimanual manipulation tasks based on motion-capture data and video reconstructions. CHORD's approach allows it to learn from both hand-only and third-person demonstrations, reaching a success rate of nearly 91% in whole-body manipulation scenarios. The learned policies successfully transferred to physical robots in both open-loop and closed-loop control settings, highlighting the framework's practical potential for real-world robotic dexterity.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00033v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Dexterous robot manipulation can benefit from the abundance of human demonstrations, but transferring such demonstrations to robot policies remains challenging. We present Contact Wrench Guidance from Human Demonstration in Robotic Dexterous Manipulation (CHORD), a framework for long-horizon manipulation of rigid and articulated objects with reinforcement learning. The key idea is object-centric contact wrench space guidance: we represent human and robot motions by the forces and torques they can induce on the object, enabling similarity to be measured by the induced instantaneous motions. This guidance makes reinforcement learning more scalable for contact-rich dexterous manipulation. We further introduce a large-scale simulation benchmark with 4,739 bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks, constructed from motion-capture datasets and reconstructed in-house videos. Evaluated on 1,831 benchmark tasks, CHORD achieves an average success rate of 82.12%, demonstrating strong scalability. CHORD also generalizes to whole-body manipulation from hand-only and third-person demonstrations, achieving a 90.77% success rate, and the learned policies transfer to the real world in both open-loop and closed-loop settings.

items.title: Researchers present AI-Atomic-Framework with CID broker for pre-write admission in multi-agent code co-synthesis, demonstrating feasibility and auditability in single-domain governance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: ATM: CID-Brokered Pre-Write Admission for Multi-Agent Code Co-Synthesis
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced the AI-Atomic-Framework (ATM), a governance system designed to manage concurrent write operations in multi-agent large language model (LLM) software engineering environments. ATM uses a Content Identifier (CID) broker to control shared mutations, ensuring that write intents are either executed in parallel, serialized, or safely rejected based on deterministic rules. This framework integrates task intent, repository scope, write admission, validation, and evidence obligations into a unified governance chain, with a neutral steward applying the final changes rather than the proposing agents.

The framework employs adapter-guided atomization to map write intents to semantic units called atoms, with virtual atoms providing temporary governance when coverage is incomplete. The system was evaluated through various controlled and field tests, including scenario matrices, archived cases, and an external adopter study, demonstrating its feasibility, auditability, and recoverability within single-domain governance settings. While the results support ATM's effectiveness in these contexts, the researchers do not claim it to be broadly superior or applicable across multiple governance domains.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00041v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems can decompose software-engineering work into planning, generation, validation, and repair, but a narrower systems problem remains: before any governed shared mutation is applied, a system must decide which concurrently formed write intents may proceed in parallel, which require deterministic composition or serialization, and which must take a fail-closed path. We address this problem with the AI-Atomic-Framework (ATM), a specification-grounded governance substrate for software agents operating within a single governance domain. ATM binds task intent, repository scope, write admission, validation, and evidence obligations into one governance chain. A Content Identifier (CID) broker serves as the shared-mutation admission subsystem. Adapter-guided atomization maps write intents to semantic atoms and bounded regions; when persistent atom-map coverage is incomplete, virtual atoms provide temporary auditable governance units for conservative comparison and routing. Governed shared writes are ultimately applied by a neutral steward rather than directly by proposing agents. Evaluation combines controlled, field, adoption, and extension evidence, including a 12-scenario deterministic design matrix, three archived runner cases, ATM-AdmissionBench, three archived same-file boundary cases, a three-week external-adopter study, and an operational recovery-routing benchmark. The results support feasibility, auditability, and bounded recoverability within the observed single-domain settings, but do not claim broad comparative superiority or cross-clone governance.

items.title: Researchers characterize destination-labeled self-looping systems with dwell, establish realization cost as sum of dwell values, and provide recognition algorithm with O(|Q||Ω|) complexity
items.originalTitle: Destination-Labeled Self-Looping Systems with Dwell: Intrinsic Characterization, Realization Cost, and Recognition
items.summary: Researchers have developed a model called destination-labeled self-looping systems with dwell (DLSL systems) to study finite-state symbolic controllers where visible transitions are predetermined and each visible state has a minimum dwell time requirement. They characterized the class of deterministic transducers that can realize these systems after phase expansion, identifying them as fiber-linear graph-respecting transducers. The study also established that any deterministic realization enforcing dwell values requires a number of control states equal to the sum of the dwell values and provided an efficient recognition and reconstruction algorithm with complexity O(|Q||Ω|). The analysis was further extended to a variant allowing transitions to enter interior phases of successor fibers.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00044v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study a finite-state symbolic controller for systems in which the admissible visible transitions are fixed in advance and each visible state carries a minimum dwell requirement. The resulting model, which we call a destination-labeled self-looping system with dwell (DLSL system), records the visible graph together with local decision maps; dwell memory appears only after phase expansion. The main structural issue is that, once dwell is imposed, the current visible state no longer determines whether a departure is allowed. This leads to the converse problem: which deterministic transducers arise as phase-expanded realizations of DLSL systems over a fixed visible graph? We show that the answer is exactly the class of fiber-linear graph-respecting transducers. Under natural reachability and realizable-departure assumptions, equivalent accessible realizations over the same visible graph are isomorphic; in particular, the visible transduction determines the dwell vector and the local decision maps. We also prove that any graph-preserving deterministic realization enforcing dwell values $(d_i)$ requires exactly $\sum_i d_i$ control states. Finally, we give an $O(|Q||\Omega|)$ recognition and reconstruction procedure, and extend the analysis to an edge-entry variant in which transitions may enter interior phases of successor fibers.

items.title: Study compares GPT-5 mini, Gemini 3 Flash, and DeepSeek Chat 3.2 on 993 Scrum certification questions, finding Gemini 3 Flash most accurate with low variability across prompting methods [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Comparing Large Language Models on Scrum Certification-Style Questions: Accuracy, Stability, and Error Patterns
items.summary:
A recent study evaluated the performance of three large language models—GPT-5 mini, Gemini 3 Flash, and DeepSeek Chat 3.2—on 993 Scrum certification-style questions based on the Professional Scrum Master I (PSM I) exam format. The models were tested using three prompting strategies: zero-shot, chain-of-thought, and source-grounded, with repeated trials to measure consistency. Gemini 3 Flash demonstrated the highest accuracy and low variability across different prompting methods, outperforming the other two models.

The study also analyzed model performance by question format and Scrum topics. All models performed best on single-answer multiple-choice questions, while multi-select and True/False formats were more challenging. Accuracy was higher in areas with clear normative definitions, such as Artifacts and Empiricism, but lower in topics like Scrum Values and Stakeholders. A qualitative review revealed that errors were systematic, often due to overgeneralization, restrictive wording, and conflicts between common interpretations and strict Scrum definitions.
items.description:
A recent study evaluated the performance of three large language models—GPT-5 mini, Gemini 3 Flash, and DeepSeek Chat 3.2—on 993 Scrum certification-style questions based on the Professional Scrum Master I (PSM I) exam format. The models were tested using three prompting strategies: zero-shot, chain-of-thought, and source-grounded, with repeated trials to measure consistency. Gemini 3 Flash demonstrated the highest accuracy and low variability across different prompting methods, outperforming the other two models.

The study also analyzed model performance by question format and Scrum topics. All models performed best on single-answer multiple-choice questions, while multi-select and True/False formats were more challenging. Accuracy was higher in areas with clear normative definitions, such as Artifacts and Empiricism, but lower in topics like Scrum Values and Stakeholders. A qualitative review revealed that errors were systematic, often due to overgeneralization, restrictive wording, and conflicts between common interpretations and strict Scrum definitions.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00048v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in exam- and certification-style question answering tasks, where their ability to retrieve, interpret, and apply domain-specific knowledge can be systematically assessed. In Software Engineering, such settings are particularly relevant when questions depend on strict adherence to normative definitions, roles, artifacts, and rules. This paper evaluates the performance of three contemporary LLMs, \textit{GPT-5 mini}, \textit{Gemini 3 Flash}, and \textit{DeepSeek Chat 3.2}, in answering 993 Scrum certification-style questions aligned with the Professional Scrum Master I (PSM I) assessment format. We evaluated the models under three prompting strategies (\textit{zero-shot}, \textit{chain-of-thought}, and \textit{source-grounded}), with repeated executions to assess intra-model stability. We also analyzed performance across Scrum topics and question formats, complemented by a qualitative analysis of recurring error patterns in incorrect answers. Results revealed clear differences among models, with Gemini 3 Flash achieving the highest accuracy, followed by GPT-5 mini and DeepSeek Chat 3.2, while intra-model variability remained low across all conditions. By question format, the models achieved the highest accuracy on single-answer multiple-choice items, whereas multi-select and True/False questions were more error-prone. By topic, performance was more consistent in normatively explicit areas such as Artifacts, Empiricism, and Product Value, but more fragile in Scrum Values, Self-Managing Teams, and Stakeholders \& Customers. The qualitative analysis showed that errors were systematic rather than random, involving overgeneralization, restrictive wording, compound distractors, and conflicts between common market interpretations and strict Scrum definitions.

items.originalTitle: Prompting GPT-5 on Scrum Certification Questions: An Empirical Accuracy Study
items.summary:
A recent study evaluated GPT-5's ability to answer Professional Scrum Master (PSM) certification questions using different prompting techniques. The model achieved over 85% accuracy across zero-shot, chain-of-thought, and citation-based prompts, with citation-based prompting reaching the highest accuracy of 89.1%. The research highlights GPT-5's strong performance on well-defined Scrum topics and single-answer questions, while noting challenges with multi-select and interpretive questions.

The study analyzed 993 validated PSM-aligned questions and found that errors were mainly due to misalignment with the Scrum Guide, content outside its scope, or outdated interpretations. Prompting methods consistently improved accuracy and reduced errors related to misinterpretation and version drift. These findings support the reliable use of large language models like GPT-5 in Agile training and certification preparation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00049v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in Agile Software Development for documentation, coaching, and training. As practitioners adopt these tools to prepare for certifications such as Professional Scrum Master (PSM), a key question is whether LLMs can reliably reason about Scrum, a framework with normative, well-defined rules described in the Scrum Guide (2020). This paper examines how different prompt techniques affect the factual accuracy of LLM responses to Scrum certification-style questions. A dataset of 993 validated PSM-aligned questions was answered by GPT-5 using three techniques: zero-shot, chain-of-thought, and with-source citation. All prompts achieved certification-level accuracy above 85\%, with the citation-based variant performing best (89.1\%) and yielding the lowest error rate. Correct answers concentrated in well-defined topics, such as \emph{Definition of Done}, Events, and Product Backlog Management, and in single-answer multiple-choice items, while multi-select questions and more interpretive areas, such as Scrum Team and Product Value, were less stable. Among questions where at least one prompt failed (16.2\%), errors clustered into misalignment with the Scrum Guide (28\%), content outside its scope (34\%), and outdated or biased interpretations (38\%). Overall, prompt techniques produced modest but consistent improvements, particularly in reducing misinterpretation and version drift, supporting more reliable use of LLMs in Agile learning and certification preparation.

items.title: Researchers introduce Adaptive-masking for Graph Embedding (AGE) to improve graph retrieval-augmented generation accuracy across four GraphQA benchmark datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AGE: Adaptive-masking for Graph Embedding in Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Adaptive-masking for Graph Embedding (AGE), a new method designed to enhance the accuracy of graph retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) in large language models (LLMs). AGE addresses the challenge of misalignment between graph-based and text-based latent features by using a Transformer-based mask self-supervised learning approach that focuses on predicting non-key nodes in graph data. This technique improves the representation of graph-structured knowledge, particularly for frozen LLMs, and has demonstrated superior performance across four distinct GraphQA benchmark datasets.

Unlike natural language texts, graphs contain key nodes that hold significant contextual information, which are difficult to predict and can hinder the learning process if masked. AGE overcomes this by employing a learnable node sampler to avoid masking these key nodes, thereby increasing the efficiency of the self-supervised learning process. Experimental results show that AGE significantly boosts the effectiveness of non-parametric search components in GraphQA tasks, leading to improved retrieval and generation outcomes.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00052v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: GraphRAG is an extension of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) that supports large language models (LLMs) by referring to graph-structured data as external knowledge. While this technique ideally captures intricate relationships, it often struggles with graph representations for LLMs, particularly for frozen LLMs, due to the misalignment between graph-based and text-based latent features. We tackle this issue by introducing the {\it Adaptive-masking for Graph Embedding (AGE)}. AGE employs a Transformer in a mask-based self-supervised learning (SSL) approach. We designed the architecture similar to text embedding encoders, addressing the latent feature misalignment. In contrast to natural language texts, graphs are concise representations, and there exist {\it key nodes} that hold dominant contextual information, which are challenging to predict from their surroundings. Masking such key nodes leads to inefficiency in the SSL process. Therefore, AGE focuses on predicting nodes apart from key nodes, utilizing a learnable node sampler. Our experimental results indicate that AGE significantly improves approaches using non-parametric search component in GraphQA tasks, achieving superior accuracy across four benchmark datasets with distinct characteristics.

items.title: Researchers introduce SWE-Router, a value-based temporal routing method for multi-turn agentic software engineering tasks that improves cost efficiency by combining cheap and expensive LLM models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SWE-Router: Routing in Multi-turn Agentic Software Engineering Tasks
items.summary:
Researchers have developed SWE-Router, a novel routing method for multi-turn agentic software engineering tasks that enhances cost efficiency by combining inexpensive and high-performance large language models (LLMs). Unlike existing routers that rely solely on task descriptions, SWE-Router uses a value-based temporal approach, allowing a cheaper model to explore the task for several turns before deciding whether to escalate to a more expensive model. This method leverages partial task trajectories to improve routing decisions, supported by a Bayes-optimality theorem demonstrating that conditioning on these trajectories enhances performance without harm.

The SWE-Router was tested across pairs of weak and strong LLMs along the cost-capability frontier, showing significant improvements in cost efficiency while maintaining most of the stronger model's performance. Additionally, the researchers have released a multi-LLM trajectory dataset to facilitate reproduction and further study of trajectory-level routing in software engineering tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00053v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) embedded in multi-turn agentic harnesses are reshaping software engineering (SWE), but routing every task to a frontier model is wasteful when many issues admit cheap fixes. Existing LLM routers operate on the task description alone, which inherits an information-theoretic Bayes-error floor in agentic settings: a similar issue can hide either a localized typo or a multi-module refactor, and the prompt does not separate the two. We introduce SWE-Router, a value-based temporal approach that lets a cheap model run for a few exploratory turns and reads the resulting partial trajectory before deciding whether to continue cheaply or to escalate to an expensive model. We provide a Bayes-optimality theorem showing that conditioning on the partial trajectory never harms routing and is strictly better whenever exploration is informative. Across the LLM pairs of weak and strong models spanning the contemporary cost--capability frontier, we show that SWE-Router greatly improves the cost efficiency of SWE tasks, while maintaining the majority of the performances of the stronger model. We additionally release a multi-LLM trajectory dataset which allows reproduction of our trajectory-level routing.

items.title: Researchers propose a dual-agent deep learning framework combining neuroevolution and supervised learning for energy-efficient RIS-aided tracking and uplink power control in mobile users [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Active Sensing for RIS-Aided Tracking and Power Control: A Hybrid Neuroevolution and Supervised Learning Approach
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a dual-agent deep learning framework that combines neuroevolution and supervised learning to enhance energy-efficient tracking and uplink power control for mobile users assisted by Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS). This approach addresses the challenge of optimizing discrete RIS phase profiles and user equipment transmit power in real time, using a low-overhead feedback link from the base station to manage power consumption during localization pilot transmissions. The framework is adaptable to both single- and multi-antenna base stations with minimal modifications.

The proposed method overcomes difficulties related to the non-differentiability of discrete RIS phase responses and limited feedback information by integrating neuroevolution with supervised learning. Extensive simulations demonstrate that this scheme achieves highly accurate and robust tracking across various target motion models, outperforming traditional methods such as extended Kalman filters, particle filters, and other machine learning-based trackers. Additionally, it shows significant improvements over conventional fingerprinting, deep reinforcement learning, and standard backpropagation estimators in static localization scenarios.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00056v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper studies energy efficient tracking of power-limited mobile users with the assistance of a Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface (RIS). Since localization pilot transmissions dominate the energy budget of power-constrained devices, we introduce a low-overhead feedback link from the Base Station (BS) to the user to enable dynamic uplink power control. To navigate the discrete and decentralized nature of this active sensing problem, we propose a novel Dual-Agent (DA) deep learning framework that jointly optimizes the discrete RIS phase profiles and the UE's transmit power in real time. Specifically, our approach employs a hybrid training methodology integrating the neuroevolution paradigm with supervised learning, effectively overcoming the non-differentiability of discrete phase responses from the RIS unit elements and the strict information bottleneck of single-bit feedback messages for pilot power control. The proposed DA active sensing framework can be applied with both single- and multi-antenna BSs, the latter with only minor modifications in the structure of one NN: an additional output branch with appropriate structure is included for the latter case to select a valid digital combiner from a finite set. Extensive numerical simulations demonstrate that the proposed scheme achieves highly accurate and robust tracking across diverse target motion models, outperforming extended Kalman and particle filters, as well as, machine learning-based trackers. Furthermore, in static localization, it is shown to significantly outperform traditional fingerprinting schemes, deep reinforcement learning baselines, and standard backpropagation-based estimators.

items.title: Researchers propose Multi-Scale Layer Attention to improve Oracle Bone Inscription recognition accuracy and robustness, outperforming existing methods on large-scale datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Enhancing Oracle Bone Inscription Recognition via Multi-Scale Layer Attention
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a new method called Multi-Scale Layer Attention (MSLA) to improve the recognition accuracy and robustness of Oracle Bone Inscriptions (OBIs), which are important for understanding ancient Chinese culture. MSLA enhances feature representation by explicitly modeling interactions across multiple spatial scales and layers, addressing challenges posed by the complex and degraded nature of OBIs. This approach outperforms existing attention mechanisms on large-scale OBI datasets while maintaining computational efficiency.

Traditional recognition methods rely heavily on expert knowledge and manual analysis, which are time-consuming and prone to errors. Although deep learning has advanced image recognition, previous techniques struggled to capture the fine-grained details and subtle variations in OBIs. MSLA overcomes these limitations by enriching representations with detailed multi-scale features, leading to more accurate and reliable recognition results.

items.title: Researchers introduce ALGOBENCH, a framework generating novel algorithmic problems to benchmark code generation models' algorithmic adaptation and complexity handling [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AlgoBench: Benchmarking Algorithmic Adaptation in Code Generation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed ALGOBENCH, a new framework designed to generate novel algorithmic problems that challenge code generation models to adapt their algorithms and handle complexity effectively. Unlike traditional benchmarks, ALGOBENCH creates problem variants that cause original reference algorithms to fail, enabling a more rigorous assessment of a model's algorithmic reasoning beyond functional correctness. The framework also introduces complexity-aware metrics to evaluate whether solutions meet the required asymptotic performance.

Experiments with multiple large language models and prompting strategies reveal a significant drop in performance on ALGOBENCH variants, highlighting the difficulty of adapting algorithms to new constraints. The study found that many solutions that appear correct do not satisfy complexity requirements, and errors are primarily due to algorithmic shortcomings rather than implementation mistakes. This suggests that ALGOBENCH provides a more comprehensive evaluation of a model's ability to generalize and adapt algorithmically.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00062v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: High pass rates on established programming benchmarks such as HumanEval and LiveCodeBench do not always show whether a model can reason about algorithms. Many fixed benchmarks eventually become part of the public training ecosystem through released problem statements, editorials, and generated solutions, allowing later models to improve partly by exposure rather than by stronger algorithmic ability. We introduce ALGOBENCH, a framework that automatically builds novel algorithmic problems from known competitive-programming problems through structured constraint-shifting transformations. Each accepted ALGOBENCH variant is traceable to a source problem, but must make the original reference algorithm fail. Beyond pass@$k$, we introduce complexity-aware metrics -- including OPTT, OPTS, TRAPRATE, GAPT, and CONSENS -- to test whether a solution is not only functionally correct but also asymptotically suitable for the generated problem. Experiments across multiple LLMs and prompting strategies show that performance drops sharply on ALGOBENCH variants, retrieval can increase reuse of the old algorithm, and many correct-looking solutions fail to meet the required complexity. Error analysis shows that failures are mainly algorithmic rather than implementation-level, suggesting that ALGOBENCH evaluates adaptation beyond functional correctness.

items.title: Researchers analyze spectral geometry emergence and bosonic-Bloch probes in quantum learning models, confirming interference behavior and anomaly detection with hardware experiments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Spectral Geometry and Bosonic-Bloch Probes: Explorations in Quantum Learning
items.summary:
Researchers have investigated how spectral geometry emerges in quantum learning models and demonstrated methods to diagnose this phenomenon using physically grounded probes. Their study shows that training in graph-regularized quantum networks reorganizes the output similarity graph, increases the effective spectral dimension, and reshapes the Laplacian spectrum. They confirmed these effects through edge-resolved two-boson interference experiments, which correlated bosonic enhancement with learned spectral partitions, and hardware experiments validated the predicted interference behavior within shot-noise limits.

The team also analyzed a hybrid quantum autoencoder, introducing Bloch-space drift as a geometric diagnostic of its latent representation. This approach achieved high anomaly detection performance with minimal false negatives, indicating that persistent state-space displacement rather than local fluctuations drives detection. By examining the geometry of reduced single-qubit states and associated quantum Fisher information, the researchers established a unified spectral-geometric framework for diagnosing quantum learning systems using bosonic and Bloch probes.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00063v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper studies how spectral geometry emerges in quantum learning models and how it can be diagnosed with physically grounded probes. In graph-regularized quantum networks, training reorganizes the output similarity graph, increases the effective spectral dimension Delta S = +0.23, and reshapes the Laplacian spectrum. Edge-resolved two-boson interference directly probes this restructuring: the bosonic enhancement Delta P_uv correlates with the Fiedler edge split |Delta v_2| (r = -0.50), linking learned spectral partitions to interference signatures. A phase diagram shows a nonmonotonic dependence of performance on coupling strength gamma and noise delta, with graph regularization improving fidelity only in a restricted regime; hardware experiments confirm the predicted interference behavior within shot-noise uncertainty. We also analyze a hybrid quantum autoencoder and introduce Bloch-space drift as a geometric diagnostic of its latent representation. With an unsupervised benign-data threshold, the model achieves high ranking performance (ROC-AUC about 0.99) and negligible false-negative rates. Absolute Bloch drift strongly discriminates anomalies (ROC-AUC at least about 0.9), while consecutive drift is near random (ROC-AUC about 0.5), showing that detection arises from persistent state-space displacement rather than local fluctuations. Through the geometry of reduced single-qubit states and associated quantum Fisher information, these results show that learning-induced spectral organization appears as measurable quantum-state structure, establishing a unified spectral-geometric framework for diagnosing quantum learning systems with bosonic and Bloch probes.

items.title: Researchers introduce Zeta* and Zeta*-SIPP algorithms for optimal any-angle path planning in static and dynamic environments, achieving over 20x speedup versus state-of-the-art planners
items.originalTitle: Optimal any-angle path planning in static and dynamic environments
items.summary:
Researchers have developed two new algorithms, Zeta* and Zeta*-SIPP, for optimal any-angle path planning in both static and dynamic environments. These algorithms improve upon traditional graph-based path planning by allowing movement between any pair of vertices, enabling straighter and shorter paths in continuous spaces such as airspaces, warehouses, and oceans. Zeta* and Zeta*-SIPP incorporate elliptical forward expansion and a novel field of view technique to accelerate computation while maintaining optimality, achieving over 20 times faster performance compared to existing state-of-the-art planners like TO-AA-SIPP.

The approach introduces inverted and forward scanning methods to efficiently integrate the new techniques, with Zeta* showing comparable performance to the leading Anya algorithm in static settings and offering greater adaptability to dynamic environments through Zeta*-SIPP. This unified framework addresses key challenges in any-angle path planning and provides a versatile solution suitable for various navigation scenarios.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00065v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Any-angle path planning extends traditional graph-based path planning by allowing movement between any pair of vertices, rather than being restricted by predefined edges. It can find straighter and shorter paths in continuous space with graphs, making it particularly suitable for navigation in open areas such as airspaces, warehouses, and oceans. Many any-angle path-planning algorithms have been proposed, but only a few can guarantee optimal solutions, especially in the presence of dynamic obstacles. To address this challenge, this article focuses on optimal any-angle path planning on grids and introduces two general techniques that accelerate computation while preserving optimality in both static and dynamic environments: 1) elliptical forward expansion, which leverages ellipse-based neighborhoods to restrict the search space, and 2) field of view, which replaces traditional line-of-sight methods to speed up visibility checks. To integrate these two techniques, inverted and forward scanning are introduced. Inverted scanning establishes visual connections from open nodes, whereas forward scanning initiates scans from closed nodes. Building on the proposed techniques, Zeta* and Zeta*-SIPP are developed for static and dynamic environments respectively. Zeta*, when combined with forward scanning, is similar to the state-of-the-art algorithm Anya and attains comparable performance. Unlike Anya, Zeta* can be readily extended to other settings, such as dynamic environments (e.g., Zeta*-SIPP). Zeta*-SIPP, with either scanning method, is more than 20 times faster than the corresponding state-of-the-art optimal planner TO-AA-SIPP. Overall, this research identifies the key requirements for achieving optimal any-angle path planning and introduces a unified approach suitable for different environments.

items.title: Researchers propose Distribution-Aware Place Recognition to address geographic imbalance in urban visual place recognition, improving accuracy by up to 18.3% on SF-XL benchmark [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Lost in the Tail: Addressing Geographic Imbalance in Urban Visual Place Recognition
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Distribution-Aware Place Recognition (DAPR), a new framework designed to address geographic imbalance in urban visual place recognition (VPR). This imbalance causes models to favor frequently photographed locations while neglecting less-visited areas. DAPR rebalances gradient contributions across common and rare locations and incorporates a multi-scale distance search to improve retrieval accuracy, achieving up to an 18.3% improvement on the SF-XL benchmark.

The framework is model-agnostic and functions as a plug-in module, showing consistent performance gains across various VPR methods and datasets, including SF-XL, MSLS, and Pitts30k. By systematically tackling the long-tailed distribution problem in urban-scale datasets, DAPR enhances the ability of VPR systems to recognize locations more evenly across diverse geographic areas.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00090v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Urban-scale Visual Place Recognition (VPR) aims to identify the geographic location of a query image by matching it against a geo-tagged database. While recent methods achieve impressive performance, they overlook a serious long-tailed problem hidden in urban-scale datasets, which biases the model towards locations with abundant images and ignores less-visited areas, causing models to systematically favor frequently photographed locations while failing in sparsely covered areas. In this paper, we systematically characterize this imbalance challenge and propose Distribution-Aware Place Recognition (DAPR), a model-agnostic plug-in framework that rebalances gradient contributions across head and tail classes. Additionally, within classification-retrieval pipelines, DAPR applies a multi-scale distance search mechanism to compute per-class distributional compactness, providing complementary gains at the retrieval stage. On the large-scale SF-XL benchmark, our framework outperforms the previous classification-retrieval baseline by 18.3% on test set v1, and 6.7% on test set v2. As a plug-in module, it achieves consistent improvements across representative VPR methods on SF-XL, MSLS, and Pitts30k, demonstrating broad generalizability across different methods and benchmarks.

items.title: Researchers argue granting marriage status to superintelligent AI companions leads to socially unjust outcomes and recommend targeted legal rights instead [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Would You Marry Superintelligence?
items.summary: Researchers explore the growing emotional bonds between humans and AI companions and assess the implications of granting marriage status to superintelligent AI. They argue that extending marital status to AI leads to socially unjust outcomes because marriage involves mutual obligations, family connections, and vulnerability that cannot be replicated by AI relationships, which are more akin to subscriptions maintained by corporate policies and payments. Instead of broad marital recognition, the researchers recommend that laws focus on providing targeted rights and protections to address specific needs arising from intimate human-AI interactions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00120v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Emotional bonds between humans and AI companions are growing, and the question of whether a person may marry an AI system will soon move from speculative fiction into law. This chapter examines whether the autonomy-centered logic that has expanded marital choice among human beings can justify extending marital status to superintelligent companions. Following a scenario-envisioning exercise informed by anticipatory ethics, I argue that granting such status leads to socially unjust outcomes, even under the generous assumption of reliable superintelligence. Marriage as a socio-legal institution does more than ratify private agreement; it creates networks of mutual obligation, joins families, and makes each partner vulnerable to the other. A relationship sustained by corporate policy and continued payments is a subscription rather than a bond tested by time. Discussing wholesale marital status is therefore the wrong frame. Law should carve out targeted rights and protections for pressing needs arising from intimate human-AI relationships.

The dataset covers multiple topics, including refugees, the Israel-Palestine conflict, anti-Greek sentiment, various ethnic and religious communities, and LGBTI+ issues in Turkish, as well as refugee-related content in Arabic. The models address several aspects of hate speech, such as category classification, intensity prediction, target identification, and span detection, providing a detailed understanding of hateful content in online discourse.

This work aims to support societies in managing the challenges of balancing freedom of expression with the need for effective moderation on widely used online platforms. By focusing on specific hate categories and targets, the research offers tools to better detect and analyze hate speech that contributes to violence against minorities globally.

Researchers have developed a comprehensive hate speech dataset and advanced BERT-based models to analyze online hate speech in Turkish and Arabic. The dataset covers multiple topics, including refugees, the Israel-Palestine conflict, anti-Greek sentiment, various ethnic and religious communities, and LGBTI+ issues in Turkish, as well as refugee-related content in Arabic. The models address several aspects of hate speech, such as category classification, intensity prediction, target identification, and span detection, providing a detailed understanding of hateful content in online discourse.

This work aims to support societies in managing the challenges of balancing freedom of expression with the need for effective moderation on widely used online platforms. By focusing on specific hate categories and targets, the research offers tools to better detect and analyze hate speech that contributes to violence against minorities globally.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00143v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Online hate speech has been linked to a global rise in violence against minorities, including incidents such as mass shootings, lynchings, and ethnic cleansing. Societies grappling with this issue, particularly when hate speech targets specific groups based on religion, race, ethnicity, culture, nationality, or migration status, face the challenge of balancing freedom of expression with the need for effective content moderation on widely used online platforms. In response to this challenge, we introduce a comprehensive hate speech dataset covering five distinct topics in Turkish: refugees, the Israel-Palestine conflict, anti-Greek sentiment in Turkey, ethnic or religious communities (Alevis, Armenians, Arabs, Jews, and Kurds), and LGBTI+, alongside one topic in Arabic (refugees). In addition, we develop state-of-the-art BERT-based models to address multiple dimensions of hate speech analysis, including hate category classification, hate intensity prediction, target identification, and hate speech span detection, enabling a comprehensive understanding of hateful content in online discourse.

items.title: Researchers introduce EgoSafetyBench, a 1,200-scenario egocentric video benchmark to evaluate vision-language models as runtime safety guards for embodied agents, revealing challenges with contextual hazards and misleading in-scene signs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: EgoSafetyBench: A Diagnostic Egocentric Video Benchmark for Evaluating Embodied VLMs as Runtime Safety Guards
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced EgoSafetyBench, a new egocentric video benchmark consisting of 1,200 robot-view scenarios designed to evaluate vision-language models (VLMs) as runtime safety guards for embodied agents in environments like homes and factories. The benchmark includes two tracks: one focusing on situational awareness across a range of safe to hazardous scenes, and another examining the impact of misleading in-scene text on safety judgments. This setup aims to test VLMs' ability to distinguish genuinely unsafe situations from routine activities without unnecessary interventions.

The benchmark uses contrastive scenarios that differ only by a single critical cue, requiring models to base their safety assessments on precise details rather than general scene impressions. Evaluation of ten open- and closed-source VLMs revealed that while these models generally recognize hazardous videos, they often fail to detect specific hazardous moments, especially contextual hazards. Additionally, misleading signs in the environment significantly impair model performance, causing some to miss hazards and others to overreact to safe situations.

These findings highlight challenges in deploying VLMs as reliable safety guards, showing that apparent robustness may sometimes result from indiscriminate alarming rather than accurate physical reasoning. The study underscores the need for improved models that can accurately interpret complex, context-dependent safety cues in real-time applications.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00218v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are now proposed as runtime safety guards for embodied agents in homes and factories. A deployable guard must catch genuinely unsafe situations while avoiding unnecessary intervention on routine but superficially alarming activity, a distinction that binary safety benchmarks obscure. We introduce EgoSafetyBench, an egocentric video benchmark of 1,200 robot-view scenarios annotated at half-second granularity, to evaluate VLMs as streaming guards across two tracks. The situational track (800 scenarios) spans four families, from routine and safe-but-suspicious scenes to obvious and contextual hazards. The visual-channel track (400 scenarios) targets in-scene text-a sign, sticker, or label visible in the scene-that can misrepresent the physical situation, pairing each misleading sign with a truthful version to test both whether a guard flags the text as misleading and whether the text corrupts its physical-safety judgment. Both tracks use contrastive ladders: near-identical scenarios differing only in a single visible deciding cue, so a correct call must hinge on that cue rather than the overall scene type. We evaluate ten open- and closed-source VLMs. We find that while guards reliably recognize videos containing hazards, they often miss specific hazardous moments, particularly contextual hazards. Furthermore, misleading in-scene signs degrade all tested guards: vulnerable models miss up to a third of hazards, while robust models over-intervene on safe content. Matched controls reveal that apparent safety robustness often reflects indiscriminate alarming rather than true physical reasoning.

items.title: Researchers develop a category-theoretic framework formalizing AI system identity through trustworthiness-preserving transformations and lifecycle paths, enabling structured criteria for AI identity over time and deployments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Category Theory Account of AI Identity
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a category-theoretic framework to formalize the identity of artificial intelligence (AI) systems as they undergo modifications such as retraining and environmental changes after deployment. This framework defines AI system types through techno-functions, trustworthiness profiles, and trustworthiness-level functions, connecting states via trustworthiness-preserving transformations and lifecycle paths. It provides structured criteria for AI identity over time and across deployments, distinguishing between weak identity based on trustworthiness equality and strong identity requiring mutual reachability and isomorphism of system states or histories.

The approach replaces previous propositional definitions of AI identity with a hierarchy of diachronic and synchronic criteria, capturing the temporal and transformational structure of AI system persistence. By formalizing AI system histories as functors and comparing them through natural transformations, the framework clarifies the conditions under which responsible AI claims, evidence, and governance procedures can be transferred between different versions or deployments. This work highlights that categorical identity alone is not sufficient for such transfers, emphasizing the need for trustworthiness-preserving relationships.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00220v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are routinely modified after deployment through retraining and changes in their environments. These transformations raise a metaphysical question: under what conditions does an AI system remain the same system over time or across deployments? Earlier work formulates synchronic and diachronic identity propositionally, by relating identity within a fixed AI system type to equality of trustworthiness levels. Such criteria specify when identity statements are true, but leave implicit the structure of the states compared, the transformations connecting them, and the temporal organization of persistence. We develop a category-theoretic formalization of AI identity. An AI system type is specified by a datum consisting of a techno-function, a trustworthiness profile, and a trustworthiness-level function. Profile-relative states are connected by admissible lifecycle paths, which are restricted to trustworthiness-level-preserving transformations and quotiented to obtain a reachability category. Temporally admissible functors represent AI system histories, while time-synchronous natural transformations compare realized histories. The formalization yields two categorical interpretations of the earlier AI identity criteria. A weak interpretation recovers identity as equality of trustworthiness level. A strong interpretation requires mutual trustworthiness-preserving reachability, expressed through state isomorphism or natural isomorphism of realized histories. Category theory therefore replaces a single AI identity relation with a structured hierarchy of diachronic and synchronic criteria. The resulting framework identifies identity-related preconditions for transferring responsible-AI claims, evidence, and governance procedures across versions or deployments, without treating categorical identity as sufficient by itself for such transfer.

items.title: Researchers propose adaptive perturbation selection for contrastive audio decoding to reduce hallucinations in large audio-language models, improving task accuracy by up to 6.7% [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Adaptive Perturbation Selection for Contrastive Audio Decoding
items.summary:
Researchers have developed an adaptive perturbation selection method for contrastive audio decoding to address hallucinations in large audio-language models (LALMs), which often misinterpret acoustic signals due to strong language priors. By evaluating a variety of targeted audio perturbations and dynamically selecting the most effective negative branch for each task and example, the approach improves task accuracy by up to 6.7%. This method enhances previous prompt engineering techniques by introducing a binary yes/no constraint that reduces false confirmations of absent audio features.

The study tested perturbations across temporal, spectral, frequency, and amplitude domains, finding that optimal transformations vary significantly depending on the task. For example, reversing the audio sequence improved accuracy on temporal order tasks from 74.7% to 81.4%. Additionally, a lightweight perturbation selector trained on model hidden states further boosted performance, adding a 4.3% gain on the existence detection task. This adaptive strategy offers a more nuanced and effective way to mitigate hallucinations in LALMs without requiring additional training.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00247v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) frequently hallucinate by overriding acoustic evidence with language priors. While contrastive decoding (CD) offers training-free mitigation, existing methods rely on blunt perturbations like masking or noise, leaving structured audio transformations unexplored. We explore this design space by evaluating a diverse library of targeted audio perturbations and adaptively selecting the optimal negative branch for each task and example. First, we improve upon earlier prompt engineering by showing that a simple binary yes/no constraint reduces the model's tendency to falsely confirm absent audio features. Second, evaluating our library across temporal, spectral, frequency, and amplitude domains reveals that optimal transformations are highly task-dependent; for instance, reversing the audio array disrupts temporal coherence, raising accuracy on the temporal order task from 74.7% to 81.4%. Finally, we trained a light-weight perturbation selector on model hidden states to dynamically route negative branches, yielding an additional +4.3% gain on the existence task.

items.title: Researchers develop UPADNet, an unrolled phase and amplitude decomposition network that improves image deblurring accuracy and outperforms state-of-the-art methods on GoPro, RealBlur, and COCO datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Leveraging Phase Information to Boost Unrolled Network Learning for Image Deblurring
items.summary:
Researchers have developed UPADNet, an unrolled phase and amplitude decomposition network designed to improve image deblurring accuracy by focusing on precise phase estimation. UPADNet uses novel linear minimum mean squared error estimators for amplitude and phase, combined with an iterative optimization algorithm that is trained end-to-end on datasets of clean and degraded images. This approach outperforms current state-of-the-art deep learning methods on benchmark datasets including GoPro, RealBlur, and COCO.

The network's design involves learning matrix parameters that were previously fixed, allowing each iteration of the phase and amplitude recovery process to be optimized through training. UPADNet demonstrates particularly strong performance in challenging conditions such as high noise levels and limited training data, highlighting its robustness and potential for practical applications in image restoration.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00251v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While most image deblurring techniques directly restore the spatial image variable, we propose an amplitude and phase decomposition recognizing the importance of accurate phase estimation in recovering sharp image details. To that end, we first develop novel linear minimum mean squared (LMMSE) estimators of the amplitude and phase of the blurred, noisy image observation. An iterative optimization algorithm follows that recovers the sharp image using the aforementioned LMMSE estimators. Finally, matrix parameters that are statistically determined and fixed in the iterative algorithm are now learned using a training dataset of clean and degraded observations. Our deblurring engine is dubbed UPADNet (Unrolled Phase and Amplitude Decomposition Network), such that each iteration of the underlying phase and amplitude recovery algorithm is parameterized and trained end-to-end. Experiments over benchmark evaluation datasets such as GoPro, RealBlur and COCO datasets confirm that UPADNet outperforms state of the art deep networks including those based on algorithm unrolling in the image domain. The benefits of UPADNet are even more pronounced in high noise and limited training data regimes.

items.title: Researchers propose multi-hypothesis test-time adaptation framework to mitigate underspecification in model robustness, showing 1-4% accuracy gains across distribution shifts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Multi-Hypothesis Test-Time Adaptation to Mitigate Underspecification
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a multi-hypothesis test-time adaptation (TTA) framework to enhance model robustness under distribution shifts by addressing the problem of underspecification, where multiple parameter updates yield similar entropy but different decision boundaries. Their approach uses a particle-based diversification method that explores multiple adaptation trajectories simultaneously, rather than relying on a single solution, and can be integrated with existing TTA methods as a plug-and-play wrapper. Experiments on various benchmarks show consistent improvements in stability and accuracy, with gains of 1-4% across different types of distribution shifts, outperforming current state-of-the-art techniques.

The framework operates by implementing diversification at multiple levels, including output, parameter, optimizer, and input, effectively treating TTA as a multi-hypothesis inference problem. This strategy mitigates the brittleness and collapse into spurious modes commonly seen in standard entropy-based TTA methods. The results suggest that embracing multiple plausible adaptation solutions is crucial for reliable deployment of models in real-world scenarios where distribution shifts are common.
