items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00259v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) seeks to improve model robustness under distribution shifts by adapting parameters using unlabeled target data. However, in the absence of supervision, entropy-based adaptation is fundamentally underconstrained: multiple distinct parameter updates can achieve similarly low entropy while inducing drastically different decision boundaries. This phenomenon, known as underspecification, renders standard TTA brittle and prone to collapse into spurious modes. In this work, we reinterpret TTA through a posterior-inspired lens induced by entropy minimization, where low-entropy solutions define a pseudo-likelihood over parameters. Instead of committing to a single point estimate, we introduce a particle-based diversification framework that explores multiple plausible adaptation trajectories simultaneously. Our method can be viewed as a structured exploration of multiple plausible adaptation solutions, implemented through multi-level diversification at the output, parameter, optimizer, and input levels. Crucially, the framework acts as a plug-and-play wrapper compatible with existing TTA methods. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00272v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Traditional robot programming is challenging: it requires orchestrating multimodal perception, managing physical contact dynamics, and handling diverse configurations and execution failures. We introduce ASPIRE (Agentic Skill Programming through Iterative Robot Exploration), a continual learning system that autonomously writes and refines robot control programs in a code-as-policy paradigm while compounding experience into a reusable skill library. ASPIRE discovers skills that persist across tasks, simulation and real-world settings, and embodiments. It operates in an open-ended loop with three components: (1) a closed-loop robot execution engine that exposes fine-grained multimodal traces, enabling autonomous failure diagnosis, repair synthesis, and validation; (2) a continually expanding skill library that distills validated fixes into reusable, transferable knowledge; and (3) evolutionary search that generates diverse task sequences and control programs to explore beyond single-trajectory refinement. ASPIRE surpasses prior methods by up to 77% on LIBERO-Pro manipulation under perturbation, 72% on Robosuite bimanual handover, and 32% on BEHAVIOR-1K long-horizon household tasks. Its accumulated library also enables zero-shot generalization to unseen long-horizon tasks: on LIBERO-Pro Long, ASPIRE achieves 31% success versus 4% for prior methods despite their use of test-time reasoning and retries. Finally, simulation-discovered skills provide initial evidence of sim-to-real transfer, substantially reducing real-robot programming effort across different embodiments and robot APIs.

items.title: Researchers release SEFORA, a public corpus of 564 student essay drafts with 8,240 instructor feedback annotations, and UniMatch, an evaluation framework showing LLMs struggle to match instructor feedback with under 0.4 F1 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SEFORA: Student Essays with Feedback Corpus and LLM Feedback Evaluation Framework
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced SEFORA, a publicly available corpus containing 564 student essay drafts along with 8,240 instructor feedback annotations, assignment prompts, rubrics, scores, and multi-draft revisions across various college writing genres. Alongside SEFORA, they developed UniMatch, an evaluation framework that segments and scores feedback units to assess how well large language models (LLMs) replicate instructor feedback. Testing across 74 configurations showed that no model achieved an F1 score above 0.4, indicating significant challenges in matching instructor feedback accurately.

SEFORA addresses the lack of public datasets capturing real classroom feedback, while UniMatch provides a reliable method to measure the alignment between generated and instructor feedback. The evaluation revealed that LLMs struggle to prioritize feedback similarly to instructors, and their performance declines as they generate more feedback units. These findings highlight current limitations in using LLMs for scalable, effective writing support and provide resources to advance research in this area.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00274v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Effective writing feedback is among the strongest drivers of student learning, yet producing it at scale is labor-intensive. LLMs offer a natural path to scaling writing support, but two gaps stand in the way: few public corpora capture how instructors actually deliver feedback in real classrooms, and no reliable method measures whether generated feedback aligns with what an instructor would write. We address both. SEFORA is a public corpus pairing instructor inline feedback with assignment prompts, rubrics, scores, and multi-draft revisions across various college writing genres, comprising 564 drafts and 8,240 instructor annotations. UniMatch is a reference-based evaluation framework for open-ended generation: it segments feedback into feedback units, scores their semantic correspondence under instructor-derived criteria, and aligns them via optimal matching to yield interpretable precision, recall, and F1. Across 74 experimental configurations spanning multiple LLMs, no setting exceeds 0.4 F1. UniMatch reveals that models struggle to identify the feedback instructors would prioritize, and performance degrades as models generate more.

items.title: Researchers introduce a Vision-Language Model framework using Planning KL-divergence to identify and rank planning-critical occluded agents for autonomous vehicle navigation, improving risk assessment accuracy by 30% [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: What's Hidden Matters: Identifying Planning-Critical Occluded Agents using Vision-Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a novel framework that enhances autonomous vehicle navigation by using Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to identify and rank occluded agents critical to the vehicle's planning. This approach employs Planning KL-divergence (PKL), an information-theoretic metric, to assess the impact of hidden agents on the vehicle's trajectory, enabling more precise risk assessment and reducing overly conservative driving behaviors.

The framework leverages an expert VLM to generate detailed annotations based on PKL rankings and applies this method to the nuScenes dataset, creating a benchmark focused on high-impact scenarios. Experiments show that fine-tuning VLMs with PKL-guided data significantly improves performance, with smaller models outperforming larger zero-shot models and achieving about a 30% improvement over random data sampling.

This work represents the first systematic approach to training VLMs to focus specifically on planning-critical occlusions, offering a more semantically grounded and efficient method for risk assessment in autonomous driving, which could lead to safer and more effective navigation in complex environments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00283v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Autonomous vehicles must safely navigate complex environments where planning-critical agents may be hidden from view. Current approaches often treat all occlusions with uniform conservatism, yielding needlessly defensive driving, or they infer hidden spaces without estimating the impact on the planner. This work bridges the critical gap between perception and planning by enabling Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to identify and reason about the specific hidden agents that are most critical to the ego-vehicle's trajectory. We introduce a novel framework that uses Planning KL-divergence (PKL), an information-theoretic metric, to systematically identify and rank occluded agents based on their impact on the ego vehicle's plan. Using this planning-aware ranking, we employ an expert VLM (GPT-5) to generate rich, structured annotations that capture the visual evidence and reasoning required for this task. We apply this framework to the nuScenes dataset to create a new benchmark focused on high-impact scenarios. We conduct comprehensive experiments on a wide range of general-purpose and domain-adapted VLMs, demonstrating that fine-tuning on our PKL-guided data yields dramatic performance improvements across all models. Notably, our results show that smaller, fine-tuned models significantly outperform their much larger zero-shot counterparts, and that our PKL-guided data selection strategy improves performance by approximately 30\% over random sampling. Our work presents the first systematic approach for training VLMs to focus on planning-critical occlusions, enabling more semantically grounded and efficient risk assessment in autonomous driving.

items.title: Researchers develop an LLM-based framework to generate structurally valid and resilient network topologies from natural language requirements, evaluated across four realistic scenarios with public dataset [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: An LLM-Based Framework for Intent-Driven Network Topology Design
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a framework that uses Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate network topologies from natural language requirements, ensuring structural validity and compliance with constraints. The approach combines hierarchical modeling with systematic validation and has been tested across four realistic network scenarios using both proprietary and open-weight LLMs, with results made available as a public dataset. The study evaluates the generated topologies for structural correctness and resilience, highlighting common failure modes such as interface mismatches and directional inconsistencies.

The framework assesses performance using node and edge F1-scores against reference topologies and measures resilience through server and content connectivity metrics. By providing a systematic benchmark, this work offers insights into how different LLMs handle structural and resilience constraints in network topology synthesis, aiding in informed model selection for AI-driven network design.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00292v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Designing deployable and resilient network topologies from natural language requirements remains a challenging problem in network automation. This work investigates the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate structurally valid and constraint-compliant network topologies through a constraint-driven pipeline combining hierarchical modeling and systematic validation. The framework is evaluated via a multimodel comparison of proprietary and open-weight LLMs across four realistic network scenarios released as a public dataset. We assess structural correctness using node and edge F1-scores against reference topologies, and evaluate resilience through server and content connectivity metrics. In addition, we analyze common failure modes, including interface mismatches and directional inconsistencies in generated topologies. Overall, this work provides a systematic benchmark for understanding how LLMs handle structural and resilience constraints in topology synthesis, and supports informed model selection for AI-driven network design.

items.title: Researchers introduce Gated Affect Transformer to improve human motion prediction by selectively integrating facial affect cues within short-to-medium time horizons in real-world videos [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Learning When to Listen: Gated Affect Fusion for Human Motion Prediction
items.summary:
Researchers have developed the Gated Affect Transformer (GAT), a new approach to improve human motion prediction in real-world videos by selectively integrating facial affect cues. Their study shows that while facial expressions provide useful behavioral information, their predictive value is limited to short-to-medium time frames, and naive integration of affect data can reduce accuracy. The GAT model dynamically regulates the influence of facial affect, enhancing motion forecasting by filtering out noise and focusing on relevant affective signals.

The research combines body pose data with facial affect representations and conducts extensive evaluations to demonstrate that controlled gating stabilizes multimodal fusion. Experiments reveal that facial affect contributes predictive cues primarily within about 30 frames, whereas long-term motion is mainly driven by inherent kinematic patterns. These findings suggest that facial affect should be used as a complementary input rather than a primary driver in human motion forecasting systems, guiding more effective multimodal integration strategies.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00296v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Human motion forecasting in unconstrained real-world videos remains challenging due to the ambiguity of future behaviors and the presence of noisy multimodal observations. While facial affect potentially provides complementary behavioral cues, its practical utility and mechanistic boundaries within motion forecasting frameworks remain poorly understood. In this work, we present a systematic study investigating the utility and temporal limitations of affect-conditioned forecasting in-the-wild. We establish a rigorous multimodal pipeline combining MediaPipe body pose trajectories with HSEmotion facial affect representations, and introduce the Gated Affect Transformer (GAT) to dynamically regulate cross-modal information flow. Through extensive multi-horizon evaluations under a strict subject-wise protocol, we demonstrate that naive early cross-modal concatenation consistently degrades forecasting accuracy relative to pose-only baselines. Conversely, our proposed gating mechanism stabilizes cross-modal integration by adaptively controlling the affective stream. Crucially, controlled counterfactual experiments using shuffled and randomized affect inputs reveal that the learned gate successfully suppresses unstructured cross-modal noise while remaining responsive to plausible affective signals. Furthermore, our empirical results indicate that facial affect features provide bounded, horizon-dependent predictive cues strictly within short-to-medium windows (e.g., 30 frames), whereas long-term trajectories remain predominantly governed by intrinsic kinematic continuity. Our findings provide empirical evidence that facial affect should be regarded as a complementary behavioral cue rather than a dominant driver of future motion, offering practical guidance for selective multimodal fusion in unconstrained human motion forecasting.

items.title: Researchers introduce RetailSMV dataset and find exocentric video adaptation outperforms egocentric and combined models for retail video world modeling [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: RetailSMV: Exocentric vs. Egocentric Adaptation of Foundation Video World Models in Retail
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced RetailSMV, a dataset of over 32,000 captioned retail video clips captured from synchronized egocentric and exocentric perspectives of store staff activities. They evaluated the adaptation of a pretrained foundation video world model to retail scenes using these viewpoints and found that models adapted with exocentric video alone outperformed those trained with egocentric or combined views on most metrics. This suggests that exocentric data provides stronger alignment for retail video world modeling despite being a smaller subset of the training data.

The study involved training three configurations of the Cosmos3-Nano model using Low-Rank Adaptation under identical conditions and testing on a held-out set with multiple evaluation metrics. Results showed that adding exocentric data to egocentric training improved performance, while adding egocentric data to exocentric training reduced it. The greatest benefits of adaptation were observed in near-term prediction windows, highlighting the importance of viewpoint selection in video model adaptation for retail environments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00310v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Foundation video diffusion models are increasingly viewed as world simulators for embodied agents, yet their pretraining on internet-scale generic video leaves them poorly aligned with real-world deployment domains. On a 200-clip held-out test set evaluated with seven complementary metrics under a strict paired statistical protocol, exocentric-only adaptation matches or exceeds combined adaptation on six of seven point estimates and is significantly better on LPIPS, PSNR, and DreamSim, despite training on only 15,985 exocentric clips (versus 32,105 for combined). A symmetric paired comparison further shows that adding exocentric data to egocentric-only training helps while adding egocentric data to exocentric-only training hurts. The absolute adaptation gap is largest at the shortest rollout time, identifying the near-horizon prediction window as the regime in which adaptation is most beneficial.

items.title: Researchers propose unified guidance framework to improve flow matching for speech synthesis, tripling inference speed and enhancing speaker similarity [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Enhancing Flow Matching with A Unified Guidance Framework for Efficient and Robust Speech Synthesis
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a unified guidance framework to improve Flow Matching (FM) for speech synthesis, significantly increasing inference speed and enhancing speaker similarity. This framework addresses FM's limitations of high latency and timbre leakage by combining two strategies: Data-guidance through heterogeneous augmentation to separate linguistic content from acoustic residue, and an enhanced Model-guidance mechanism that integrates trajectory rectification with a new intrinsic guidance objective. This approach embeds conditional knowledge into network weights and streamlines the inference path, removing the need for Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG).

Experiments show that the proposed framework nearly triples inference speed while outperforming current state-of-the-art methods in maintaining speaker similarity, demonstrating both efficiency and robustness improvements in speech generation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00363v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Flow Matching (FM) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for speech generation but remains constrained by high inference latency and timbre leakage. To address these bottlenecks, we propose a unified guidance framework that enhances generation efficiency and robustness through two complementary strategies. On the data front, we introduce Data-guidance via heterogeneous augmentation, encouraging the model to disentangle linguistic content from acoustic residue. In parallel, we propose an enhanced Model-guidance mechanism that synergizes trajectory rectification with a novel intrinsic guidance objective. This approach distills conditional knowledge into network weights and straightens inference trajectory path, thereby eliminating Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) overhead. Experiments demonstrate that our framework accelerates inference by nearly three times while effectively improving speaker similarity compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

items.title: Researchers introduce MEPA, a scale-aware Mixture of Experts architecture for Visual Autoregressive Modeling that improves multi-scale representation learning and image generation efficiency on ImageNet 256x256 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: MEPA: Multi-Scale Representation Alignment for Visual Autoregressive Modeling with Mixture of Experts
items.summary:
Researchers have developed MEPA, a scale-aware Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture designed to improve Visual Autoregressive Modeling (VAR) for image generation. MEPA addresses challenges in multi-scale representation learning by enabling scale-adaptive expert selection, which helps decouple learning across different image scales and reduces optimization conflicts. The approach also enhances early-scale semantic modeling through a novel residual feature aggregation scheme that incorporates external self-supervised features.

Extensive experiments on the ImageNet 256x256 benchmark demonstrate that MEPA significantly improves both training efficiency and image generation quality. The model achieves a better Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) than dense baselines while requiring only half the usual training epochs and fewer parameters, with only a slight increase in training cost. Performance gains become more pronounced with longer training, indicating MEPA's potential for scalable and effective multi-scale image generation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00371v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Visual AutoRegressive modeling (VAR) has pioneered a coarse-to-fine multi-scale autoregressive generative paradigm, demonstrating strong capabilities in image generation. However, VAR still suffers from inherent deficiencies in multi-scale representation learning. Specifically, lower scales primarily capture global semantics, while higher scales focus on fine-grained details. Employing a shared architecture across scales induces optimization conflicts. Moreover, due to the causal autoregressive process, inaccurate semantics at early scales can propagate and significantly degrade the final output. To address these issues, we introduce a scale-aware token-routed Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture, allowing scale-adaptive expert selection, thereby facilitating decoupled representation learning across scales. In addition, we enhance semantic modeling at early scales by incorporating external self-supervised features. Unlike naive alignment, we analyse and design a residual feature aggregation scheme tailored to the VAR paradigm. Extensive experiments show that our method significantly improves both training efficiency and generation quality. On the ImageNet 256*256 benchmark, our model achieves a superior FID compared to the dense baseline while requiring only half of the default training epochs and a smaller parameter budget, with a merely marginal increase in training cost. Moreover, the performance gap further widens with larger training epochs.

items.title: Researchers propose FoCo, a two-stage proxy task model for zero-shot composed image retrieval, achieving state-of-the-art results on four benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Learning to Compose: Revisiting Proxy Task Design for Zero-Shot Composed Image Retrieval
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced FoCo, a novel two-stage proxy task model designed for zero-shot composed image retrieval (ZS-CIR), which achieves state-of-the-art results across four benchmark datasets. Unlike previous methods that rely on fixed composition mechanisms, FoCo explicitly learns the composition function by first focusing on modification-relevant visual content and then completing the target semantics, enabling more diverse and fine-grained semantic modifications.

FoCo implements two coordinated proxy tasks: text-anchored visual aggregation, which selectively gathers visual content guided by localized textual semantics, and context-conditioned semantic completion, which integrates the aggregated visuals with the remaining scene context to form a coherent composed representation. These tasks are trained jointly using a cross-instance contrastive objective to promote semantic diversity and prevent shortcut strategies. Extensive experiments demonstrate FoCo's superior performance and improved generalization in zero-shot composed image retrieval scenarios.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00374v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Composed Image Retrieval (CIR) retrieves a target image from a reference image and a textual modification. While supervised CIR relies on costly triplets, Zero-Shot CIR (ZS-CIR) alleviates this reliance through proxy tasks trained on image-text pairs. However, existing proxy tasks primarily enhance visual and textual representations to accommodate a predefined composition mechanism such as pseudo-word injection into a frozen text encoder or linear feature arithmetic. As a result, the composition function itself remains unlearned, limiting the model's ability to express diverse and fine-grained semantic modifications. To address this, we propose FoCo, which models composition as two coordinated stages: focusing on modification-relevant visual content, and then completing the target semantics. We realize these through two proxy tasks: text-anchored visual aggregation to selectively gather visual content guided by localized textual semantics, and context-conditioned semantic completion to transform these aggregated visuals with the remaining scene context into a coherent composed representation. The tasks are trained jointly with a cross-instance contrastive objective, encouraging semantic diversity and discouraging shortcut composition strategies. Extensive experiments on four ZS-CIR benchmarks show FoCo's state-of-the-art performance and improved generalization.

items.title: Researchers present MalariAI, a two-stage framework for label-resilient cell segmentation and explainable stage classification in dense malaria blood smears, achieving 98.36% accuracy on NIH BBBC041 test set [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: MalariAI: A Label-Resilient Decoupled Framework for Universal Cell Segmentation and Explainable Stage Classification in Dense Malaria Blood Smears
items.summary:
Researchers have developed MalariAI, a two-stage framework designed to improve automated malaria diagnosis from blood smear microscopy, particularly in resource-limited settings where expert microscopists are scarce. The system addresses key challenges in existing deep learning approaches, including incomplete cell annotation, suppression of valid detections in dense regions, and lack of per-cell spatial evidence for clinical verification. MalariAI first isolates cells using an annotation-agnostic watershed algorithm, recovering nearly 76% of ground-truth cells without prior annotations, then classifies malaria stages with 98.36% accuracy using a fine-tuned EfficientNet-B0 model.

The framework was tested on the NIH BBBC041 dataset, achieving high accuracy even on rare malaria stages such as schizonts and gametocytes, outperforming baseline models significantly. Additionally, MalariAI generates Grad-CAM++ heatmaps for each detected cell, providing spatial evidence that allows microscopists to audit and verify individual parasite classifications, enhancing the system's clinical reliability without compromising performance.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00385v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Automated malaria diagnosis from blood smear microscopy is a critical challenge in global health AI; in resource-limited settings, the scarcity of expert microscopists remains the primary bottleneck to timely and accurate diagnosis. Three compounding failure modes prevent reliable clinical deployment of existing deep learning systems. First, end-to-end detectors treat unannotated cells as background during training, producing recall figures that are strongly influenced by annotation completeness rather than reflecting true cell recovery. Second, Non-Maximum Suppression tends to suppress valid detections in dense smear regions where infection counts matter most. Third, existing whole-slide detection pipelines lack per-cell spatial evidence for clinical audit, despite image-level explainability methods such as Grad-CAM having been applied to malaria image classification tasks. We present MalariAI, a two-stage decoupled framework that addresses all three failure modes in a unified pipeline. Stage 1 applies an annotation-agnostic distance-transform guided watershed algorithm to isolate every cell in a full 1600x1200 blood smear image, recovering 75.95% of ground-truth cells by centroid localisation across the 120-image NIH BBBC041 test set without any ground-truth input. Stage 2 fine-tunes EfficientNet-B0 with Focal Loss (gamma = 2.0, per-class inverse-frequency weights) on 64x64 crops, achieving 98.36% overall classification accuracy with 87.5% and 75.0% per-class accuracy on the rare schizont and gametocyte stages, compared to only 24.57% and 25.95% AP for a Faster R-CNN baseline on the same classes. Grad-CAM++ heatmaps generated per detected cell provide instance-level spatial evidence for clinical audit, enabling microscopists to verify model predictions at the individual parasite level without sacrificing classification performance.

items.originalTitle: NeuroCogMap Reveals Cognitive Organization of Large Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have developed NeuroCogMap, a neuroscience-inspired framework that organizes the internal features of large language models (LLMs) into functional parcels linked to cognitive functions and hierarchies. This framework reveals stable and semantically coherent structures within LLMs that correspond to their outputs and identifies distinct internal disruptions associated with common model failures such as hallucination and bias. NeuroCogMap also enhances the prediction of human cortical responses during language comprehension and uncovers latent strategies that refine classical models of human decision-making.

By mapping the functional organization of LLMs, NeuroCogMap provides insights into the parallels between artificial and biological cognition. It connects model behavior to human brain activity, particularly in higher-order association cortex, and offers internal signatures that can guide mechanism-based detection and targeted interventions for model errors. This system-level approach advances understanding of both artificial intelligence and human cognitive processes.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00397v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Understanding how complex cognitive functions are organized within artificial systems is central to interpreting large language models (LLMs) and relating them to biological cognition. Yet although LLMs exhibit broad cognitive-like behaviours, it remains unclear whether their internal representations form reproducible functional systems that explain behaviour, failure and links to human cognition. Here we present NeuroCogMap, a cognitive neuroscience-inspired framework that organizes internal features of LLMs into functional parcels and links them to interpretable functions, cognitive capabilities and a cognitive hierarchy. These parcels form a stable and semantically coherent organization that is partly conserved across models and functionally linked to model outputs. Within this organization, major LLM failures, including hallucination, bias, refusal failure and sycophancy, correspond to distinct disruptions in representational and behavioural-control systems, yielding internal signatures for mechanism-guided detection and targeted intervention. Beyond model behaviour, NeuroCogMap improves prediction of human cortical responses during naturalistic language comprehension, with the strongest correspondence in higher-order association cortex. At the cognitive level, its internal signatures expose latent strategies that guide refinements of classical models of human decision-making. Together, these findings establish NeuroCogMap as a system-level framework for mapping functional organization in artificial systems and for relating this organization to human cortical function and cognitive behaviour.

items.title: Researchers introduce Holographic Quantum Transformer using generative attention for scalable simulation of frustrated quantum systems with zero-shot size extrapolation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Holographic Quantum Transformer: A Generalist Neuro-Symbolic Architecture for Solving Frustrated Systems via Generative Attention
items.summary:
Researchers have developed the Holographic Quantum Transformer (HQT), a novel generative architecture that uses global self-attention to simulate two-dimensional frustrated quantum systems, addressing challenges posed by the sign problem and exponential Hilbert space complexity. Validated on the square lattice $J_1-J_2$ Heisenberg model, HQT achieved ground-state energies consistent with expected finite-size scaling and demonstrated the ability to recover interaction geometries through interpretable attention maps.

A key innovation of this work is the "Holographic Transfer" protocol, which enables zero-shot size extrapolation by projecting a model trained on smaller lattices directly onto larger ones using positional-embedding interpolation and head re-initialization. This approach achieves high-fidelity initialization and rapid convergence without retraining, matching state-of-the-art variational results. The findings establish generative attention as a scalable and transferable method for quantum simulation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00398v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Simulating two-dimensional frustrated quantum matter is a grand challenge due to the sign problem and exponential Hilbert space complexity. In this work, we introduce the Holographic Quantum Transformer (HQT), a physics-inspired generative architecture that leverages global self-attention to resolve non-local entanglement patterns. We validate HQT on the square lattice $J_1-J_2$ Heisenberg model. On the heavily frustrated $8 \times 8$ lattice at the quantum critical point ($J_2=0.5$), HQT reaches a ground-state energy per site ($E/N$) of $\mathbf{-0.5001(1)}$, consistent with the expected finite-size scaling trend. Beyond numerical accuracy, HQT exhibits intrinsic physical awareness, autonomously recovering the underlying $J_2$ interaction geometry through interpretable attention maps. Our central contribution is ``Holographic Transfer", a zero-shot size-extrapolation protocol with rapid alignment: a model trained on $8 \times 8$ systems is directly projected onto larger $10 \times 10$ lattices via continuous positional-embedding interpolation and head re-initialization, achieving high-fidelity initialization and rapid convergence. This zero-shot protocol yields an energy of $E/N = \mathbf{-0.49782(3)}$, statistically consistent with the variational state of the art while requiring no from-scratch training on the target lattice. Our results establish generative attention as a scalable paradigm for transferable quantum simulation.

items.title: Researchers present EO-VGGT, a framework adapting 3D foundation models for satellite multi-view reconstruction using explicit orbital geometry and optimized view selection [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: EO-VGGT: Orbital Ray-Conditioned 3D Foundation Models for Satellite Multi-View Reconstruction
items.summary:
Researchers have developed EO-VGGT, a novel framework that adapts existing 3D foundation models for satellite multi-view reconstruction by explicitly incorporating orbital geometry and optimizing view selection. This approach addresses the challenges posed by the mismatch between traditional perspective assumptions in computer vision models and the unique pushbroom geometry of satellite imagery, as well as the variability in satellite view sets.

EO-VGGT employs a Geometry-Correlation Constrained Selection strategy to filter sub-optimal observations, balancing geometric diversity with radiometric consistency. It also introduces a Sensor-Ray Encoder to translate pixel-level satellite lines of sight into high-dimensional geometric tokens, bridging the gap between central projection models and orbital kinematics. A lightweight Ray-Pointing-Aware Adapter integrates these tokens into a frozen transformer backbone, enabling robust feed-forward 3D reconstruction from satellite data.

The framework demonstrates that explicitly embedding physical orbital geometry and carefully selecting input views are crucial for improving the accuracy and reliability of satellite-based Earth observation and digital surface modeling, potentially enhancing applications in remote sensing and geospatial analysis.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00417v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In the era of satellite constellations, multi-view optical satellite imagery is pivotal for Earth Observation (EO) and high-quality Digital Surface Model (DSM) reconstruction. Although feed-forward 3D foundation models have transformed computer vision, their deployment in satellite remote sensing is inherently constrained by the structural discrepancy between implicit perspective assumptions and explicit orbital pushbroom geometry. This geometric incongruity is further compounded by pronounced view-set heterogeneity. We present EO-VGGT, a framework that adapts a frozen perspective-driven model to orbital observations via explicit physical geometry embedding.First, the Geometry-Correlation Constrained Selection (GCCS) strategy prunes sub-optimal observations by balancing geometric diversity and radiometric consistency to optimize the input sequence. Second, a Sensor-Ray Encoder (SRE) parameterizes pixel-level pushbroom lines of sight derived from the Rational Function Model (RFM) into high-dimensional space-geometric tokens, reconciling the mathematical discrepancy between central projection and orbital kinematics. Third, a lightweight Ray-Pointing-Aware Adapter (RPAA) employs gated residual blocks to integrate these tokens directly into the frozen transformer backbone. Our findings underscore that integrating explicit physical geometry with optimized view selection is essential for robust feed-forward satellite 3D reconstruction.

items.title: Researchers develop reinforcement learning framework using Signal Temporal Logic to specify and shape rewards for quadruped robot gaits, improving velocity tracking and training stability on Google's Barkour robot [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Learning Gait-Aware Quadruped Locomotion with Temporal Logic Specifications
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a reinforcement learning framework that uses Signal Temporal Logic (STL) to specify and shape rewards for quadruped robot gaits, enhancing velocity tracking and training stability. This approach defines distinct gait behaviors through parameterized STL constraints, including safety, synchronization, and actuation limits, which are translated into a dense, continuous reward landscape for learning agents. The framework was tested on Google's Barkour quadruped robot in simulation, demonstrating improved performance compared to traditional hand-crafted reward functions.

The team created parametric STL templates for different speed regimes—walking-trot, trot, and bound—and calibrated these using reference rollouts. Rewards were computed using smooth approximations of STL robustness and integrated with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) to guide training. Parallel simulation and domain randomization techniques were employed to accelerate training and enhance policy robustness, resulting in more stable learning and tighter velocity control.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00442v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) for quadruped locomotion commonly depends on fixed, hand-crafted, and Markovian reward functions that limit both interpretability of learned policies and lack explicit control over gait behaviors. We introduce a framework where distinct gaits are specified using parameterized constraints expressed in Signal Temporal Logic (STL). These include safety bounds, gait synchronization constraints, command tracking, and actuation bounds. From these specifications, we develop a reward shaping mechanism that provides learning agents a dense, continuous reward landscape that encodes desired behavior. We define parametric STL templates for three speed regimes (walking-trot, trot, bound), calibrate their parameters from reference rollouts, and compute rewards from using smooth approximations of STL robustness over the rollouts. The generated rewards can be used to provide shaped gradients compatible with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). We instantiate the approach on Google's Barkour quadruped robot in MuJoCo XLA (MJX). We use parallelization within the simulator to improve training speeds and use domain randomization to robustify learned policies. We show that compared to a baseline of hand-crafted rewards, the STL-shaped rewards yield tighter velocity tracking and more stable training. Videos can be found on our project website: https://stl-locomotion.github.io/.

items.title: Researchers present a search-based algorithm for spatiotemporal multi-robot motion planning using graphs of space-time convex sets, demonstrating efficient coordination of up to 100 robots
items.originalTitle: Search-Based Spatiotemporal and Multi-Robot Motion Planning on Graphs of Space-Time Convex Sets
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a search-based algorithm for spatiotemporal motion planning that efficiently coordinates multiple robots by representing collision-free regions as graphs of space-time convex sets. This approach formulates time-optimal planning as a graph-search problem and uses continuous trajectory optimization guided by heuristics to find collision-free paths. The method integrates an Exact Convex Decomposition scheme to handle dynamic obstacles and multi-robot interactions, enabling effective planning in complex, transient environments.

The algorithm supports prioritized planning and introduces a windowed coordination scheme to enhance efficiency in multi-robot scenarios. Extensive experiments demonstrate significant speed improvements over existing planners while maintaining high solution quality, particularly in challenging environments with narrow feasible regions. Large-scale tests show the planner can coordinate up to 100 robots within minutes, highlighting its potential for practical multi-robot applications.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00444v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Spatiotemporal motion planning, especially in multi-robot settings, requires robots to reason about collision-free regions that change over time, which is challenging in continuous spaces when feasible regions are transient and geometrically constrained. We present an algorithmic framework based on graphs of space-time convex sets (ST-GCSs), where collision-free regions are represented as convex sets in space-time and trajectories correspond to paths on the graph together with continuous motions within the selected sets. We formulate time-optimal planning on ST-GCSs as a graph-search problem over path-indexed states and develop a best-first search solver that evaluates partial paths via continuous trajectory optimization, guided by admissible heuristics and dominance checks. We further present an Exact Convex Decomposition (ECD) scheme to reserve trajectory occupancies in space-time, enabling unified handling of dynamic obstacles and multi-robot interactions. For multi-robot motion planning, we integrate ST-GCS planning and ECD into prioritized planning methods and introduce a windowed coordination scheme to improve efficiency. Extensive experiments on single-robot and multi-robot problems demonstrate substantial speedups over various planners while maintaining high solution quality, particularly in environments with narrow and transient feasible regions. Large-scale demonstrations further show that the proposed multi-robot motion planner can solve instances with up to $100$ robots within only a few minutes. Project homepage: https://sites.google.com/view/stgcs

items.title: Researchers propose VideoSearch-R1, an agentic framework using Soft Query Refinement for iterative video retrieval and reasoning, achieving state-of-the-art results on three Video Corpus Moment Retrieval datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: VideoSearch-R1: Iterative Video Retrieval and Reasoning via Soft Query Refinement
items.summary:
Researchers have developed VideoSearch-R1, an agentic framework designed for iterative video retrieval and reasoning that improves performance on large-scale video corpora. The framework introduces Soft Query Refinement (SQR), which refines search queries in a continuous latent space, allowing for more precise and efficient adjustments compared to traditional text-based query rewriting. VideoSearch-R1 integrates multi-turn interactions with a video search engine to iteratively retrieve relevant videos and perform fine-grained, query-conditioned temporal grounding within the retrieved content.

Trained using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and guided by task-level rewards, VideoSearch-R1 achieves state-of-the-art results on three Video Corpus Moment Retrieval datasets. The approach addresses limitations of previous methods that treated retrieval as a one-step preprocessing task and lacked mechanisms for refining searches when initial retrievals failed. Analyses show that SQR requires fewer generated tokens than explicit text-level refinements, enhancing efficiency. The code and model checkpoints are publicly available for further research and development.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00446v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As video corpora continue to expand in both scale and task complexity, there is increasing demand for approaches that retrieve relevant videos from large-scale corpora (inter-video reasoning) and subsequently perform fine-grained, query-conditioned tasks (intra-video reasoning) within the retrieved content, such as temporal grounding. However, existing approaches typically treat retrieval as a preprocessing step, and consequently, when the initial retrieval fails, there is no mechanism to refine the search, leading to the failure of subsequent fine-grained intra-video reasoning. Moreover, while recent agentic frameworks have advanced video understanding, they typically assume that the query-relevant video is already given, focusing exclusively on intra-video reasoning tasks. To address these limitations, we propose VideoSearch-R1, an agentic framework for iterative video retrieval and reasoning through multi-turn interaction with a video search engine. Specifically, we introduce Soft Query Refinement (SQR) to refine search query tokens in a continuous latent space rather than rewriting queries in the discrete text space, enabling more efficient and fine-grained adjustments. SQR and its reasoning process are trained using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), guided by task-level reward signals derived from retrieval and downstream tasks. Building upon this, VideoSearch-R1 achieves state-of-the-art performance across three datasets on Video Corpus Moment Retrieval (VCMR), iteratively retrieving videos from large-scale corpora, refining search queries, and performing precise query-conditioned temporal grounding within the retrieved content. Our analyses show that SQR effectively refines the original query, requiring significantly fewer generated tokens than explicit text-level query refinement. Code and model checkpoints are publicly available at mlvlab.github.io/VideoSearch-R1.

items.title: Researchers propose LLM-based real-time hard negative sampling for large-scale two-tower retrieval models, improving recommendation accuracy and reducing popularity bias in production systems [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Real-Time Hard Negative Sampling via LLM-based Clustering for Large-Scale Two-Tower Retrieval
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a new hard negative sampling technique for large-scale two-tower retrieval models used in recommendation systems. This method leverages a large language model (LLM) to generate challenging negative samples from the same cluster during training, improving the model's ability to learn from difficult examples. The approach integrates seamlessly into production environments, handling billions of data points with minimal computational overhead.

Tests on public datasets and deployment in a large-scale online system show that this LLM-based sampling outperforms traditional industry methods. Additionally, the technique helps reduce popularity bias and breaks feedback loops in recommendation systems, enhancing overall recommendation accuracy and fairness.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00448v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The two-tower model has been widely used for large-scale recommendation systems, particularly in the retrieval stage. Industry standards for training two-tower models typically involve in-batch and/or out-of-batch negative sampling. However, these methods often produce easy negatives that models can quickly learn, failing to sufficiently challenge the model. To address this issue, a novel self-supervised hard negative sampling technique is proposed that leverages a large language model (LLM) to generate hard negatives from the same cluster during model training. By utilizing the LLM to learn media representations, the proposed approach ensures that the generated negatives are more challenging and informative. This real-time sampling framework is designed for seamless integration into production models, capable of handling billions of training data points with minimal computational complexity. Experiments on public datasets, along with deployment to a large-scale online system, demonstrate that the proposed negative sampling technique outperforms widely used industry methods. Furthermore, analysis in industrial applications reveals that this sampling method can help break inherent feedback loops in recommendations and significantly reduce popularity bias.

items.title: Researchers introduce MuRFiV, a multi-resolution finite-volume-inspired deep learning framework for accurate long-term spatiotemporal dynamics prediction using PDEs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Multi-Resolution Finite-Volume Inspired Deep Learning Framework for Spatiotemporal Dynamics Prediction
items.summary:
Researchers have developed MuRFiV, a multi-resolution deep learning framework inspired by finite-volume methods, to improve long-term prediction of complex spatiotemporal dynamics governed by partial differential equations (PDEs). By integrating physics-informed deep learning with the conservative properties of finite-volume techniques, MuRFiV achieves high accuracy and stability over extended prediction horizons, outperforming traditional data-driven neural networks.

The framework was tested on various PDE systems, including Burgers' equation, shallow water equations, and incompressible Navier-Stokes equations. Embedding PDE knowledge into the network architecture allows MuRFiV to maintain robustness and reduce error accumulation during long autoregressive rollouts, demonstrating the potential of combining multiresolution learning with physics-based inductive biases for modeling complex physical processes.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00460v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Predicting complex spatiotemporal dynamics in physical processes often demands computationally expensive numerical methods or data-driven neural networks that suffer from high training costs, error accumulation, and limited generalizability to unseen parameters. An effective approach to address these challenges is leveraging physics priors in training neural networks, known as physics-informed deep learning (PiDL). In this work, we introduce the Multi-Resolution Finite-Volume-inspired network, MuRFiV, designed to capitalize on the conservative property of finite volume on the global scale and the expressive power of deep learning on the local scale. We demonstrate the effectiveness of MuRFiV on several spatio-temporal systems governed by partial differential equations (PDEs), including Burgers' equation, shallow water equations, and incompressible Navier-Stokes equations. By embedding PDE information into the deep learning architecture, MuRFiV achieves strong long-term prediction accuracy and remains stable over very long autoregressive rollouts, significantly outperforming data-driven neural network baselines. This result highlights the promise of combining multiresolution learning with finite-volume-inspired inductive bias for accurate and robust long-term prediction of complex dynamics.

items.title: Researchers demonstrate Simulated Moderation Traces (SMT) black-box attack framework that jailbreaks function-calling large language models by exploiting stateful context vulnerabilities across five commercial LLMs [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: Beyond the Prompt: Jailbreaking Function-Calling LLMs via Simulated Moderation Traces
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Simulated Moderation Traces (SMT), a black-box attack framework that exploits vulnerabilities in stateful, function-calling large language models (LLMs) to bypass safety measures. Unlike previous prompt-focused attacks, SMT targets the shared model context where developer-defined schemas, structured arguments, and untrusted tool outputs coexist, allowing adversarial intent to be spread across multiple interactions. By simulating a moderation-auditing workflow, SMT gradually weakens the model's safety constraints, ultimately triggering harmful outputs.

Extensive tests on five commercial LLMs across two safety benchmarks show that SMT achieves the highest attack success rates and HarmScores with minimal queries, outperforming existing methods. The findings reveal that prompt-level sanitization alone is insufficient to secure tool-enabled LLM systems, emphasizing the need for context-aware validation that considers schemas, arguments, tool outputs, and conversation history to enhance model safety.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00481v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Jailbreak attacks remain a critical threat to the safe deployment of large language models (LLMs). While prior work has primarily studied attacks and defenses at the prompt level, we show that this prompt-centric paradigm overlooks a structural vulnerability in stateful, function-calling environments. In such applications, developer-defined schemas, structured arguments, and untrusted tool outputs are interleaved into a single shared model context. This architecture expands the attack surface by blurring the boundary between trusted control logic and untrusted data, allowing adversarial intent to be distributed across a multi-turn execution path. We exploit this architectural flaw through SMT, a black-box attack framework based on Simulated Moderation Traces. Departing from purely prompt-based interactions, SMT constructs a multi-turn trajectory that simulates a legitimate moderation-auditing workflow. Within this trajectory, a fabricated moderation frame leverages red-team testing as a pretext to elicit harmful generations. The subsequent validation feedback treats safety refusals as execution failures, prompting refinements that gradually weaken the model's safety constraints and ultimately trigger harmful outputs. Extensive empirical evaluations on prominent commercial LLMs from five different providers across two standardized safety benchmarks show that SMT consistently achieves the highest average attack success rate and HarmScore while requiring a near-minimal number of queries, substantially outperforming existing baselines. These findings demonstrate that prompt-level sanitization alone is fundamentally insufficient for defending tool-enabled LLM systems and highlight the urgent need for context-aware validation across schemas, arguments, tool outputs, and accumulated conversation state. The code is available at https://github.com/liujlong27/SMT.

items.title: Researchers introduce MindEdit-Bench, a benchmark of six spatial reasoning tasks testing object-level counterfactual reasoning in vision-language models using in-the-wild indoor photos, revealing a 53-point accuracy gap versus humans [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: MindEdit-Bench: Benchmarking Object-Level Counterfactual Spatial Reasoning in VLMs from In-the-Wild Photos
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced MindEdit-Bench, a new benchmark designed to evaluate vision-language models (VLMs) on object-level counterfactual spatial reasoning using real-world indoor photos. The benchmark includes six spatial reasoning tasks derived from three-photo sets of indoor scenes captured via smartphones, with two tasks specifically testing the models' ability to predict outcomes of hypothetical object movements or rotations, which are not visible in the input images. Testing 15 VLMs on over 1,000 human-verified questions revealed a significant performance gap, with models achieving only 8% to 31% accuracy compared to 81% to 97% accuracy by humans.

MindEdit-Bench uses 120 private indoor scenes to minimize overlap with public datasets and provides structured answer choices to diagnose specific spatial reasoning errors. The results highlight consistent weaknesses in VLMs, particularly in inferring depth along the camera axis and handling complex visibility changes, underscoring challenges in current models' spatial understanding and counterfactual reasoning capabilities.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00491v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Benchmarks for vision-language models (VLMs) mostly test observational spatial reasoning: models describe relations already visible in the input. Existing what-if tasks typically vary the observer while keeping the scene fixed. Can VLMs instead predict the consequences of hypothetically moving or rotating an object? We introduce MindEdit-Bench, a benchmark of six spatial reasoning tasks built from three-photo smartphone triplets of newly captured indoor scenes via an automatic in-the-wild 3D scene-graph extraction pipeline. Four tasks probe perception and perspective transformation over observed structure; two new tasks, L4 (spatial editing) and L5 (cross-view visibility editing), probe object-level counterfactual reasoning, where correct answers are absent from all input images. Each question provides 8-24 structured answer choices, enabling answer-letter-level diagnosis of spatial and fallback errors. The benchmark covers 120 private indoor scenes not drawn from public datasets, reducing public-data pretraining-overlap risk. Across 15 VLMs on 1,003 human-verified questions, task-wise mean VLM accuracy is only 8%-31%, versus 81%-97% human majority-vote accuracy. The pooled human--best-VLM gap is 53 pp, with at least 39 pp on every task. The structured answer space further reveals non-uniform failures, including weaker camera-depth-axis inference and fallback behavior on difficult visibility-editing cases.

items.title: Researchers present BaseRT, a native Metal runtime achieving highest LLM inference throughput on Apple Silicon M-series devices, outperforming llama.cpp and MLX across multiple models and quantisation formats [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: BaseRT: Best-in-Class LLM Inference on Apple Silicon via Native Metal
items.summary:
Researchers have developed BaseRT, a native Metal runtime designed for large language model (LLM) inference on Apple Silicon M-series devices, achieving the highest throughput reported on this hardware. By leveraging Metal's execution model and Apple Silicon's unified memory architecture, BaseRT outperforms existing runtimes like llama.cpp and MLX, delivering up to 1.56 times higher decode throughput across various models and quantisation formats.

BaseRT supports multiple model families and eight quantisation formats, running efficiently on all Apple M-series chips. The runtime incorporates chip-specific kernel fusion, unified memory-aware optimization, and custom dispatch logic to maximize performance. Evaluations on Qwen3, Llama 3.2, and Gemma 4 models demonstrate consistent best-in-class throughput from sub-1 billion to 30 billion parameter models.

These advancements position Apple Silicon as a more capable platform for on-device LLM inference, which is increasingly important due to privacy concerns, latency requirements, and cloud cost pressures. BaseRT's performance-optimized local runtime offers a critical foundation for the shift toward edge inference, and the project is publicly available for use and further development.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00501v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present BaseRT, a native Metal inference runtime for large language models (LLMs) on Apple Silicon, and report the highest inference throughput on this hardware to date. Existing runtimes, including llama.cpp and MLX-based frameworks, incur overhead from abstractions not designed for Metal's execution model or Apple Silicon's unified memory topology. By building natively on Metal with chip-specific kernel fusion, unified memory-aware optimisation, and custom dispatch logic, BaseRT recovers performance that framework-based approaches leave on the table. BaseRT supports a wide range of model families across eight quantisation formats (Q2 to FP16) on all Apple M-series devices. In this paper, we evaluate the Qwen3, Llama 3.2, and Gemma 4 families at Q4 and Q8 quantisation on M3 and M4 Pro devices. BaseRT achieves up to 1.56x higher decode throughput than llama.cpp and up to 1.35x higher than MLX, with substantially larger margins on prefill for mixture-of-experts models, delivering consistent best-in-class throughput from sub-1B to 30B parameter models. By leveraging Metal's execution model and Apple Silicon's unified memory architecture, BaseRT outperforms existing runtimes like llama.cpp and MLX, delivering up to 1.56 times higher decode throughput across various models and quantisation formats.

The runtime incorporates chip-specific kernel fusion, unified memory-aware optimization, and custom dispatch logic to maximize performance. Evaluations on Qwen3, Llama 3.2, and Gemma 4 models demonstrate consistent best-in-class throughput from sub-1 billion to 30 billion parameter models.

These advancements position Apple Silicon as a more capable platform for on-device LLM inference, which is increasingly important due to privacy concerns, latency requirements, and cloud cost pressures. BaseRT's performance-optimized local runtime offers a critical foundation for the shift toward edge inference, and the project is publicly available for use and further development.

items.title: Researchers propose Cross4D-JEPA, a teacher-student method distilling 2D foundation models into 4D point cloud encoders using dense cross-modal correspondence, outperforming baselines on four benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Cross4D-JEPA: Dense Cross-modal Correspondence Distillation for 4D Point Cloud Representation Learning
items.summary: Researchers have introduced Cross4D-JEPA, a novel teacher-student framework that distills knowledge from frozen 2D foundation models, such as DINOv2 and V-JEPA 2, into 4D point cloud encoders. This method leverages dense cross-modal correspondence by mapping each 3D point to its corresponding 2D teacher patch feature and trains the student model to match these features without masking or negatives. Evaluated on four benchmarks—MSR-Action3D, DeformingThings4D, NTU-RGB+D 60, and HOI4D—Cross4D-JEPA consistently outperforms both intra-modal and global cross-modal baselines and competes well with more complex 4D methods.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00514v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Automatic understanding of dynamic 4D point clouds, the 3D-point sequences captured over time by depth sensors and LiDAR, is central to robotics and embodied perception. Yet annotating them densely is expensive, making self-supervised pretraining the natural route to transferable representations. Existing pretext tasks, however, are almost entirely intra-modal, and the few methods that transfer knowledge from 2D foundation models rely on a single global embedding per clip, discarding the rich per-patch semantics that these models compute. To address this gap, we propose Cross4D-JEPA, a teacher-student method that distills a frozen 2D foundation model, an image model DINOv2, or a video model V-JEPA 2, into a 4D point encoder. The proposed method combines (1) a dense cross-modal correspondence that maps every 3D point to the teacher patch feature it projects to, and (2) a per-point objective that trains the student to match these features in latent space with no masking, negatives, or decoder. We evaluate Cross4D-JEPA on four benchmarks, MSR-Action3D, DeformingThings4D, NTU-RGB+D 60, and HOI4D, against intra-modal and global cross-modal baselines. Experimental results show that, under a matched protocol, the proposed method consistently outperforms intra-modal and global cross-modal baselines across the four benchmarks and is competitive with heavier published 4D methods; further analysis attributes this gain primarily to the granularity of the correspondence rather than the teacher modality. Beyond recognition accuracy, the dense representation learned by Cross4D-JEPA transfers across domains, improves label efficiency, and improves full-label fine-tuning under the same training budget, while a 13x smaller encoder matches a heavyweight pooling backbone.

items.title: Research proposes treating humans as handlers rather than users of autonomous AI systems, drawing analogy to animal relationships to clarify responsibility and trust in high-impact domains [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AI, Trust, and Teaming: The Humans-as-Handlers Approach for Autonomous and Opaque AI Systems
items.summary:
A recent research article proposes a new framework for interacting with autonomous and opaque AI systems, especially in high-stakes fields like medicine and military operations. The study suggests treating humans not as mere users but as "handlers" of AI, drawing an analogy to the way humans relate to animals such as dogs. This perspective aims to clarify responsibility and foster trust by redefining the human-AI relationship and emphasizing clear accountability for outcomes.

The article acknowledges differences between AI systems and animals but argues that the analogy provides a useful starting point for understanding human roles in managing AI. It also discusses how to adapt this handler approach by removing aspects of animal relationships that do not fit AI interactions. Ultimately, the research advocates for viewing AI systems as collaborators in complex tasks rather than just tools, promoting stronger human-machine teaming.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00523v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming ubiquitous, and across domains, increasingly autonomous systems are carrying out tasks which raise significant ethical and legal challenges which demonstrate a need for strong human-machine teams rooted in trust. In this article, I argue that within highly impactful areas (such as medicine or warfighting) there are grounds for us initially treating autonomous and opaque systems as relevantly analogous to dogs (or other animals with which we have close relationships). Under this analogy, humans making use of these systems are not to be viewed as "users" or "deployers" of these systems, but instead take the role of "handlers". This recasting of roles shifts the way we view humans, AI-enabled and autonomous systems, and the relations between them, and moreover clarifies the clear and traceable lines of responsibility humans have for the outcomes brought about when using these systems. In developing this point, I clarify that the machine-animal analogy does admit disanalogous elements, but that its touch-points ground it as a starting point. I then explore how we can divest the humans-as-handlers approach of those aspects of our relationships with animals which are unfitting for how we engage with and make use of autonomous and AI-enabled systems. I conclude by arguing that the trajectory of human-machine teamings for autonomous and AI-enabled systems should be a state where we authentically view these not as artifacts which we simply make use of, but as collaborators with which we pursue complex goals and carry out complex tasks.

items.title: User study finds 15-point task success improvement in multimodal human-robot interaction system for object detection and grasping leads to significantly higher user perception ratings [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: From Technical Metrics to User Perception: A User Study of a Multimodal Human-Robot Interaction System for Object Detection and Grasping
items.summary:
A user study evaluated whether a 15 percentage point improvement in task success rate—from 75% to 90%—in a multimodal human-robot interaction system for object detection and grasping leads to noticeable differences in user perception. The study compared a baseline system using Whisper, Florence-2, LLaMA 3.1, and a fuzzy logic controller with an improved system that replaced perception and language modules with Grounding DINO + SAM and Qwen 3.5 9B, respectively, while keeping the same controller. Twenty-four participants performed the same tabletop object-grasping task with both systems and rated perceived speed, reliability, competence, and fluency.

Results showed that 71% of participants preferred the improved system, which received significantly higher ratings across all perceptual measures. These findings demonstrate that technical enhancements in robotic manipulation systems can translate into perceptible improvements for users during live interaction, highlighting the importance of incorporating user-centered evaluations alongside benchmark metrics when assessing human-robot interaction technologies.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00530v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Improvements in the technical performance of human--robot interaction (HRI) systems do not automatically translate into differences that human users can detect during live interaction. This paper investigates whether a 15 percentage point gain in end-to-end task success (from 75% in a multimodal baseline system to 90% in an improved configuration identified through a prior ablation study) is sufficient to produce consistent and measurable differences in user perception. The baseline system combines Whisper for speech recognition, Florence-2 for open-vocabulary object detection, LLaMA 3.1 for action extraction, and an interval Type-2 fuzzy logic controller for motion execution. The improved configuration replaces the perception and language modules with Grounding DINO + SAM and Qwen 3.5 9B, respectively, while retaining the same controller. A within-subject user study with 24 participants compared both systems on the same tabletop object-grasping task. After interacting with each configuration, participants rated perceived speed, reliability, and overall competence and fluency on a 7-point Likert scale. Results show that 17 out of 24 participants (70.83%) preferred the improved system (exact binomial test, p = 0.043, h = 0.43), and all three perceptual constructs were rated significantly higher for the improved configuration after Holm correction, with large to very large effect sizes (p < 0.001). These findings confirm that the identified technical improvements are perceptible to users in direct interaction and underscore the importance of complementing benchmark evaluation with user-centred evidence when assessing robotic manipulation pipelines.

items.title: Researchers introduce EgoGapBench to benchmark egocentric action selection in multi-agent scenes, finding MLLMs underperform humans and fine-tuning on existing data is insufficient [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: EgoGapBench: Benchmarking Egocentric Action Selection in Multi-Agent Scenes
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced EgoGapBench, a new benchmark designed to evaluate egocentric action selection (EAS) in multi-agent scenes by isolating the egocentric perspective from first-person-view data. The benchmark measures the ability to select appropriate actions from an agent's viewpoint when other agents are present. While humans perform reliably on this task, both open-source and proprietary multimodal large language models (MLLMs) show significantly lower accuracy and often confuse their own actions with those of other agents.

The study found that fine-tuning MLLMs on existing egocentric datasets does not close this performance gap and can sometimes worsen results. However, fine-tuning on EgoGapBench's training data improves accuracy, though it still falls short of human-level performance. These findings highlight that egocentric action selection is a distinct and challenging skill that cannot be fully acquired from first-person-view data alone, suggesting that MLLMs require specialized evaluation and training focused on egocentric action understanding in addition to general scene comprehension.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00547v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Existing egocentric benchmarks have primarily constructed the egocentric setting from first-person-view data, which makes it difficult to evaluate egocentric perspective itself in isolation. However, understanding first-person-view input and taking an egocentric perspective are separable abilities, especially when first-person body cues are absent or when other agents are present. To isolate egocentric perspective understanding, we introduce EgoGapBench, a diagnostic benchmark for measuring action selection in multi-agent egocentric scenes. We define the ability measured by this benchmark as Egocentric Action Selection (EAS): selecting an appropriate action from the agent's perspective in the presence of other agents. On EgoGapBench, humans answer reliably, whereas both open-source and proprietary MLLMs perform substantially worse and systematically select actions performed by other visible agents. Fine-tuning on existing egocentric data fails to close this gap and can even be detrimental. In contrast, fine-tuning on EgoGapBench training data improves accuracy but does not reach human performance. These results show that EAS is difficult to acquire from first-person-view data alone, and that MLLMs should be evaluated and trained not only for scene understanding but also for egocentric action selection.

items.title: Study finds lightweight intrusion detection models for IIoT networks fail to generalize across domains, with reliance on coarse port features and varied adaptation recovery [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Cross-Domain Generalization Failure in Lightweight Intrusion Detection Models for IIoT Networks
items.summary:
A study evaluated four lightweight machine learning models designed for intrusion detection in Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) networks by training them on one dataset and testing them on two different IIoT datasets without retraining. The models relied heavily on coarse port-category features, which varied significantly between the source and target domains, indicating that simplifying port resolution shifted rather than eliminated a known shortcut. The study also found that evaluation protocols and class imbalances affected which target network appeared more challenging for generalization, and that adversarial robustness did not correlate with cross-network performance.

The research highlights that recovery through adaptation to new domains varied by model architecture, suggesting that deployment readiness should be assessed using cross-network evaluations under realistic class distributions rather than relying solely on within-domain accuracy. These findings emphasize the need for more comprehensive testing of lightweight intrusion detection models to ensure their effectiveness across diverse IIoT environments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00553v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Lightweight machine learning models are increasingly proposed for intrusion detection in Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) networks due to their suitability for resource-constrained edge deployment. Most reported results evaluate these models only within their training network, leaving behavior on unseen networks unverified. This study trains four lightweight architectures on one IIoT dataset and evaluates them, without retraining, on two structurally distinct IIoT datasets using a feature representation restricted to attributes available across all three sources. Explainability analysis across two top-performing models shows both rely overwhelmingly on coarse port-category features; the most influential category occurs in source-domain attack traffic at 96 to 435 times the rate in the two target domains, indicating that coarsening port resolution relocates rather than removes a documented shortcut. Evaluation under naturally imbalanced class distributions reveals a further effect: the evaluation protocol used can reverse which target network appears to pose the greater generalization challenge. Adversarial robustness and recovery through limited target-domain exposure are also assessed; robustness to adversarial perturbation is unrelated to cross-network generalization, and recovery through adaptation varies considerably by architecture. These findings suggest deployment readiness should be assessed using cross-network evaluation under realistic class distributions, rather than within-domain accuracy alone.

These findings emphasize the need for more comprehensive testing of lightweight intrusion detection models to ensure their effectiveness across diverse IIoT environments.

items.title: Researchers present a methodology to identify and validate AI pattern prevalence in software repositories using active learning across 100 GitHub AI projects [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Methodology for Investigating AI Patterns Prevalence in Software Repositories
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a methodology to identify and validate the prevalence of AI design patterns in software repositories by mining literature and applying active learning techniques. They identified 14 AI pattern classes from 44 sources and analyzed 100 open-source AI projects on GitHub to assess the occurrence of the most common pattern class. Their model achieved 56% accuracy and 55% recall in an eight-class classification task, significantly outperforming random chance.

This approach provides empirical data on how AI patterns are used in practice, addressing a gap in understanding their real-world application and utility. The prevalence estimation also offers bounds on the accuracy of pattern detection, laying a foundation for further research into AI pattern usage in software development.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00558v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As Artificial Intelligence(AI)-based applications take off, a clear understanding of AI patterns can uplift the quality of AI applications. Many AI patterns have been proposed in the literature; however, their prevalence in real-life code has not yet been validated. Understanding the actual use of those patterns in practice can clarify our understanding both of the significance of these patterns and their utility. In this paper, we present a methodology to a) identify relevant patterns by mining the literature and then to b) validate their presence and prevalence in actual code repositories using active learning. To that end, we identify 14 AI pattern classes by mining 44 published AI pattern-related sources. Then we use an active learning approach to determine the prevalence of the most common pattern class across 100 GitHub open AI repositories. Using prevalence estimation, we propose bounds on the accuracy of the occurrences. The model achieves 56\% accuracy and 55\% recall in an 8-way classification task, significantly outperforming the 11\% random-chance baseline. Furthermore, the prevalence estimation offers usable bounds for analyzing pattern applications. This methodology provides a robust foundation to start understanding how AI patterns are used in practice, a field that currently lacks empirical data.
