items.title: Researchers propose Compositional Primitive Fields to reshape vision model features for improved generalized category discovery by identifying low-rank compositional structures in images [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Identifying Latent Concepts and Structures for Generalized Category Discovery
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Compositional Primitive Fields (CPF-GCD), a new framework designed to improve Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) by reshaping vision model features to reveal low-rank compositional structures in images. This approach addresses the limitations of current vision backbones, which produce high-rank, entangled representations that hinder the unsupervised discovery of latent concepts. CPF-GCD models images as compositions of a finite set of learnable visual primitives arranged spatially, enabling the identification of both known and novel categories through structured, reusable components.

CPF-GCD operates by inserting a spatial field mechanism between the backbone and classification head, rewriting noisy patch tokens into mixtures of low-rank primitives that capture atomic parts and their layouts. This explicit modeling of spatial distributions allows novel categories to emerge naturally as new activation patterns over a shared vocabulary. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CPF-GCD can be integrated as a plug-and-play module to consistently enhance performance across various GCD baselines, highlighting the importance of leveraging low-rank compositional structures for open-world recognition tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00620v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) aims to recognize known classes while autonomously discovering novel ones in open-world settings. However, current approaches primarily focus on designing clustering objectives, often overlooking a critical bottleneck: standard vision backbones yield high-rank, entangled token representations that are ill-suited for unsupervised discovery of latent concepts and structures. In this paper, we propose Compositional Primitive Fields (CPF-GCD), a novel representation learning framework that reshapes the feature space to make such latent structure identifiable by enforcing a low-rank compositional organization. Our core hypothesis is that all categories, whether known or novel, can be expressed as compositions and spatial arrangements of a finite set of learnable visual primitives that capture reusable concepts. CPF instantiates this geometric constraint via a spatial field mechanism. Inserted between the backbone and the head, it rewrites noisy patch tokens through low-rank primitive mixtures, effectively decomposing images into reusable atomic parts and their spatial layouts. By explicitly modeling the spatial distribution of primitives, CPF enables novel categories to emerge naturally as new activation patterns over a shared vocabulary. This shifts the focus of representation from merely partitioning global embeddings to constructing a structured and separable primitive field. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CPF serves as a generic, plug-and-play module that consistently boosts performance across diverse GCD baselines, validating that identifying and leveraging low-rank compositional structure is a crucial inductive bias for open-world recognition.

items.title: Researchers present a Natural Semantic Metalanguage-based interface for event-based emotion analysis with causal faithfulness and release EmoExpl-1200 dataset and rule set [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Faithful by Definition: Emotion Analysis via Natural Semantic Metalanguage Explications
items.summary:
Researchers have developed an interface for event-based emotion analysis that uses the Natural Semantic Metalanguage (NSM) framework to provide explanations that are causally and definitionally faithful to the emotion classification process. Their approach involves a parser that converts input text into a structured explication using a fixed vocabulary and a decision list of rules derived from semantic definitions, ensuring that the emotion label is computed transparently from the explication rather than through a black-box model. This method allows for auditability and verification of the classification process.

The team fine-tuned the parser on crowd-sourced event descriptions, achieving moderate accuracy while prioritizing interpretability over raw performance. Alongside this interface, they released the EmoExpl-1200 dataset, which includes per-line verification metadata and the complete rule set, supporting further research and evaluation in explainable emotion analysis.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00661v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Explanations for emotion classifiers are usually produced post hoc, with no guarantee that they reflect the computation behind the label. We present an explication interface for event-based emotion analysis. A parser maps the input text to an explication, a short script in the closed vocabulary of Natural Semantic Metalanguage organized into twelve typed slots, and a fixed decision list of rules transcribed from published semantic definitions computes the label from the explication alone. The faithfulness guarantee is therefore causal and definitional, while all empirical risk lives in the learned parser, which the per-line entailment interface makes auditable against the input. On crowd-sourced event descriptions, our fine-tuned parser reaches 0.33 accuracy and 0.48 selective accuracy on a small held-out set, suggesting that the interface trades insignificant accuracy difference to a black-box model for a verifiable, inspectable decision basis for first-person event-based emotion analysis. We also release EmoExpl-1200 with per-line verification metadata and the full rule set.

items.title: Researchers introduce LLVM-Bench and LLVM-Gym to benchmark and improve large language models for LLVM compiler issue resolution, achieving up to 21.99% resolution rate with LLVM-Ens ensemble approach [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: LLVM-Bench: Benchmarking and Advancing Large Language Models for LLVM Compiler Issue Resolution
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced LLVM-Bench, the first large-scale benchmark designed to evaluate large language models (LLMs) on issue resolution within the LLVM compiler infrastructure, which is known for its complexity and scale. Alongside LLVM-Bench, they developed LLVM-Gym, an automated platform that facilitates issue reproduction, patch application, compiler building, and testing. Their study assessed multiple LLMs and configurations, revealing that current LLM-based methods face challenges such as patch invalidity and build failures when applied to LLVM issues.

To address these limitations, the team proposed LLVM-Ens, a lightweight ensemble approach that combines patches generated by diverse techniques, filters out incorrect or redundant solutions, and selects the most promising fixes. This method improved the resolution rate to 21.99%, demonstrating enhanced effectiveness in resolving LLVM compiler issues and advancing the application of LLMs in complex system-level software maintenance.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00700v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLVM is a widely used compiler infrastructure whose scale and complexity make issue resolution labor-intensive and challenging. Although large language models (LLMs) have recently achieved remarkable success in issue resolution, their effectiveness on complex system-level LLVM compiler remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we introduce LLVM-Bench, the first large-scale benchmark for LLVM issue resolution, containing 423 real-world, validated tasks collected from the LLVM project. We further develop LLVM-Gym, a scalable evaluation platform that automates issue reproduction, patch application, compiler building, and test execution. Using LLVM-Bench and LLVM-Gym, we conduct a comprehensive study of four representative LLMs, six retrieval configurations, and three agents. Our results show that current LLM-based issue resolution techniques remain limited on LLVM-Bench, with patch invalidity and build failures as the dominant failure modes. We further reveal a strong complementarity among different LLMs and agents, motivating LLVM-Ens, a lightweight ensemble approach that expands the patch space through integrating the patches generated by diverse techniques, filters incorrect and redundant candidates, and identifies the most promising solution. Our results show that LLVM-Ens achieves a resolution rate of up to 21.99%, further improving LLVM issue resolution.

items.title: Researchers publish strategic framework for designing impactful autonomous driving datasets, analyzing major datasets and introducing the KITScenes dataset family [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Creating Impactful Autonomous Driving Datasets: A Strategic Guide from Research Gap to Benchmark
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a strategic framework for designing impactful autonomous driving datasets, addressing a gap in existing literature that focuses more on dataset content than on strategic creation. Their approach emphasizes diagnosing whether research challenges stem from data or evaluation issues and selecting minimal data operations to efficiently close these gaps, recording new data only when necessary. This framework is illustrated through an analysis of major autonomous driving datasets and a case study of the newly introduced KITScenes dataset family.

The framework covers key aspects such as identifying research gaps, choosing appropriate data operators, designing sensor suites, and developing annotation strategies. By applying this method, the researchers aim to help smaller labs and startups optimize resource use and avoid costly missteps in dataset creation. The KITScenes datasets are publicly available for further research and development in autonomous driving.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00710v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Well-designed autonomous driving datasets have fundamentally shaped research progress, yet existing literature primarily describes what datasets contain rather than how to strategically design impactful ones. This is especially limiting for small and medium-sized labs and startups that cannot afford to misallocate scarce resources. We argue that impactful dataset creation begins with a diagnosis: whether a research question is blocked by a data problem or an evaluation problem, and proceeds by selecting the minimal data operator(s) that closes the resulting gap, recording new data only when no cheaper operator(s) suffices. We analyze the evolution of major autonomous driving (AD) datasets through this lens and distill a strategic framework spanning gap identification, operator choice, sensor suite design, and annotation strategy. We ground the framework in a running case study of our KITScenes dataset family. The datasets are available at: https://kitscenes.com/

items.title: Researchers propose fixed-point flows to enhance self-conditioned flow map language models, improving one- and few-step text generation performance on OpenWebText [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Self-conditioned Flow Map Language Models via Fixed-point Flows
items.summary:

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00714v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-conditioning is a core technique that enhances continuous flow-based language models, where the model learns to denoise generated text by conditioning on its own denoising estimate. While empirically successful, its performance improvements are poorly understood. Moreover, there is growing interest in the use of few-step generators based on flow maps, for which how to leverage self-conditioning is unclear. Here, we show that flow language models with self-conditioning solve a fixed-point iteration that bootstraps the performance of the learned denoiser. We use this viewpoint to formulate fixed-point flows, a two-dimensional class of self-conditioned flows, where the first dimension represents the flow process and the second represents the fixed-point iteration. We show that fixed-point flows define valid flow maps, and show that they can be distilled from self-conditioned flow models by compressing both fixed-point iterations and the flow process, the former with fixed-point distillation and the latter with flow map distillation. Our resulting flow map language model, FMLM$^\star$, outperforms state-of-the-art self-conditioned models and few-step models in one- and few-step generation on OpenWebText. Code is available at https://github.com/Ugness/self-conditioned-fmlm.

items.title: Researchers introduce PartialVisGraph, a hypergraph framework for robust skeleton-based action recognition under constrained field-of-view, achieving up to 68.8% accuracy gains on NTU RGB+D benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Partial Skeleton Visibility for Action Recognition: A Constrained Field-of-View Approach
items.summary:
Researchers have developed PartialVisGraph, a novel hypergraph-based framework designed to improve skeleton-based action recognition in scenarios with limited field-of-view (FoV), where joint visibility is often incomplete. This approach introduces learnable virtual hyperedges and a Single-Head Sample-Adaptive Transformer that incorporates a visibility prior to prevent occluded joints from degrading feature propagation. PartialVisGraph demonstrates significant accuracy improvements, achieving up to 68.8% gains on NTU RGB+D benchmarks under severe FoV constraints compared to existing methods.

The framework addresses challenges common in real-world applications such as egocentric vision, crowded surveillance, and wearable devices, where partial visibility of skeletal joints can severely impact recognition performance. By constructing expressive hypergraphs and selectively gating information flow based on joint visibility, the method maintains robust action recognition even with substantial joint dropout. Extensive evaluations on NTU RGB+D 60 and 120 datasets validate its effectiveness, showing consistent state-of-the-art results both under partial and full visibility conditions.

This advancement offers a practical solution for deploying skeleton-based action recognition systems in unconstrained environments, enhancing their reliability and applicability in diverse real-world settings where sensor viewpoints are limited or obstructed.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00716v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Skeleton-based action recognition has achieved remarkable success by exploiting joint coordinates and their topological connections, yet prevailing methods overwhelmingly assume complete and clean skeleton inputs. In real-world deployments, such as egocentric vision, crowded surveillance, wearable devices, or edge robotics, limited field-of-view (FoV) frequently causes substantial joint visibility dropout, leading to severe performance degradation that existing models are largely unprepared to handle. To bridge this critical yet underexplored gap, we introduce PartialVisGraph, a novel hypergraph framework tailored for robust skeleton action recognition under constrained FoV. We first construct highly expressive hypergraphs by introducing learnable virtual hyperedges that form a soft incidence matrix, capturing flexible high-order dependencies beyond conventional pairwise graphs. We then propose the Single-Head Sample-Adaptive Transformer, which adaptively aggregates joint features onto hyperedges while explicitly incorporating a visibility prior. This prior selectively gates information flow, preventing occluded or out-of-view joints from corrupting reliable feature propagation. We further establish rigorous evaluation protocols with realistic FoV simulation benchmarks on NTU RGB+D 60 and 120. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PartialVisGraph consistently achieves state-of-the-art accuracy under partial visibility, with gains of up to 68.8\% on subsets with severe FoV restrictions compared to recent strong baselines, while remaining superior on full-visibility settings. Our approach offers a principled and practical pathway toward deployable skeleton-based action understanding in unconstrained environments.

items.title: Researchers propose ConRTF, a real-time Transformer-based table structure recognition method using edge-constrained boundary refinement and fine-grained localization loss, improving accuracy on PubTables-1M with minimal training data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ConRTF: Edge-Constrained Boundary Distribution Refinement for Realtime TransFormer Table Structure Recognition
items.summary:
Researchers have developed ConRTF, a real-time Transformer-based method for table structure recognition that improves the accuracy of identifying row and column layouts in document images. This approach introduces an Edge-constrained Fine-grained Localization loss (EFL) that accounts for the distinct structural roles of rows and columns by emphasizing their respective boundary orientations during training. ConRTF integrates this loss with a distribution-based boundary refinement technique, enhancing boundary precision without altering the inference process.

The method demonstrates data efficiency, maintaining strong performance with as few as 2,000 to 3,000 annotated tables. Evaluations on the PubTables-1M dataset and two private datasets show that ConRTF consistently outperforms optimized baselines and several real-time detectors, including RT-DETRv2 and YOLOv10-11, achieving up to a 1.6-point improvement in GriTS score at comparable inference speeds.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00734v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Table Structure Recognition (TSR) aims to recover the row and column layout of tables from document images, a key step in document understanding pipelines. Accurate TSR depends on precise boundary localization: small errors in row or column boundaries can propagate into incorrect cell assignments and structural inconsistencies. Yet detection-based approaches treat table elements as generic objects, ignoring a fundamental property of table layout: rows and columns play structurally distinct roles and their boundaries carry unequal importance. We propose an Edge-constrained Fine-grained Localization loss (EFL) that formalizes this structural asymmetry by encoding table-specific geometric priors into the training objective: row-like elements are supervised with emphasis on their horizontal boundaries, while column-like elements prioritize vertical boundaries. Implemented within a real-time detector with distribution-based boundary refinement (D-FINE), EFL operates during training only and guides boundary refinement toward structurally meaningful adjustments with no change to the inference pipeline. The proposed approach, ConRTF, is also data-efficient, maintaining robust accuracy with as few as 2k--3k annotated tables. Experiments on PubTables-1M and two private datasets show consistent improvements over the optimized baseline and several real-time detectors including RT-DETRv2 and YOLOv10-11, with gains of up to +1.6 GriTS points at equal inference speed.

items.title: Researchers find hallucinated citations in peer-reviewed papers at ICLR, ICML, NeurIPS, and USENIX Security, with about 5% of 2025 NeurIPS and USENIX papers containing multiple likely fake references [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Phantom References: Hallucinated Citations That Survive Peer Review at Top-Tier Conferences
items.summary:
Researchers have identified the presence of hallucinated citations—references to non-existent or mismatched scholarly works—in peer-reviewed papers from major conferences such as ICLR, ICML, NeurIPS, and USENIX Security. Using a tool called RefChecker, which verifies bibliography entries against multiple sources, they found that about 5% of papers at NeurIPS and USENIX Security in 2025 contained at least two likely fake references. This issue has increased following the rise of AI language models like ChatGPT, with some papers even containing five or more such citations, including award-winning works.

The study highlights that while the overall rate of hallucinated citations is below 1% at the reference level, the scale of these conferences means that paper-level failures are significant. The researchers emphasize that peer review alone does not reliably prevent citation errors, but automated auditing using tools like RefChecker is feasible and cost-effective. They have made RefChecker open-source to support routine citation verification before publication, aiming to improve the integrity of scientific literature.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00738v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models can generate polished scientific text that includes unsupported claims, allowing hallucinations to enter the archival record. Assessing this risk via technical statements is difficult and often requires expert judgment, but citations provide a more auditable surface: a reference either resolves to a real scholarly work with compatible authorship, or it does not. We measure citation hallucination in peer-reviewed proceedings using a conservative definition limited to identity-level failures: non-existent works and substantial author-list mismatches. We explicitly exclude ordinary bibliographic drift (e.g., venue/year differences, publication-status updates, minor name variants). To audit citations at scale, we build RefChecker, a verification pipeline that resolves bibliography entries against multiple bibliographic sources and escalates unresolved cases to web-search re-verification. We apply RefChecker to accepted camera-ready papers from ICLR, ICML, NeurIPS, and USENIX Security. Hallucinated citations have entered the archival record. While reference-level rates are usually below 1%, proceedings are large enough that paper-level failures are visible: in 2025, roughly one in twenty NeurIPS and USENIX Security papers contains at least two likely hallucinated academic-paper-like references under our strict definition. We also observe post-ChatGPT increases in several venues, including a tail of papers with 5+ failures in a single bibliography, and likely hallucinated citations even among award-winning papers. These results suggest peer review alone does not reliably enforce citation integrity, yet auditing is tractable (about 0.04$ per paper in one venue-scale scan). We open-source RefChecker for routine, reproducible citation verification before publication (https://github.com/markrussinovich/refchecker).

items.originalTitle: Prototype Memory-Guided Training-Free Anomaly Classification and Localization in Prenatal Ultrasound
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a training-free framework for classifying and localizing multiple prenatal ultrasound anomalies using only a few reference images per category. This approach addresses challenges in prenatal screening, such as the rarity and variability of anomalies and the difficulty of obtaining large annotated datasets. The framework includes a memory bank with multi-granular prototypes, a prototype-driven feature merging mechanism for anomaly detection, and a class-aware refinement strategy to enhance category prediction.

The method was extensively tested on a multi-center dataset comprising 1,149 cases and 2,357 images across nine anomaly categories, demonstrating superior performance compared to existing techniques. This training-free approach offers a practical solution for resource-limited clinical settings by eliminating the need for fine-tuning on new categories, potentially improving prenatal anomaly diagnosis and management.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00744v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Prenatal anomaly classification and localization is of critical importance for fetal health and pregnancy management. Although ultrasound (US) is the primary modality for prenatal screening, accurate diagnosis remains challenging due to the low prevalence and high heterogeneity of anomalies. Existing deep learning methods for prenatal tasks rely on large-scale annotated datasets, which are difficult to obtain in practice. Although few-shot learning alleviates data scarcity, it typically requires fine-tuning for new categories, limiting its practicality in resource-limited clinical settings. To address these challenges, we propose a training-free framework for multi-class prenatal US anomaly classification and localization that operates with only a few reference images per class, representing the first exploration of this setting. Our framework comprises three key components: (1) a memory bank with multi-granular prototypes that explicitly models both class-level semantics and anomaly characteristics; (2) a prototype-driven soft merging mechanism that aggregates discriminative features to detect the anomaly region; and (3) a class-aware refinement strategy that leverages prototype consistency to improve category prediction. Extensively validated on a multi-center prenatal US dataset containing 1,149 cases, with a total of 2,357 images and 9 categories, our proposed method outperforms the competitors.

items.summary:

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00746v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The bird's-eye view (BEV) representation enables multi-sensor features to be fused within a unified space, serving as the primary approach for achieving comprehensive 3D perception. Its variant surpasses GaussFormer on 3D semantic occupancy with 1.55 mIoU improvement while using only 30% of the Gaussians and achieving a 450% speedup.

items.title: Researchers adapt Uncertainty Herding active learning to cascaded table extraction pipelines, proposing RankFusion and CAPA extensions that improve annotation efficiency across multiple datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Active Learning for Cascaded Object Detection: Balancing Coverage and Uncertainty in Table Extraction Pipelines
items.summary:
Researchers have adapted the Uncertainty Herding active learning method to improve annotation efficiency in cascaded table extraction pipelines, which involve Table Detection (TD) and Table Structure Recognition (TSR). They introduced two pipeline-aware extensions, RankFusion and CAPA, that leverage the dependency between TD and TSR to better balance coverage and uncertainty during sample selection. Experiments on multiple public and private datasets demonstrate that these methods outperform existing baselines, with CAPA showing the most consistent improvements across datasets.

The study addresses the high cost of building task-specific training sets for TSR, which requires detailed structural annotations. By incorporating dual-manifold coverage and stage-dependent uncertainty calibration, the proposed extensions effectively reduce annotation efforts while maintaining performance. RankFusion achieves higher expected gains but with more variance, whereas CAPA provides stable results, making it a promising strategy for active learning in complex cascaded detection tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00747v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Table extraction from business documents relies on a cascaded pipeline where Table Detection (TD) first localizes tables and Table Structure Recognition (TSR) then recovers their internal layout. Building task-specific training sets for this pipeline is costly, particularly for TSR which requires fine-grained structural annotations. Active learning (AL) can reduce this annotation burden, yet most AL strategies are designed for single-model tasks and do not account for inter-stage dependencies in cascaded architectures. In this work, we present the first adaptation of Uncertainty Herding (UHerding), a hybrid coverage-uncertainty sampling method originally proposed for image classification, to cascaded object detection pipelines. We propose two pipeline-aware extensions that exploit the TD-to-TSR dependency: RankFusion adds dual-manifold coverage over both detection and structure representation spaces, while CAPA further incorporates stage-dependent gating and per-task uncertainty calibration. Extensive experiments across two public (PubTables-1M and FinTabNet) and two private table extraction datasets, with various annotation budgets (from 71 to 500 documents) show that UHerding generalizes well to table extraction, outperforming each baseline. Among pipeline-aware variants, RankFusion achieves higher expected gains but at the cost of greater variance, while CAPA emerges as the most consistent strategy, outperforming standard UHerding on three out of four datasets.

items.title: Researchers introduce LeVLJEPA, the first fully non-contrastive end-to-end vision-language pretraining method that improves dense semantic features without negatives or momentum encoders [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: LeVLJEPA: End-to-End Vision-Language Pretraining Without Negatives
items.summary:
Researchers have developed LeVLJEPA, the first fully non-contrastive end-to-end vision-language pretraining method that enhances dense semantic features without relying on negatives, temperature scaling, momentum encoders, or teacher-student training schedules. This approach uses cross-modal prediction with stop-gradient targets and per-modality distributional regularization, enabling stable large-scale training.

LeVLJEPA's encoder demonstrates superior performance as a frozen backbone in vision-language models across multiple benchmarks, including GQA, VQAv2, and POPE, outperforming contrastive baselines in semantic segmentation tasks while maintaining comparable results in global feature evaluations like linear probing. These findings highlight non-contrastive pretraining as an effective strategy for generating dense semantic vision features in vision-language applications.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00784v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-language pretraining remains dominated by contrastive objectives, whereas vision-only self-supervised learning has largely adopted non-contrastive methods. At the same time, the role of vision-language encoders has shifted: they are increasingly deployed not as zero-shot classifiers but as the frozen visual backbone of vision-language models and dense prediction systems, which consume the full grid of patch tokens rather than a single pooled embedding. We introduce LeVLJEPA, the first fully non-contrastive end-to-end vision-language pretraining method. LeVLJEPA learns through cross-modal prediction with stop-gradient targets and per-modality distributional regularization, without negatives, temperature, momentum encoder, or teacher-student schedule, and trains stably at large scale. We find that the resulting encoder provides markedly stronger dense semantic features for downstream use: as a frozen vision-language-model backbone, LeVLJEPA is the strongest of the evaluated encoders across GQA, VQAv2, and POPE under two distinct language models, and outperforms contrastive baselines on semantic segmentation, while remaining on par on global readouts such as linear probing. These results establish non-contrastive pretraining as an effective means of producing dense semantic vision features.

items.title: Researchers present LRAT-Catcher, a tool importing SAT solver LRAT certificates into Lean 4 via reflection to verify combinatorial theorems including Schur and Ramsey numbers
items.originalTitle: LRAT-Catcher: Importing SAT Solver Certificates into Lean4 by Reflection
items.summary:
Researchers have developed LRAT-Catcher, a tool that imports SAT solver LRAT certificates into the Lean 4 theorem prover using reflection. This tool enables the verification of complex combinatorial problems, such as Schur and Ramsey numbers, by converting DIMACS formulas and LRAT certificates into Lean theorems. LRAT-Catcher leverages a formally verified LRAT checker compiled as native code, allowing it to handle larger instances than previous methods that relied on explicit proof-term imports.

LRAT-Catcher also supports composing cube-and-conquer solving runs entirely within Lean, combining per-cube refutations with a cover-completeness certificate into a single unsatisfiability theorem. Verified encodings link CNF-level results to the original combinatorial problems, enhancing the reliability of the proofs. The tool was evaluated by successfully establishing the Schur number S(4) = 44 and the Ramsey number R(4,4) = 18 as Lean theorems, demonstrating its effectiveness compared to existing proof-term imports and external checkers.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00815v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: SAT solvers settle combinatorial problems beyond the reach of interactive theorem provers and produce LRAT certificates for independent verification. We present LRAT-Catcher, a standalone, general-purpose tool that imports a DIMACS formula together with an LRAT certificate into Lean 4 as a theorem. LRAT-Catcher runs the formally verified LRAT checker from Lean core as compiled native code via reflection. This scales to instances where Mathlib's explicit proof-term import exhausts memory. LRAT-Catcher also composes cube-and-conquer solving runs entirely inside Lean. Per-cube refutations are combined with a cover-completeness certificate, itself an LRAT proof, into a single unsatisfiability theorem. Verified encodings connect CNF-level results to the original combinatorial problems. We evaluate the tool against Mathlib's proof-term import and the external checker cake_lpr on establishing the Schur number S(4) = 44 and the Ramsey number R(4,4) = 18 as Lean theorems.

items.title: Study finds 153 operationalization failures in 236 agent-generated analytical workflows across finance, HR, and public safety, highlighting a semantic gap in agentic data systems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Exploring the Semantic Gap in Agentic Data Systems: A Formative Study of Operationalization Failures in Analytical Workflows
items.summary:
A study analyzing 236 agent-generated analytical workflows across finance, human resources, and public safety found 153 operationalization failures despite successful workflow generation and execution. The research identified five main types of failures—comparative grounding, process reasoning, quantitative reasoning, role confusion, and policy grounding—highlighting a semantic gap between user-level analytical concepts and the information available in current workflow-generation systems. This gap suggests that existing data systems may lack the necessary semantic richness to fully translate analytical intent into executable operations.

The study emphasizes that while large language models have improved the generation and execution of analytical workflows, the semantic information needed to operationalize complex analytical concepts often extends beyond what is explicitly represented in database schemas and data values. These findings raise important questions about the limitations of current agentic data systems and point to the need for enhanced semantic representations to better bridge the divide between analytical intent and computational execution.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00828v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate queries, invoke tools, and construct analytical workflows. Although recent advances have substantially improved workflow generation and execution, the semantic information required to operationalize analytical concepts often lies beyond what is explicitly represented in database schemas and data values. We present a cross-domain formative study of operationalization failures in agent-generated analytical workflows. Across 236 analytical intents spanning finance, human resources, and public safety domains, we identify 153 recurring failures despite successful workflow generation and execution. Our analysis reveals five recurring classes of failures: comparative grounding, process reasoning, quantitative reasoning, role confusion, and policy grounding. These findings suggest a semantic gap between user-level analytical concepts and the information available to workflow-generation systems. More broadly, they raise questions about the admissibility of analytical operations and suggest that future agentic data systems may require richer semantic representations to bridge the gap between analytical intent and executable computation.

items.title: Researchers present Pano2World, an end-to-end method converting single indoor panoramas into persistent, explorable 3D Gaussian scenes with improved multi-view consistency and novel-view synthesis performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Pano2World: End-to-End 3D Generation via Unified Multi-View Sequences
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Pano2World, an end-to-end method that converts a single indoor panorama into a persistent, explorable 3D Gaussian scene, enabling free-viewpoint navigation beyond the limitations of traditional panoramic viewing. The approach reconstructs a coarse 3D proxy from the input panorama and uses a panoramic diffusion model with View-Aware Attention Routing to jointly denoise multiple target views, ensuring geometric alignment and semantic consistency across views. A novel Latent Feature Adapter module preserves multi-view hidden features during decoding, enhancing the quality of the final 3D scene.

Pano2World addresses challenges in existing methods that rely on iterative per-view completion or video generation models constrained by continuous trajectories, which can lead to error accumulation or limited scene coverage. Experimental results demonstrate that Pano2World significantly outperforms current techniques on benchmarks for multi-position panoramic novel-view synthesis, offering improved multi-view consistency and novel-view synthesis performance for indoor scene exploration.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00832v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A single panorama captures the full visual sphere from one camera center, yet confines users to looking around in place without enabling true scene exploration. Converting a single panorama into a persistent, renderable 3D representation for free-viewpoint navigation has attracted growing interest; existing methods either adopt iterative per-view completion that propagates inpainting results to update the underlying geometry, leading to progressive error accumulation and cumbersome multi-step pipelines, or leverage the temporal consistency priors of video generation models, yet the continuous-trajectory constraint intrinsic to such models limits their flexibility in covering scenes from multiple directions simultaneously. We present Pano2World, which takes a single indoor panorama as input and directly outputs a persistent, explorable 3D Gaussian scene. Given the source panorama, Pano2World first reconstructs a coarse 3D Gaussian proxy and renders it at adaptively sampled nearby poses to obtain geometrically aligned guidance panoramas; a panoramic diffusion model then jointly denoises all target views via View-Aware Attention Routing, where each target view simultaneously receives geometric constraints from its corresponding guidance panorama and global semantic guidance from the source panorama, naturally enforcing cross-view consistency. To avoid the information loss incurred by decoding the multi-view hidden features formed during joint denoising back to the pixel domain via VAE, we introduce Latent Feature Adapter, a geometry-aware bridge module that directly distills these hidden features into a scene latent, subsequently decoded into the final 3D Gaussian scene. Experiments demonstrate that Pano2World significantly outperforms existing methods on the multi-position panoramic novel-view synthesis benchmark.

items.summary:
The tutorial presented in arXiv:2607.00836 offers a comprehensive overview of world models and world action models in robotics, framing them as action-conditioned predictive models that forecast the future states or observations relevant to tasks. It categorizes existing approaches into observation-space and state-space models, highlighting their differences in visual fidelity, spatial structure, physical interpretability, and control applicability. Additionally, the tutorial introduces world action models that link predicted futures to executable robot actions, outlining four key paradigms for embodied prediction and control.

By clarifying the conceptual boundaries and providing a structured taxonomy, this work aims to unify understanding across communities involved in embodied intelligence and generative simulation. The tutorial's insights help in comparing methods and guiding the design of predictive models that support robotic decision-making and control.

items.title: Study analyzes gradient-based inversion of GPT-2 last-layer hidden states to recover input text, achieving up to 97.5% exact-match on 10-token prompts with continuous embedding optimization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Recovering Input Text from Hidden States: Study of Gradient-Based Inversion of Decoder-Only Language Models
items.summary:
A recent study investigates the problem of recovering original input token sequences from the last-layer hidden states of decoder-only language models like GPT-2. The researchers approach this inversion as a continuous embedding-space optimization, avoiding hard-token projections during the search and committing tokens only at the end of the process. This method reveals detailed internal signals and allows for precise assessment of recovery accuracy, achieving up to a 97.5% exact-match rate on 10-token prompts by expanding the candidate window.

The study identifies that reconstruction failures predominantly occur with space-prefixed, high-frequency function words located in dense embedding regions, while content-bearing tokens are nearly perfectly recovered. Compared to previous methods using per-step hard projection, this continuous optimization approach is slower but provides greater observability and detectability of failures. The findings demonstrate that GPT-2's last-layer hidden states retain sensitivity comparable to the original input text, offering insights into the model's internal representations and potential for input reconstruction.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00852v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work studies the hidden-state inversion problem: recovering the original input token sequence of a decoder-only language model from its last-layer hidden states. Rather than treating inversion as a one-shot reconstruction, we study it as a continuous embedding-space optimisation in which a soft proxy is driven towards the leaked target without any hard-token projection during the search, and a token is committed only once, at the end of the inner loop. This design choice has two consequences which are the main focus of this paper. First, keeping the optimisation entirely in continuous space exposes a rich set of internal signals: rank trajectories of the ground-truth token, per-position loss curves, and a discrete loss measured at commit time. Second, the discrete loss allows assessing the correctness of recovery via cumulative discrete loss. We further analyse which tokens break the reconstructions and find a sharp categorical asymmetry: space-prefixed, high-frequency function words in dense regions of the embedding matrix dominate the failures, while content-bearing tokens are recovered almost perfectly. On 10-token C4 prompts the exact-match rate rises from 66.9% to 97.5% (mean similarity 0.994) as the candidate window is widened, confirming that most errors are recoverable near-misses rather than genuine ambiguities. A comparison with the released SIPIT reference situates these findings: per-step hard projection is faster, but the continuous formulation is what makes the optimisation observable and its failures detectable. The results show that last-layer hidden states of GPT-2 are as sensitive as the original text.

items.title: Researchers propose MTL-BA, a meta-transfer learning framework for mmWave beam alignment in MISO systems that reduces adaptation cost and meta-training budget while maintaining performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Meta-Transfer Learning for mmWave Beam Alignment
items.summary:
Researchers have developed MTL-BA, a meta-transfer learning framework designed to improve millimeter-wave (mmWave) beam alignment in multiple-input single-output (MISO) wireless systems. This approach freezes a pre-trained convolutional backbone and adapts only lightweight Scale-and-Shift adapters and a classifier head, significantly reducing adaptation costs and meta-training requirements while maintaining high prediction performance.

MTL-BA addresses limitations of existing meta-learning and transfer learning methods by combining the benefits of both: it avoids the high parameter update and training costs of full network adaptation and leverages episodic meta-learning to optimize adaptation. Simulation results using the DeepMIMO dataset demonstrate that MTL-BA achieves comparable accuracy and spectral efficiency to full fine-tuning, updates about 17 times fewer parameters, outperforms last-layer fine-tuning, and requires 60% fewer meta-training epochs than Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML).

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00860v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Millimeter-wave (mmWave) beam alignment plays a critical role in next-generation wireless systems, yet its efficient implementation remains challenging. Meta-learning and transfer learning have been explored to enable deep learning-based beam prediction models to rapidly adapt to unseen environments; however, existing meta-learning approaches adapt the entire network and are trained from random initialization, leading to a large number of updated parameters and a high meta-training cost, while transfer learning approaches restrict adaptation to part of the network but do not exploit episodic meta-learning, which explicitly trains the model over multiple tasks, to optimize the adaptation process itself. To overcome these limitations, we propose MTL-BA, a meta-transfer learning framework for beam alignment in millimeter-wave multiple-input single-output (MISO) systems that freezes a pre-trained convolutional backbone and meta-learns only lightweight Scale-and-Shift (SS) adapters together with a classifier head. Warm-starting from the pre-trained model and restricting adaptation to the SS adapters and classifier head reduce both the adaptation cost and the meta-training budget without sacrificing prediction performance. Simulation results on the DeepMIMO ray-tracing dataset show that MTL-BA matches the accuracy and spectral efficiency of full fine-tuning across various SNR levels despite updating approximately $17\times$ fewer parameters than both full fine-tuning and Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML), outperforms last-layer fine-tuning while updating a comparable number of parameters, and approaches MAML's performance while requiring $60\%$ fewer meta-training epochs.

items.title: Researchers propose Confidence-Adaptive Thinking (CAT) to improve Large Reasoning Models' efficiency by modulating reasoning length based on confidence, outperforming baselines on multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: CAT: Confidence-Adaptive Thinking for Efficient Reasoning of Large Reasoning Models
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Confidence-Adaptive Thinking (CAT), a new framework designed to enhance the efficiency of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) by adjusting the length of reasoning processes based on the model's confidence. This approach addresses the issue of overthinking on simple queries, which leads to unnecessary token use and slower inference, by modulating reasoning length according to problem difficulty. CAT leverages the model's intrinsic self-certainty signals to optimize reasoning preferences, enabling it to shorten reasoning for confident responses while allowing more deliberation for uncertain ones.

Experimental evaluations demonstrate that CAT consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in reasoning accuracy across multiple benchmarks and different base models. This advancement offers a promising solution for balancing accuracy and latency in practical applications, potentially improving the efficiency of LRMs in industrial scenarios without compromising performance on complex tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00862v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) have achieved remarkable success on complex tasks by leveraging long chain-of-thought (CoT) trajectories, yet they frequently exhibit overthinking on simple queries, resulting in significant token overhead and reduced inference efficiency. However, existing compression methods predominantly apply uniform length reduction or rely on coarse-grained difficulty estimation, often leading to performance degradation on difficult problems. To address this limitation, we propose Confidence-Adaptive Thinking (CAT), a framework that incorporates the model's intrinsic self-certainty signals as confidence into the preference optimization process, which autonomously modulates reasoning lengths based on problem difficulty. Experimental results show that CAT consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on reasoning accuracy across multiple benchmarks on different base models. Our work enables LRMs to effectively compress confident responses while deliberating on uncertain ones, offering a potentially robust solution for balancing accuracy and latency in practical industrial scenarios.

items.title: Researchers propose flat minima optimization with controlled Gaussian perturbations and periodic reinitialization to improve sparse-view 3D Gaussian Splatting generalization in neural rendering [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Improving Sparse-View 3DGS Generalization via Flat Minima Optimization
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a method to improve the generalization of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) in neural rendering when training data is limited to sparse views. By applying flat minima optimization principles, which favor solutions stable under small parameter changes, they introduce controlled Gaussian perturbations and periodic reinitialization of certain parameters. This approach enhances the robustness of 3DGS against overfitting and preserves fine details without altering the existing architecture.

The proposed technique adapts flat minima concepts to the unique geometric and dynamic characteristics of 3DGS, using a lightweight training framework. Experiments on LLFF and Mip-NeRF360 datasets show that this method yields sharper, more stable reconstructions with better generalization to novel viewpoints under sparse-view supervision, improving both quantitative metrics and perceptual quality.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00885v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent advances in neural rendering have established 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) as a highly efficient representation for novel view synthesis, enabling fast training and real-time rendering with strong fidelity. However, when supervision is limited to sparse input views, 3DGS tends to overfit to the observed images and generalize poorly to unseen viewpoints. We address this challenge from the perspective of flat minima (FM) optimization, which seeks solutions that remain stable under small parameter perturbations. Viewing Gaussian parameters as trainable weights, we adapt FM principles to the geometric and dynamic nature of 3DGS with a lightweight training framework. Our method regularizes optimization with controlled Gaussian perturbations that account for each Gaussian's anisotropy and the training progress, preserving fine details while improving robustness to sparse-view overfitting. To further stabilize this flat minima optimization process, we introduce periodic reinitialization, which temporarily returns non-positional parameters to their initial states for a short window. Together, these techniques integrate seamlessly into existing 3DGS pipelines without architectural changes. Experiments on LLFF and Mip-NeRF360 datasets demonstrate improved quantitative metrics and perceptual quality under sparse-view supervision, producing reconstructions that are sharper, more stable, and better generalized to novel viewpoints.

items.title: DeWorldSG framework generates spatio-temporally robust 3D semantic scene graphs using depth-guided filtering and world-model priors, improving triplet recall by 77.4% on 3DSSG and ReplicaSSG datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: DeWorldSG: Depth-Aware 3D Semantic Scene Graph Generation via World-Model Priors
items.summary:
DeWorldSG is a new framework designed to generate spatio-temporally robust 3D Semantic Scene Graphs from RGB-D sequences, addressing challenges in existing methods such as unstable 3D object representations and missing relational data due to frame-wise inference. items.title: Researchers introduce MAGNET, a multi-agent framework for long-form narrative generation that reduces hallucinations and improves coherence using persona-grounded character agents and world-state tracking [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: From Personas to Plot: Character-Grounded Multi-Agent Story Generation for Long-Form Narratives
items.summary:
Researchers have developed MAGNET, a multi-agent framework designed to improve long-form narrative generation by reducing hallucinations and enhancing coherence. MAGNET uses persona-grounded character agents that interact based on a shared world state and evolving story goals, while a complementary system called ATLAS detects inconsistencies by comparing scene-level world representations. Evaluations show that MAGNET significantly decreases narrative errors and hallucinations compared to traditional single-model approaches and other methods like IBSEN, demonstrating its effectiveness in producing coherent and consistent long-form stories.

The framework's success is attributed to its explicit tracking of the story's world state and goal-driven multi-agent generation, which together support controllable and structurally coherent storytelling. This approach offers a promising foundation for future advancements in automated long-form narrative creation, addressing key challenges faced by large language models in maintaining plot consistency over extended texts.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00918v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive creative fiction generation, they struggle to maintain narrative consistency and coherent plot lines in long-form stories. In this work, we introduce a unified framework for long-form narrative generation and verification. MAGNET, a multi-agent goal-driven narrative engine for storytelling, generates stories with persona-grounded character agents that propose actions based on a shared world state and evolving story goals, while ATLAS is a graph-based pipeline that compares scene-level world representations across a generated story to detect hallucinations. By evaluating MAGNET using an LLM editor, pairwise rubric scoring, and ATLAS, we show that our framework produces coherent narratives compared to single-model prompting and IBSEN. At 100 pages, MAGNET reduced annotations and hallucinations by 41 and 50%, respectively, compared to the single model baseline and by 34 and 45%, respectively, compared to IBSEN, with pairwise rubric evaluation showing similar results. These results suggest that long-form narratives can emerge from explicit world-state tracking and goal-driven multi-agent generation, providing a foundation for controllable and structurally coherent long-form narrative generation.

items.title: Researchers propose DiT-Pruning method for post-training pruning of Diffusion Transformers, preserving image quality at 50% sparsity with minimal CLIP score loss [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Post-Training Pruning for Diffusion Transformers
items.summary:
Researchers have developed DiT-Pruning, a novel post-training pruning method tailored for Diffusion Transformers (DiTs), which are known for high computational demands in image generation. This approach introduces customized saliency criteria and pruning granularity that account for DiTs' unique architecture and parameter distribution, enabling effective pruning without significant loss in image quality. Evaluations demonstrate that DiT-Pruning maintains performance even at 50% sparsity, with minimal impact on CLIP scores, outperforming existing pruning techniques.

The method balances the contributions of weights and activations using an energy-based metric and incorporates clustering-aware pruning granularity based on observed patterns in the weight space. This allows for more precise identification and removal of less important elements, addressing limitations of prior pruning methods designed for large language models. Extensive testing on various DiT models confirmed consistent preservation of image quality, particularly under high sparsity conditions.

DiT-Pruning's ability to reduce computational overhead while maintaining output quality has significant implications for deploying diffusion-based image generation models more efficiently. By enabling effective sparsity without degrading performance, this technique could facilitate broader adoption of DiTs in resource-constrained environments and advance research in model compression for generative AI.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00927v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have demonstrated impressive performance in image generation but suffer from substantial computational overhead and resource consumption. Post-training pruning offers a promising solution; however, due to DiTs' unique architectural design and parameter distribution, traditional pruning methods are inapplicable, leading to significant performance degradation. Specifically, prior methods developed for LLMs, which derive metrics through a series of approximations, amplify the relative contribution of weights in the saliency metric. In addition, weights in DiTs exhibit significantly larger magnitudes than those in LLMs. Moreover, existing pruning granularity overlooks variations in model structures. In this paper, we propose DiT-Pruning, which improves pruning performance by introducing customized saliency criteria and pruning granularity. We design a novel metric that balances the contributions of weights and activations from an energy-based perspective, enabling more effective identification of important elements. Furthermore, we observe distinct clustering patterns in the two-dimensional weight space. Accordingly, we adopt a clustering-aware pruning granularity, enabling effective sparse allocation. Extensive evaluations on various DiTs show that our method consistently preserves image quality, especially under high sparsity. For FLUX.1-dev at 512x512 resolution on MJHQ, DiT-Pruning achieves only a 0.001 loss in CLIP score at 50% sparsity, dramatically outperforming recent pruning methods.

items.title: Researchers compare four strategies for learning cardiac motion priors in implicit neural representations using UK Biobank MRI data, finding meta-learning achieves best adaptation over 50 iterations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Learning Cardiac Motion Priors for Implicit Neural Representations
items.summary:
Researchers evaluated four methods for learning cardiac motion priors in implicit neural representations (INRs) using short-axis tagged cardiac MRI data from the UK Biobank. The study compared a population prior learned by joint optimization, a consensus prior via weight averaging, auto-decoders, and meta-learning to improve the fitting of INRs, which are typically time-consuming and sensitive to optimization paths. All learned priors enhanced early adaptation performance compared to random initialization, with meta-learning showing the best overall adaptation trajectory over 50 iterations.

The analysis revealed that while the consensus prior was effective, auto-decoders enabled faster recovery of large deformations during early adaptation. Meta-learning combined strong early performance with sustained improvement, suggesting it as a promising approach for guiding optimization towards plausible cardiac motion fields in INRs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00955v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Implicit neural representations (INRs) are well suited to cardiac motion estimation, providing continuous, compact representations of motion fields. However, fitting an INR to each image sequence is time-consuming and sensitive to the optimisation trajectory. Learned priors can help guide optimisation towards plausible motion fields and enable faster adaptation, but learning priors for cardiac motion INRs remains under-explored. In this work, we compare four strategies for learning cardiac motion priors, including a population prior learned by joint optimisation, a consensus prior obtained by weight averaging, auto-decoders, and meta-learning. Using short-axis tagged cardiac magnetic resonance images from the UK Biobank, we evaluate their impact on tracking accuracy, motion behaviour, and adaptation trajectory. All learned priors substantially improved early adaptation performance compared with random initialisation. While the simple consensus prior was effective, auto-decoders recovered large deformations faster during early adaptation. Meta-learning achieved strong early performance and maintained the best adaptation trajectory over 50 iterations.
